entries.title: How to use this reference
entries.description: Six parts, numbered clauses, every entry dated and attributed. How the reference is organised, what the numbering means, and where to start depending on why you are here.
sources: ISO/IEC Directives Part 2, rules for the structure of standards

blocks.html:
This is a reference work, not a course. Entries are numbered like clauses in a
standard so you can cite them, link into them, and find your way back.

Six parts, each opening at x.0 with what that part of the function actually produces, then working outward. Every entry cites its sources, because a claim about a framework is worth exactly as much as the thing it cites.

The number before an entry is its clause. 3.2 is the second entry in Part 3; 3.2.1 is the first section inside it. Every section heading is deep-linkable twice, by its slug and by its clause number, so #c3-2-1 and #the-difference-stated-plainly reach the same place.

Clause numbers are stable. If an entry is retired the number is not reused, and if the corpus is renumbered the old anchors redirect.

items.term: You are new to the field
items.html: Read 1.1, then 1.3, then 3.1. That is roughly ninety minutes and gets you to the point where a risk register makes sense.
1.4 for the boundary question, 3.2 for the vocabulary people get wrong, and Part 6 for the rest.
Search, or use the A-Z index. The index uses inverted headwords, so “appetite, risk” and “risk appetite” both land.
Part 2 for the decisions, Part 4 for the obligations, Part 5 for the framework you have been asked for.

blocks.html:
It is not a substitute for the standard. Where an entry describes ISO 27001 or the Trust Services Criteria, it describes them accurately and cites the clause, but the certifiable text is the standard’s and you will need a copy.

It is also not a template library. A few entries link to worked examples; most describe how the artefact behaves and how it fails, which is the part that does not come in a template.
Claims are checked against the standard they cite. Where an entry is wrong, it is corrected against that source.

entries.title: What governance, risk and compliance is
entries.description: Governance, risk and compliance is the coordinated set of practices used to direct objectives, understand what could stop them, and prove obligations are met. Definition, the three pillars, and how the frameworks fit.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information security management systems, requirements
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, February 2024
IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100), 2017, revised 2022

blocks.html: Governance, risk and compliance is the coordinated set of practices an organisation uses to direct what it is trying to achieve, understand what could stop it, and prove it meets the obligations that apply to it.

The three are administered by different people and fail together. Governance sets the appetite that risk measures against; compliance supplies most of the evidence that governance reviews. Run them as three teams with three spreadsheets and the first audit finds the contradictions for you.

The label is younger than the work. Boards have directed, risk functions have measured and compliance officers have evidenced for as long as there have been regulated companies. What changed around 2002 was that the same board committee started receiving all three reports in the same meeting, and noticed they did not agree.

items.html: Who decides, on what authority, and where the decision is recorded: the policy set, the committee calendar, the delegated authority matrix, board reporting.
Identifying what could obstruct the objectives, sizing it, deciding what to do, then watching it: the register, the appetite statement, the treatment plan, the issue log.
Knowing which obligations bind you (law, contract, standard), mapping each to a control, and keeping the proof that the control ran.

blocks.html: Each pillar owns artefacts, not opinions. A governance function that cannot produce the minutes recording a decision has not governed it. A risk function whose register has no owners and no dates is a list. A compliance function holding a policy but no evidence the policy was followed has documented an intention.

blocks.name: grc-loop
blocks.caption: FIG. 1 - The GRC loop. Break any edge and the function becomes paperwork: appetite nobody set, controls nobody asked for, evidence nobody reads.

blocks.html:
Read the loop clockwise and it describes a quarter of work. Governance publishes an appetite statement: say, no accepted risk above a residual score of 12 without board sign-off. Risk applies that threshold to the register and produces a treatment plan for everything above it. Compliance runs the controls those treatments name and keeps the evidence. Assurance reports the whole picture back, and governance revises the appetite it set.

Read it anticlockwise and it describes how the function fails. Evidence accumulates with no control mapped to it. Controls run with no risk behind them. Risks are scored against an appetite that was never written down.

The amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its
objectives, stated by governance and used by risk to decide what must be
treated.

columns.html: Most of a GRC analyst’s week is spent moving a risk or a control through a small number of states, and keeping the record of that movement legible to someone who was not there. The interview, the register update, the evidence request, the follow-up when the evidence does not arrive.

columns.caption: FIG. 2 - Risk matrix (5 × 5), the most-used artefact on the job.
columns.note: Outlined cell: a possible / moderate risk, the band where appetite, not arithmetic, decides the answer.

columns.name: register-row
columns.caption: FIG. 3 - A risk register row. The fields that make a score defensible, and the same record is keyed into any GRC tool.

blocks.html: The matrix is the argument, not the answer. Two people scoring the same incident will land in adjacent cells and both be defensible; what makes the score usable is that the scale is written down, applied the same way twice, and challenged in a forum with minutes. A 5 × 5 grid with no documented criteria behind each band produces numbers that cannot survive a question.

Framework Type Answers the question Output
ISO/IEC 27001 Certification Is the ISMS working? Certificate
NIST CSF 2.0 Framework How mature are we? Profile
SOC 2 Attestation What can we show a customer? Auditor report
COSO ERM Model How does risk reach the board? Risk view

They are not alternatives, and picking between them is usually the wrong question. ISO 27001 and SOC 2 answer different buyers: a certificate travels, an attestation report is read. NIST CSF 2.0 is a language for describing where you are, not a bar to clear. Its 2024 revision added a sixth function, Govern, precisely because organisations were maturing controls without anyone owning the decisions behind them. COSO ERM sits above all of it and is about how risk reaches a board at all.

Most organisations of any size end up mapping between at least two of them. That mapping, the crosswalk, is the single most reused artefact in the discipline, because one control almost always satisfies several obligations at once.

items.q: Is GRC a technical job?
items.html:
No, but it is a literate one. You need to read a system diagram and challenge an engineer’s answer; you do not need to configure the system. The daily tools are documents, interviews and evidence.

The failure mode is not being insufficiently technical. It is accepting an answer you did not understand because asking again felt awkward.

items.q: Is GRC the same as cyber security?
items.html:
No. Cyber security is one obligation domain among several. GRC also covers financial reporting, privacy, health and safety, supplier conduct, and whatever else the organisation is bound by.

The overlap is large in technology companies, which is why the two are often staffed from the same team, and why “GRC” is frequently used as shorthand for “security compliance”. That shorthand is what makes the boundary confusing. Security engineering builds and operates the control; GRC decides the control is required, tests that it ran, and keeps the proof.

items.q: Which certification should I start with?
items.html:
If you want the vocabulary, ISO/IEC 27001 Lead Implementer or the ISACA CRISC syllabus will both give you it. If you want an employer to recognise the letters, CISA is the most widely asked-for in audit-adjacent roles and does not require a technical background.

Certification is not the gate people entering the field assume it is. A candidate who can walk an interviewer through a risk they assessed end to end (how it was raised, scored, treated, and closed) outperforms one with three certificates and no artefact to describe.

items.q: Can I move into GRC from IT support?
items.html:
It is one of the more common routes in. Service desk work already teaches the two things the role is built on: reading a system you did not build, and writing down what happened in a way someone else can act on.

The gap to close is the evidence habit: knowing what makes a screenshot admissible, why a date matters, and what an auditor will ask for next. That is learnable in months, and considerably faster than teaching a compliance specialist how a directory service works.

entries.title: Terms and definitions
entries.description: The words the rest of the reference assumes. Risk, control, obligation, evidence, assurance and the rest, defined once, in the sense the standards use them.
sources: ISO Guide 73:2009 - Risk management, vocabulary
ISO/IEC 27000:2018 - Information security management systems, overview and vocabulary
IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Glossary

sections.text: Why the precision earns its keep

blocks.html:
Most arguments inside a GRC function are vocabulary arguments wearing a
disguise. These are the words the rest of the reference uses, in the sense the
standards use them.

Where a term has a precise definition in a standard, that definition is given and cited. Where practice has drifted from the standard (and it has, in several places), the drift is named rather than smoothed over.

items.html: The effect of uncertainty on objectives. Note the direction: a risk is defined against something you are trying to achieve, which is why a register with no objectives behind it drifts into a list of things people dislike.
A risk that has occurred. The distinction is operational: risks are managed on a review cycle, issues are managed to a closure date.
The thing that could cause the event, not the risk itself. “Ransomware” is a threat; “ransomware encrypts the order database and we cannot ship for four days” is a risk.
A measure that modifies risk. Includes process, policy and practice, not only technology. A control that is not operating is not a control.
A requirement that binds the organisation, from law, regulation, contract or a standard it has committed to. The source is part of the obligation; one with no citation cannot be tested.
A dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient for a reviewer who was not present.
A conclusion about whether something works, given by someone with the standing to give it. First party from management, second party from a customer, third party from an independent auditor.
The amount of risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives.
The acceptable variation around a specific objective. Distinct from appetite, and confused with it constantly.
The level before controls are taken into account. Useful mainly for showing what the controls are earning.
The level after existing controls. This is the number appetite is applied to.
What is being done about a risk: accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid.
One named person with the authority to decide. Not a team, not a function, not a role that is currently vacant.
What sits inside the boundary of a certification, an assessment or a register, and by implication what sits outside it and is therefore unexamined.

blocks.html:
Compliant. Nothing is compliant in the abstract. Something is compliant with a named obligation, at a point in time, on the evidence available. A vendor that says its product is “GDPR compliant” has said nothing testable.

Framework. Used for four different things: a certifiable standard (ISO 27001), a descriptive model (NIST CSF 2.0), an attestation criteria set (SOC 2) and an internal control model (COSO ERM). The difference determines what you can do with the output, which is why it is worth keeping straight.

Maturity. A statement about how consistently a process runs, not about how good it is. A consistently bad process scores well on maturity, which is why a maturity score alone never answers “are we safe”.

The one named person accountable for a risk staying inside appetite, with the
authority to approve its treatment. Distinct from the control owner, who
operates the measure.

blocks.text: Why the precision earns its keep

blocks.html:
An auditor’s first move on a register is to read three risk statements and check they are risks rather than threats or issues. It takes ninety seconds and tells them how much of the rest to trust. The same is true of a control inventory full of aspirations, or an obligation register with no citations.

Getting the words right is not pedantry. It is the cheapest available signal that the function knows what it is doing.

entries.title: The four artefacts every GRC function keeps
entries.description: Every functioning GRC programme keeps the same four records: a policy set, a risk register, a control inventory and an evidence store. What each one is for, and how to tell when one has stopped working.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, clause 6.1.3 and Annex A
ISO 31000:2018 - Risk management, guidelines
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100)

blocks.html:
Strip a GRC programme of its tooling, its committee names and its reporting
templates, and four records remain. Everything else in the function exists to
create, maintain or read one of them.

The four are a policy set, a risk register, a control inventory and an evidence store. A programme missing one is not necessarily failing, but it will be unable to answer a specific class of question, and the question always arrives.

The written answer to what are we required to do, and who said so. A policy states the rule; a standard states the measurable version of the rule; a procedure states the steps. Three levels, and the confusion between them is the most common documentation problem in a young programme.

The test of a policy set is not whether it exists. It is whether an employee who breaks a rule can be shown the sentence they broke, and whether the person who approved that sentence can be named.

The list of things that could obstruct the objectives, with a score, an owner and a decision attached to each. See 3.1 for how to read one.

A register goes stale in a predictable way: entries stop changing. If nothing in a register has moved a band in two quarters, either the environment is extraordinarily stable or nobody is reviewing it. In practice it is the second.

The list of things you actually do to keep those risks inside appetite, each one mapped to the obligations it satisfies. This is the artefact that makes multiple frameworks affordable: one access review can satisfy an ISO 27001 Annex A control, a SOC 2 criterion and an internal policy at the same time, but only if something records that it does.

An inventory with no mapping column is a to-do list. The mapping is the artefact.

The proof that the controls ran. Screenshots, exports, tickets, signed attestations, meeting minutes, all with dates and with a name attached to whoever produced them.

The quality bar is not “we have a folder”. It is that a stranger can pick a control, pull the evidence for a specific month, and tell from the evidence alone that the control operated. If the evidence needs a colleague to explain it, an auditor will treat it as absent.

A dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient for a
reviewer who was not present to conclude the control ran as described.

The four are not independent. A control inventory with no risk register behind it produces controls nobody can justify the cost of. A risk register with no policy set behind it produces scores nobody can challenge, because there is no stated threshold to challenge them against. An evidence store with no inventory is a warehouse.

The order to build them in, when starting from nothing, is register first, then policy, then inventory, then evidence. Starting with policy is the intuitive choice and the slow one: you end up writing rules for risks you have not yet established you carry.

entries.title: GRC vs internal audit vs security engineering
entries.description: GRC designs and operates controls, internal audit independently tests whether they work, and security engineering builds the systems both are talking about. Who owns what, and why the boundary matters.
sources: IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020
IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Standard 1100 (Independence and Objectivity)

blocks.html:
GRC designs and runs the controls. Internal audit independently tests whether
they work. Security engineering builds the systems both are describing. The
three overlap in vocabulary and almost never in accountability.

The confusion is worth resolving early, because from outside the roles look identical. All three read system documentation, all three ask engineers questions, all three write findings. The difference is entirely about who they answer to.

sides.name: GRC
sides.html:
Designs the control, writes the policy, keeps the register, gathers the
evidence, answers the customer questionnaire. Accountable to management.

sides.name: Internal audit
sides.html:
Samples the same controls without having designed them, forms an opinion,
reports to the audit committee. Independence is the whole job.

blocks.html:
Internal audit’s constraint is the important one. An auditor who helps rewrite the control they will later test has compromised the opinion they exist to give. That is why an internal auditor will point at a gap and decline to close it, which is not obstruction but the only position from which the finding is worth anything.

GRC has the opposite mandate. Finding a gap and leaving it open is the failure.

Three-quarters of the confusion is caused by one thing: in organisations under roughly 500 people, the same person often does both. The company has a “compliance manager” who writes the policy, runs the access review, and then signs the attestation saying the access review happened.

That is a self-review, and every framework names it. It is workable while the organisation is small and honest about it; it stops being workable the moment an external party is relying on the attestation.

The impairment created when the party assessing a control is the party that
designed or operated it. Managed by separating the roles, not by declaring
independence.

Security engineering builds and operates the control. GRC establishes that the control is required, defines what “working” means, tests that it ran, and keeps the proof.

In practice the boundary is drawn at the console. If the work involves changing a configuration, it is engineering. If it involves deciding the configuration must be a certain way, or demonstrating to a third party that it was, it is GRC.

The productive relationship between the two is narrower than either expects: GRC should be able to state precisely what evidence it needs and why an obligation demands it, and should not be specifying how the system produces it.

Ask who receives the output. Management receives GRC’s. The audit committee receives internal audit’s. If the answer is “the same person who asked for the work”, it is not audit, whatever the job title says.

entries.title: The three lines model
entries.description: The IIA's 2020 Three Lines Model replaced the older three lines of defence. What each line owns, why "defence" was dropped, and where GRC sits.
sources: IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020
IIA, Position Paper: The Three Lines of Defence in Effective Risk Management and Control, 2013

blocks.html:
The three lines model describes how accountability for risk is distributed:
the people doing the work own it, a second group provides expertise and
challenge, and a third gives an independent opinion to the governing body.

The Institute of Internal Auditors published the current version in 2020, replacing a 2013 paper that used the phrase three lines of defence. The rewrite was not cosmetic. “Defence” implied risk was something arriving from outside to be repelled, and implied the lines were sequential barriers. Both readings produced organisations where the first line assumed the second would catch its mistakes.

items.html: The people who deliver the product or service. They own the risks their activity creates and operate the controls inside it. Not a junior line: most control operation happens here.
Specialist functions providing expertise, frameworks, challenge and monitoring. Risk, compliance, and most GRC roles sit here. It supports the first line and reports to management.
Internal audit. Independent assurance to the governing body on the effectiveness of everything the first two lines do. It reports to the audit committee, not to management.

blocks.html: The governing body sits above all three, and management sits between the body and the first two lines. External assurance providers (a certification body, a SOC 2 auditor, a regulator) sit outside the model entirely.

Three things worth knowing if you were taught the older version.

Collaboration replaced separation. The 2013 framing encouraged lines to operate independently of each other. The 2020 model states explicitly that the lines should collaborate, with independence required only for the third.

The lines are roles, not teams. A person can hold first-line and second-line responsibilities in different parts of their job. The model constrains the combination (you cannot independently assure your own work) but does not require three org charts.

Risk is upside as well as downside. The current model frames the lines around achieving objectives, not only avoiding harm.

Second line, in almost every case. GRC provides the frameworks the first line operates within, monitors whether they are being followed, and escalates when they are not.

The common exception: in a small organisation, GRC frequently ends up operating first-line controls too, running the access review rather than checking it ran. That is a resourcing reality rather than a model violation, but it needs to be visible, because it removes the challenge the second line exists to provide.

entries.title: Who does GRC work
entries.description: In a small company one person does all of it. At scale the work splits into risk, compliance, privacy and vendor management. What each seat owns, and who they answer to.
sources: IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020
ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025

sections.text: The seats, roughly in the order they appear
The trap in a small company

blocks.html:
In a company of thirty, one person does all of it alongside another job. In a
company of three thousand, the same work is four teams with different reporting
lines. The seats change; the artefacts do not.
The useful way to read an organisation chart here is to ask which of the four artefacts each seat is accountable for, and who receives their output. Titles vary far more than that does.

blocks.text: The seats, roughly in the order they appear

items.html: The first dedicated hire. Runs the register, chases evidence, answers questionnaires, keeps the policy set current. The job is 70% writing things down so somebody else can act on them.
Owns the obligation register and the audit relationship. Appears when there is a second framework, or a first regulator.
Owns the register, the appetite statement and the reporting into committee. Appears when the register outgrows the analyst who started it.
Owns a distinct obligation set with its own regulator and its own artefacts. In the EU the DPO role has statutory independence requirements that make it a poor fit for a general compliance seat.
Owns supplier due diligence and the ongoing monitoring. Usually the first specialisation, because the volume is relentless.
Owns the programme, the budget and the board narrative. Answers for the function’s opinion, not its paperwork.

blocks.html:
Most commonly the CISO, in technology companies where the obligations are security-led. Increasingly the General Counsel where the obligation set is regulatory rather than technical, and occasionally the CFO where it grew out of financial controls.

The reporting line matters less than one thing: whoever it is must not also own the systems being assessed. A GRC function reporting to the engineering leader whose controls it tests is second line in name only.

blocks.text: The trap in a small company

blocks.html:
One person writing the policy, running the access review, and signing the attestation that the access review happened is performing a self-review. Under about a hundred staff this is unavoidable and everybody knows it.

The way to handle it is not to pretend otherwise. Record it in the register as an accepted risk with a named approver, and get a second pair of eyes (a peer, a board member, an external reviewer) on the attestations that leave the building. An auditor who finds the acceptance already written respects it. One who finds it themselves writes a finding.

entries.title: Risk, issue and incident: the difference
entries.description: A risk is a possible future effect of uncertainty, an issue is one that has materialised and an incident is a discrete event that has already occurred.
keywords: difference between a risk and an issue
what is an issue in risk management
is an issue a realised risk
sources: ISO 31000:2018 - Risk management, guidelines (risk defined as the effect of uncertainty on objectives, clause 3.1)
ISO/IEC 27000:2018 - Information security management systems, overview and vocabulary (information security event and information security incident)
ISO/IEC 27035-1:2023 - Information security incident management, principles and process
"Issue" has no single ISO definition; the term is used in common operational and project-management practice for a present problem already affecting delivery

sections.text: Where each is logged, and who owns it
Why mixing them corrupts the register

blocks.html:
A risk is a possible future effect of uncertainty. It has not happened yet. An
issue is a risk that has materialised, or a present problem demanding action
now. An incident is a discrete event that has already occurred, often a control
failure or a security event.

The distinction is one of tense. Risk is future and uncertain, issue is present and certain, incident has already occurred, though its consequences may still be unfolding. Where each is logged, who owns it and what happens next all follow from where the thing sits on that timeline.

Practitioners collapse the three constantly, and the collapse is not cosmetic. An incident filed as a risk overstates open exposure: it counts a thing that already happened as a thing that might. A live issue left in the register as a “risk” hides that action is already overdue. Either way the register stops describing the world.

items.html: A possible future effect of uncertainty on objectives, something that has not happened and may not. ISO 31000:2018 defines it as the “effect of uncertainty on objectives”, where an effect is a deviation from the expected, in either direction.

A risk that has materialised, or a present problem that needs action now. It has no single ISO definition; in common operational and project-management usage it names a condition already affecting delivery that must be managed, as distinct from a risk that only might.

A discrete event that has already occurred, typically a control failure or, in security, an unwanted event that harms operations. ISO/IEC 27000 separates an information security event (something happened that may matter) from an incident, an event or series with significant potential to compromise operations.

blocks.html:
Concept Tense Where it is logged Who acts Worked example
Risk Future, uncertain Risk register Risk owner A key supplier could fail and take checkout down
Issue Present, certain Issue log Action owner The supplier has raised prices past budget and a decision is needed this quarter
Incident Past, occurred Incident log or ticketing Incident responder The supplier’s outage took checkout down for 90 minutes on 14 August

The example column runs one thread through all three deliberately. The same supplier is a risk while the failure is hypothetical, an issue the moment a present problem needs deciding, and an incident once an event has actually landed. Nothing about the supplier changed; the tense did.

blocks.text: Where each is logged, and who owns it

blocks.html:
These arrangements are common practice rather than anything a standard mandates. A risk lives in the risk register and, in most schemes, belongs to a named risk owner, one person who can authorise its treatment rather than a team (see 3.1). An issue lives in an issue log, sometimes a tab on the same spreadsheet and sometimes a separate action tracker, and belongs to whoever owns closing it. An incident lives in an incident log or the ticketing system and belongs to the responder handling it until it is contained and reviewed.

They are kept as separate records for the same reason the three concepts are separate (see 1.3): a single document that mixes future exposure with present problems and past events cannot be sorted, counted or reported without first pulling the three back apart.

A risk becomes an issue at the moment it materialises. The uncertain future effect is now a present fact, and it moves from the register (where it was being watched) to the issue log, where it gets an action owner and a due date. The risk line does not simply vanish; it is marked as realised and cross-referenced, so the history survives the question an auditor asks after the fact. Nor does the risk always close: recurrence or knock-on uncertainty can keep a line open on the register even after this instance has landed.

An incident runs the other way. A single event can open several new risks (what else is exposed the same way) and several issues that must be fixed now, and closing it well usually means adding or strengthening a control. That control changes the residual score of the risk the incident sat under, which is the point at which the incident log, the issue log and the register are meant to reconcile. When they do not, one of the three is lying.

blocks.text: Why mixing them corrupts the register

blocks.html:
A register that quietly fills with issues and incidents is no longer a risk register; it is a to-do list with scores on it. Two specific corruptions follow, and both are common.

An incident logged as a risk overstates open exposure. Risk reporting counts what is open and above appetite, so a past event sitting in that total is read as a live threat and the risk picture looks worse than reality, or the incident’s one-off severity inflates a score that then never comes back down.

A live issue left in the register as a “risk” does the opposite and hides that action is already required. A risk carries a treatment decision and a review date; an issue carries an owner and a deadline. Dressed as a risk, an overdue problem reads as something merely being monitored, and the deadline that should be escalating does not exist.

The tell, when reviewing someone else’s register, is a row whose statement is in the past tense. “Supplier X failed and checkout was down” is not a risk. It already happened. It belongs in the incident log, with whatever new risk it exposed rewritten as its own forward-looking line.

items.q: Is an issue just a realised risk?
items.html:
Often, but not only. Many issues began as a risk on the register that then materialised: the supplier you flagged did raise its prices. But an issue can also be a present problem nobody had logged as a risk: a defect found in production, a control that turns out never to have run. The test is not where it came from but its tense: an issue is a problem that exists now and needs a decision now, whatever its history.

Treating every issue as a “realised risk” also tempts you to reopen the risk line and re-score it, when what the issue actually needs is an action owner and a date, not a fresh likelihood.

items.q: What is the difference between an issue and an incident?
items.html:
An incident is a discrete event that occurred at a point in time (an outage, a breach, a control failure), and in security ISO/IEC 27000 draws a further line between an event (something happened that might matter) and an incident (an event, or series, likely to harm operations). An issue is broader and need not be a single event: a supplier that keeps missing SLAs, a project running over budget or an unresolved control gap are all issues without being incidents.

Put plainly, an incident is something that happened; an issue is something that is wrong. An incident is closed once it is contained and reviewed; an issue is closed once the underlying problem is resolved.

items.q: Does every incident create a risk?
items.html:
No, but a serious one usually should. The value of an incident to the risk function is what it reveals: an incident that exploited a control gap is evidence the residual risk was understated, and the post-incident review is where that score gets corrected and a new treatment added. An incident fully contained by controls working as designed confirms the existing risk rather than opening a new one.

The failure mode is the incident that closes with a “lessons learned” slide and never touches the register, so the same event recurs against a risk line that still reads green.

entries.title: GRC vs cyber security
entries.description: Cyber security builds and operates the defences; GRC governs, measures and evidences them. Where the two meet, and why GRC is not a technical security role.
keywords: does GRC sit under the CISO
sources: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, February 2024 (the Govern function)
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information security management systems, requirements

blocks.html: GRC and cyber security are different disciplines that meet at the control. Cyber security builds and operates the defences; GRC governs, measures and evidences them. GRC is not a technical security role.

The two get merged because in a technology company they are often the same budget and sometimes the same team. A security engineer configures the firewall; the GRC analyst three desks away writes the standard that says the firewall must exist, checks that it does and hands the proof to an auditor. Same subject, different sentence: one operates, the other governs and records.

The distinction holds even where the org chart hides it, because the two roles fail in different ways. Security fails when the defences do not stop or contain the attack. GRC fails when the control worked and nobody can prove it did.

sides.name: GRC
sides.html:
Decides which controls the organisation is obliged to run, defines what
“working” means, checks that they run and keeps the evidence a customer or
auditor will ask for.

sides.name: Cyber security
sides.html:
Designs, builds and operates the defences (firewalls, identity, monitoring and
incident response), and answers to whether an attack is stopped, not to whether
the paperwork exists.

rows.a: Can we prove the control is required, owned and operating?
rows.b: Does the defence actually stop the attack?

rows.a: Varies: CISO, risk, legal or COO
The control worked but nobody can prove it
rows.b: The defence does not stop or contain the attack

blocks.html: The “relationship to the control” row is where the two most often get miscast. Security operates the control; GRC establishes that it is required, that a named person owns it and that it ran, while the control itself is usually owned by the business or system owner, not by either function. Neither role covers the other, which is why one function cannot simply absorb the work of the other.

Both live at the control, and that is the whole source of the confusion. A single access-review control is designed and run by security, and separately recorded by GRC as required, owned by a named person and operated on a schedule. That last part is the evidence. Neither produces the audit outcome alone: a control that runs but is undocumented fails the audit, and a documented control that does not run fails the attack.

NIST CSF 2.0 made the split easier to see. Its February 2024 revision added a sixth function, GOVERN, alongside the five operational functions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) precisely because organisations were maturing defences with nobody owning the decisions, roles and oversight behind them. GOVERN is not a seventh silo, though: it sits across the framework and informs how the other five are run. It elevates the governance and risk-oversight outcomes a security-GRC role tends to concentrate on, while the operational functions are where the defences are built and run, a single framework holding both kinds of work.

Two mistakes recur. The first is imagining a GRC analyst configures firewalls. The daily tools of GRC are documents, interviews and evidence requests; the analyst reads a system diagram and challenges an engineer’s answer but does not touch the console. Hiring a GRC analyst to harden systems, or a security engineer to run an ISO 27001 audit programme, produces someone doing half of each job badly.

The second is assuming a strong security team makes GRC redundant: that if the defences are genuinely good, the governance layer is overhead. It does not follow. An auditor does not accept “our security team is excellent” as evidence, and a customer’s procurement questionnaire does not accept it either. ISO/IEC 27001 certification assesses whether the ISMS is implemented and effective, which turns on documented information and objective evidence that the controls operate, not on the operator’s confidence that they do. Excellent security with no evidence trail struggles to demonstrate an effective ISMS, and cannot be sold to a buyer who requires certification.

There is no single answer, and the honest one is that the reporting line varies by organisation. GRC reports to the CISO in many technology companies, where the work is mostly security compliance and that is where it already sits. It reports to a Chief Risk Officer where risk is a board-level function in its own right, common in financial services. It reports to legal or the General Counsel where the binding obligations are contractual and regulatory more than technical, and to the COO where GRC is treated as operational assurance spanning more than security.

What drives the choice is the breadth of the mandate. A function scoped to information security alone tends to sit under the CISO. One that also covers privacy, financial reporting, health and safety or supplier conduct cannot sit cleanly under security, because it would then be governing controls its own boss operates, the self-review problem under another name.

items.q: Is GRC cyber security?
items.html: No, though in a technology company the two overlap enough to be staffed from one team. Cyber security is one obligation domain GRC covers, alongside privacy, financial reporting and whatever else binds the organisation. Security builds and operates the defence; GRC decides the defence is required, checks it runs and keeps the proof. Where a company does only security compliance, “GRC” and “security” can look like the same job. The boundary gets clearer the broader the mandate is.

items.q: Is GRC a technical role?
items.html: Not in the sense of configuring systems, though it is a literate one. You need to read a network diagram, follow an engineer’s explanation and challenge it; you do not need to build or run the system. The daily work is documents, interviews and evidence. It varies with seniority and company (a GRC engineer automating evidence collection sits closer to the console than a compliance analyst chasing a quarterly access review), but the core skill is judgement about obligations and proof, not hands on the firewall.

items.q: Does GRC sit under the CISO?
items.html: Sometimes, not always. It reports to the CISO where its scope is information security; to a Chief Risk Officer, legal or the COO where the mandate is broader than security. A GRC function that governs controls the CISO’s own team operates has an independence problem if it also reports to that CISO, which is one reason larger organisations move it out from under security as it grows.

entries.title: Risk vs compliance
entries.description: Risk and compliance use the same controls to answer different questions: is our exposure within appetite, and can we prove we meet our obligations.
keywords: is compliance part of risk management
sources: ISO 31000:2018 - Risk management, guidelines
ISO 37301:2021 - Compliance management systems, requirements with guidance for use
COSO, Internal Control - Integrated Framework, 2013

blocks.html: Risk and compliance use the same controls to answer different questions. Risk asks what could hurt the organisation and whether the exposure sits within appetite. Compliance asks what the organisation is required to do and whether it can prove it did.

Most of the time the two answers agree, which is why the same overlapping team runs both off one register. A single quarterly access review treats the risk of excessive access and evidences the obligation to review it: one control, logged twice. The distinction only becomes load-bearing when the two answers disagree: when a control passes its compliance test and the risk behind it is still outside appetite, or when a risk the business is willing to carry runs straight into an obligation it is not allowed to carry.

sides.name: Risk
sides.html:
Begins with what could go wrong, sizes it against the objectives and asks
whether the residual sits inside appetite. The register is never finished; the
exposure keeps moving.

sides.name: Compliance
sides.html:
Begins from the obligations that bind it (law, contract, standard), maps each to
a control and keeps the proof it operated. Each obligation is either evidenced
or open.

rows.a: "What could hurt us, and is it within appetite?"
rows.b: "What are we required to do, and can we prove it?"

rows.a: Never; re-scored as the exposure moves
rows.b: Per obligation, when its evidence is current; the system itself never stops

rows.a: Exposure sits above appetite and nobody owns the treatment
rows.b: A control has no evidence, or an obligation no control

blocks.html: ISO 31000 defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives and has the organisation evaluate it against risk criteria, which typically encode the appetite governance has set. ISO 37301 builds the other side into an ongoing management system (one of monitoring, evaluation and improvement) whose unit of work is the compliance obligation: a requirement you must meet or a commitment you have chosen to. COSO supplies the join: a control is the response to a risk to an objective, and the same control is often what a compliance regime points to as proof. The controls are shared. The questions asked of them are not.

In most teams the two live in one register, and a control carries two keys: the risk it treats and the obligation it evidences. The access review above is the ordinary case: raised as a treatment for an access risk, cited as evidence against an access-control obligation, closed once with a single artefact.

Running them as two registers is the common mistake in a young programme. It produces two control inventories that drift apart, two owners for the same review and a control that is marked effective on the compliance side while the risk it was meant to reduce sits open on the other. One register with two keys, however it is physically stored, is the arrangement that tends to survive an audit.

The value is in the two cases where a clean answer on one side is worthless on the other.

A fully compliant control can still leave risk above appetite. Compliance is a floor, not a ceiling. Multi-factor authentication is required by policy and the evidence shows it running: the obligation is met and the test passes. If it is not enforced on a legacy login path, the account-takeover exposure is still outside appetite. The compliance answer is green; the risk answer is red; both are correct. Meeting the obligation says only that the obligation’s bar was cleared, never that the bar was set where your exposure actually is.

An accepted risk can still breach an obligation you cannot accept your way out of. Acceptance (retaining a risk by informed decision, in ISO 31000’s terms) is a legitimate treatment: the business may formally decide to carry a risk. That decision has no force against a binding obligation. A retention rule fixed in law is breached whether or not the risk committee signed off carrying it. You can accept a risk; you cannot accept a statute. When acceptance is the treatment, the compliance question has to be asked separately, because it is the one the acceptance cannot answer.

The two answers go to different rooms, in different shapes.

Risk reports exposure against appetite to a risk committee: where the residual sits, which items have moved and what is above appetite still waiting on a treatment. The unit is a risk, and the question in the room is whether the organisation is carrying more than it agreed to.

Compliance reports obligations met against obligations open to a compliance or audit committee: which obligations have current evidence, which have gaps and which are in breach. The unit is an obligation, and the question in the room is whether anything the organisation is bound by is unproven or unmet.

An item can be comfortable in one report and alarming in the other. That is not a reporting error. It is the two functions doing their separate jobs on the same control.

Ask which question is on the table. If it is “are we carrying more than we agreed to”, it is risk, and the answer is measured against appetite. If it is “can we prove we meet what binds us”, it is compliance, and the answer is measured against the obligation. The controls are the same; treat the two answers as independent, because the day they disagree is the day both matter.

items.q: Is compliance part of risk management?
items.html:
It depends who you ask, and both answers are defensible. To a risk function working in COSO or ISO 31000 terms, non-compliance is one category of risk, so compliance sits inside enterprise risk as a subset. To a compliance function under ISO 37301, compliance is its own management system with obligations that exist whether or not anyone has scored them as risky: a peer, not a subset.

In practice it is both. The obligation exists on its own footing; the exposure created by failing it is managed as a risk. Teams that insist on one framing usually do it to settle who owns the register, which is a reporting-line question dressed up as a definitional one.

items.q: Can you be compliant but not secure?
items.html:
Routinely. Compliance is a floor: it confirms the obligation’s bar was cleared, not that the bar matches your exposure. A control can pass every compliance test and still leave a risk above appetite, because the obligation demanded less than your situation needs: an old standard, a narrow contract clause, a control that runs but not everywhere it has to.

The reverse happens too. A well-secured system can hold an obligation open because the evidence was never captured in the form an assessor accepts. Secure and compliant are correlated, not the same measurement.

items.q: Which comes first, risk or compliance?
items.html:
It turns on the trigger. If a regulator, contract or standard already binds you, compliance comes first: the obligation exists regardless of how your risk assessment comes out, and you cannot risk-assess your way out of it. If you are deciding where to spend a fixed control budget, risk comes first, because it tells you which threats to objectives are worth the money.

In a mature programme the ordering dissolves: obligations and risks feed one register, and each control is justified by both the exposure it reduces and the obligation it satisfies.

ISO 37301:2021 - Compliance management systems, requirements with guidance for use

entries.title: What auditing is
entries.description: Auditing is independent examination of evidence against a stated criterion to form an opinion someone else can rely on. Internal vs external, and the cycle.
sources: IIA, International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing, 2017
IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020
ISO 19011:2018 - Guidelines for auditing management systems
IAASB, ISA 200 - Overall objectives of the independent auditor

blocks.html:
An audit is an independent examination of evidence against a stated criterion (a
standard, a policy, a regulation, a set of accounts) carried out to form an
opinion that someone who was not there can rely on.

Three words carry the definition. Independent: the person forming the opinion did not design or operate the thing being examined. Criterion: there is a written bar, fixed before the work starts, so the opinion is a comparison and not a preference. Opinion: the output is a judgement about conformity, not a repair: an auditor who fixes the finding has stopped being one.

An audit is not a review, an assessment or a health check. Those words are used loosely, but an audit specifically produces assurance: a signed statement, at a defined level of confidence, that a reader outside the process can act on. That is why the independence rule is not negotiable. The moment the examiner has a stake in the answer, the assurance is worth nothing.
The two are often confused because both sample controls and write findings. What separates them is who they answer to and what they are for.

rows.a: The organisation, within an approved charter
rows.b: Statute, listing rules or a standard

rows.a: Any part of the organisation, risk-ranked
rows.b: Fixed: the accounts, or the certified management system

rows.a: Findings and recommendations, tracked to closure
rows.b: A formal opinion, published or lodged

blocks.html: Internal audit is the third line in the three lines model: it gives the board assurance that the first line’s controls and the second line’s oversight are actually working. External audit sits outside the model entirely. It serves people outside the organisation who need an independent read before they rely on its statements.

A stated level of confidence, given by someone independent, that a thing is as
described. Reasonable assurance is a high bar expressed as an opinion; limited
assurance is a lower bar expressed as the absence of anything found.
Every audit, internal or external, financial or ISO, runs the same five stages. The names vary by scheme; the sequence does not.

items.html: Fix the scope, the criterion and the sample. Decide what evidence would be sufficient before asking for any. A scope agreed loosely is renegotiated under pressure later.
Gather evidence: documents, system extracts, walk-throughs, re-performance. Test a sample against the criterion and record what was seen, where it came from and when.
Compare findings to the criterion. Rate each gap by consequence, not by how easy it was to spot. Distinguish an isolated slip from a control that never operated.
State the opinion, then the findings behind it. Each finding names the criterion missed, the evidence, the effect and a recommended owner. The auditee responds with a dated remediation plan.
Re-test that the agreed actions closed the gap. A finding is open until evidence shows the fix works, not when someone says it is done.

blocks.html: The stage that fails most often is follow-up. Findings are agreed, a management action plan is filed, and nobody re-tests. The next audit re-raises the same issue, and the audit function’s credibility erodes because its findings turned out to be optional.

An auditor tests three things about a control, in order, and stops at the first that fails.

  1. Design. Would this control, as described, prevent or detect the thing it is meant to? A control that cannot work even on paper fails here.
  2. Implementation. Does the control exist in reality: is it turned on, is someone assigned, did it run at all?
  3. Operating effectiveness. Did it run every time it should have, across the whole period, on evidence? This is what a SOC 2 Type II or an ISO surveillance audit is really checking, and it needs a population, not one screenshot.

A finding at the design level is more serious than one at the operating level, because a redesign is a bigger commitment than tightening execution.

items.q: What is the difference between an audit and an assessment?
items.html: An audit forms an opinion against a fixed criterion and is carried out by someone independent of the work. An assessment is usually broader, more advisory, and can be run by the team that owns the process. An audit produces assurance a third party can rely on; an assessment produces input the owner can choose to act on. The words are used interchangeably in marketing, which is why contracts specify which one is meant.

items.q: What are the main types of audit?
items.html: By subject: financial (the accounts), compliance (against a law or regulation), operational (efficiency and effectiveness of a process), information systems (controls over technology), and certification (against a standard such as ISO/IEC 27001). By provider: internal, external and second-party, where a customer audits a supplier directly.

items.q: Do auditors fix the problems they find?
items.html: No. An auditor who designs or implements the remediation has audited their own work and cannot then give an opinion on it: the self-review threat. Auditors recommend; the auditee owns the fix. Internal auditors may advise on a solution within limits, but someone else must implement it and a later audit must test it.

items.q: What makes audit evidence sufficient?
items.html: Enough of it, relevant to the criterion, and reliable at its source. A system- generated log is stronger than a manager’s assertion; a sample large enough to represent the population is stronger than one convenient example; evidence dated inside the audit period is stronger than evidence produced the week of the audit. Sufficiency is a judgement the auditor has to be able to defend.

entries.title: What governance produces
entries.description: Governance is not a meeting. It is four artefacts (a policy set, a committee calendar, a delegated authority matrix and a board pack) and the decisions recorded in them.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, Govern (GV) function, 2024

sections.text: What a decision record looks like
Where it goes wrong at small scale

blocks.html:
Governance answers one question in four artefacts: who decided this, on what
authority, and where is it written down.
The test of a governance function is not whether it meets. It is whether, six months later, somebody can find the decision, the person who made it, and the authority they held when they made it.

items.html: The written rules and the standards beneath them. See 2.1 for the three levels and why collapsing them is the standard failure.
Which forums exist, what each one decides, who sits on it, and when it meets. A committee with no terms of reference is a meeting.
Who may approve what, up to what value or severity, without going higher. The artefact that turns “escalate if significant” into something a person can act on at 4pm on a Friday.
What the governing body is told, in what form, on what cycle. See 2.3.

blocks.html:
The distinction is the one COSO and the NIST CSF’s Govern function both turn on. Management runs the organisation. Governance sets the direction management runs in, and holds it to account for the result.

Practically: management decides how to close a gap; governance decides whether the gap is acceptable in the first place, and hears about it either way. When the same forum does both, the challenge disappears: the group approving the plan is the group that wrote it.

blocks.text: What a decision record looks like

blocks.html:
The minimum that survives a year: the question put, the options considered, the decision, the person or forum that made it, the date, and the authority relied on. Six lines.

Most governance failures found in audit are not bad decisions. They are good decisions with no record of who made them, discovered at the moment somebody needs to know whether they were entitled to.

The specific power a role holds to decide without escalating, stated with its
limit. An authority with no limit is not delegated; it is assumed.

blocks.text: Where it goes wrong at small scale

blocks.html:
A twenty-person company does not need four committees. It needs the four artefacts to exist in some form, and one of them is usually a shared document rather than a governance platform.

The failure at this size is not absent governance; it is undocumented governance. The founders genuinely do decide things, consistently, on defensible grounds, and none of it is written down, so the first customer security review finds a company that cannot show it governs anything.

entries.title: Policy, standard, procedure: the document hierarchy
entries.description: A policy states the rule, a standard states the measurable version, a procedure states the steps. Getting the three levels wrong is the most common documentation failure in a young GRC programme.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, clause 5.2 (Policy) and clause 7.5 (Documented information)
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, GV.PO (Policy)

blocks.html: Three levels, and each answers a different question. The policy says what is required. The standard says how much is enough. The procedure says how to do it.

Collapsing them is the standard failure. An organisation writes one forty-page “Information Security Policy” containing password lengths and step-by-step joiner instructions, then discovers it must go back to the board every time a tool changes.

Level Answers Changes Approved by
Policy What is required, and why Rarely, annually at most Board or delegated committee
Standard How much is enough, measurably When the threat or tooling moves Function head
Procedure How the work is done, step by step Whenever the tool changes Process owner

The approval column is the reason the split exists. Different levels change at different speeds and warrant different levels of scrutiny; binding them into one document forces the slowest approval path onto the fastest-moving content.

Policy: access to systems holding customer data is granted on the principle of least privilege and reviewed at defined intervals.

Standard: privileged access is reviewed quarterly; standard access semi-annually; reviews are completed within 15 working days of issue.

Procedure: export the entitlement report from the identity provider, filter to the in-scope groups, distribute to the named owners, track responses in the review tracker, revoke on instruction, attach the completed tracker to the control record.

Note what moves where. Replace the identity provider and only the procedure changes. Tighten the cadence to monthly and only the standard changes. The policy is untouched by either.

The principle that an identity holds only the access required for its current
duties, for only as long as those duties last.

A policy that names a product is a standard. A standard with no number in it is a policy. A procedure that requires judgement to follow is a standard pretending.

One more, useful when reviewing someone else’s document set: pick any rule and ask who approved it and when. If nobody can answer for a rule the organisation is enforcing against employees, the hierarchy has failed regardless of how many levels it has on paper.

entries.title: Committees and delegated authority
entries.description: A committee with no terms of reference is a meeting, and an authority with no limit is not delegated. How to write both so a decision at 4pm on a Friday does not need an escalation.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017
IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020

sections.text: Terms of reference, in six lines
The escalation trigger that actually works
How many forums a company actually needs

blocks.html:
A committee exists to make a class of decision that no individual should make
alone. If you cannot name that class, you have scheduled a meeting.
Two artefacts do this work: terms of reference, which say what a forum decides, and a delegated authority matrix, which says what everybody else may decide without it.

blocks.text: Terms of reference, in six lines

blocks.html:
Purpose: the class of decision this forum owns. Membership: by role, with a quorum. Cadence. Inputs: what must be tabled, by whom, how far in advance. Outputs: minutes, decisions, actions with owners and dates. Escalation: what this forum sends upward, and on what trigger.

Anything longer is usually a description of the organisation rather than a mandate. Anything shorter cannot settle an argument about whether a decision was in scope.
One row per decision type, one column per level, and a limit in every cell.

The badly written version is the common one, and it fails in a specific way: it cannot be applied by the person holding it. “Escalate if significant” means the holder must guess at the threshold, and every guess is defensible afterwards, which means nothing is.

blocks.text: The escalation trigger that actually works

blocks.html:
Tie it to the appetite statement. If governance has published no accepted risk above a residual score of 12 without board sign-off, the matrix inherits that number and the trigger is arithmetic rather than judgement.

Where appetite is qualitative, the trigger has to be categorical instead: any risk touching customer funds, any obligation with a regulatory penalty attached. Either works. What does not work is a trigger that requires the person pulling it to already know the answer.

The minimum attendance for a forum’s decisions to stand. Worth setting low
enough that the committee can actually meet, and specific enough that three
people from the same team cannot constitute it.

blocks.text: How many forums a company actually needs

blocks.html:
One, until it does not. A single risk and compliance forum, meeting quarterly, with the CEO or COO in the chair, covers most organisations under two hundred people and produces a real minute trail.

Split it when the agenda stops fitting, usually when privacy or a regulator arrives with its own reporting obligations. Splitting earlier produces forums that meet without a decision to make, which is how a governance calendar starts being ignored.

entries.title: Board reporting
entries.description: A board pack answers three questions in one page: what changed, what is outside appetite, and what we need from you. Everything else is an appendix.
sources: COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, GV.OV (Oversight), 2024

blocks.html:
A board has perhaps twelve minutes for your item. The pack that works answers
three questions in that time: what changed, what sits outside appetite, and
what you need the board to decide.
Everything else (the register extract, the control coverage, the audit timetable) belongs in an annex nobody is expected to read in the room, and everybody can read afterwards.

What changed. Since the last meeting, in the language of the business. Two new risks above appetite because the payments integration went live; one closed because the supplier was replaced. Not a delta count.

What is outside appetite. The specific entries, their owners, the treatment and the date. This is the only part of the pack that requires a decision, and it should be visually obvious which items they are.

What you need. A decision, a budget, or an acknowledgement. Say which. A pack that asks for nothing trains the board to skim it.

A four-colour grid with dots on it is the most requested and least useful board artefact in the discipline. It shows position without showing movement, compresses away the ownership, and invites an argument about whether something is amber or red rather than about what to do.

If the board wants one, give them one, and put the movement beside it. An arrow per entry showing where it was last quarter turns the same picture into a narrative, which is what a board is actually assembling.

The papers issued in advance of a governing-body meeting. Issued late, it is a
document read in the room; issued a week ahead, it is a document the board has
questions about.

Three questions come up in almost every session, and the pack is stronger if it pre-empts them.

Is this getting better or worse? Answered by trend, not by level.

What would you do with more money? Answered by the treatments currently deferred, with what deferring them costs.

What are we not seeing? Answered honestly by naming the parts of the estate outside scope, which is uncomfortable and builds more credit than anything else in the pack.

Quarterly, with an out-of-cycle path for anything material. Monthly reporting to a board produces packs nobody reads and a function that spends its time reporting rather than working; annual reporting produces surprises.

The out-of-cycle path matters more than the cadence. A board that learns about a significant incident from the quarterly pack six weeks later will not trust the quarterly pack again.

entries.title: Governance vs management
entries.description: Governance sets direction, appetite and accountability; management runs the organisation within it. Where the deciding-versus-doing line blurs and fails.
sources: ISO 37000:2021 - Governance of organizations, guidance
COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017
IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020

blocks.html: Governance and management divide along deciding versus doing: governance sets the direction, the risk appetite and the lines of accountability; management runs the organisation within them. They are distinct functions (usually held by the board and the executive respectively), not two words for one, so that the people who set the target are not the sole judges of whether it was hit.

The separation is the whole point, and it is the first thing to erode. A board that starts approving individual purchases has stopped governing; an executive that starts deciding how much risk is acceptable has started governing without a mandate. Both are ordinary, and both are named at the foot of this entry.

When something goes wrong, the first useful question is which of the two failed, because the remedies do not overlap. A governance failure is answered by changing a strategy, an appetite or a person on the board; a management failure is answered by changing how the work is run. Blur the two and the right fix lands on the wrong body.

sides.name: Governance
sides.html:
Sets the direction, fixes the risk appetite, appoints the executive and holds it
to account. Owns the destination and runs nothing itself.

sides.name: Management
sides.html:
Runs the organisation day to day within the direction and appetite the board set,
and reports back on whether it is working. Owns the journey and sets nothing
above itself.

rows.a: The board, largely non-executive, acting collectively
rows.b: The executive: the CEO and the management team

rows.a: The long term: strategy, appetite, succession
rows.b: The operating cycle: this quarter, this year

rows.a: Direction, risk appetite, who holds authority
rows.b: How to execute within that direction
Delivery and daily operation, to the board

rows.a: Approved strategy, appetite statement, terms of reference
rows.b: Operating results, running controls, reports up

rows.a: Periodic: the board and committee calendar
It drifts into running the operation
rows.b: It sets the appetite it is judged against

blocks.html: The Accountable for row does the real work. Both bodies answer to someone, but not to the same someone and not for the same thing. Management answers to the board for delivery; the board answers to shareholders, members or the public for whether the organisation was directed and overseen well. ISO 37000 puts this at the centre of governance and draws the line most people miss: responsibility can be delegated to management, but accountability is retained by the governing body. The board can hand over the running of the place; it cannot hand over answering for it.

Two bodies exist rather than one because of separation of duties, applied at the top of the house. It is the same principle that stops the person who raises an invoice from being the person who approves it: whoever sets a target should not also be the only judge of whether it was met. Fold direction-setting and delivery into one pair of hands and the appetite quietly bends to fit the results.

The three lines model draws the same line lower down (the governing body above, management owning the first and second lines, independent assurance in the third), and the whole arrangement rests on the governing body being distinct from the management it oversees. What joins the two bodies without merging them is delegated authority. The board does not run the organisation, so it grants the executive the power to, within limits it writes down and can withdraw, recorded in the committee and delegation structure beneath it.

The board’s grant of decision-making power to the executive, within limits it
sets and can revoke. The hinge between the two bodies: governance decides what
the organisation is for, then delegates the authority to run it, and keeps the
accountability.

The clean two-body picture assumes a board of non-executives and a separate executive team, which describes a listed company and not much else.

In an owner-managed business the founder chairs the board on Monday and runs the operation for the rest of the week, and the two roles share one diary. The distinction has not vanished; it has become a discipline the individual has to keep in their own head: knowing, at any given decision, whether they are setting the appetite or spending it. Small firms fail here not by collapsing the roles but by never noticing they hold both.

The executive director is the deliberate blur. Most boards seat at least one (the CEO, often the finance director) as a full member of the governing body who is also part of the management it oversees. They govern in the boardroom and manage outside it, which is why a functioning board structures itself so the executive members cannot dominate the governance decisions: non-executive majorities, committees chaired by non-executives, sessions the executives leave.

The distinction still matters where one person holds both roles, because accountability does not merge just because the diary did. When the owner-manager’s company is sued or audited, whether this was a governance failure or a management failure still has to be answered, by the same person, in the right role, if the answer is to be worth anything.

Two failures sit either side of the line, and each is the other’s mirror.

The first is a board that drifts into managing. It fills its meetings approving individual hires, signing off line items and reading operational dashboards, rubber-stamping the detail the executive was appointed to own. The detail feels like diligence, but it crowds out the work only the board can do: setting direction, testing the strategy and holding the executive to account. A board deep in operational minutiae is usually a board that has quietly stopped overseeing, because no time is left for it.

The second is an executive that makes governance-level calls without saying so. The clearest case is an executive that sets its own risk appetite, deciding how much risk is acceptable, then reporting performance against a bar it set for itself. COSO puts risk appetite under board oversight for exactly this reason: the executive may propose it, but the board reviews and concurs, so that the body measured against the appetite is not the body that fixes it. Left to itself, an executive can widen the appetite whenever the results demand, and no one above it is the wiser. It is self-review raised to the level of strategy: the body being held to account has taken over defining what account looks like.

items.q: Is governance the same as management?
items.html: No. Governance decides what the organisation is for, how much risk it will run and who holds authority; management operates inside those decisions and reports back. Same organisation, two jobs: one sets the frame, the other works within it. The words are used loosely in everyday speech, which is where the confusion starts, but every governance standard treats them as distinct functions.

items.q: Who actually does governance?
items.html: The governing body: in a company, the board and its committees, acting collectively rather than through the chair alone. In a charity it is the trustees, in a public body the accountable board. In a very small organisation it may be one or two people who put the governance hat on at set moments (approving the annual plan, signing the accounts) and take it off to run the place the rest of the time. Governance is a role a body performs, not a department on the chart.

items.q: Can a manager do governance work?
items.html: Yes, but only when acting in a governance capacity, not by virtue of being senior. A manager who sits on a governance committee, or the executive director on the board, is doing governance in that seat, bound by its terms of reference and its record. The moment they leave the seat they are managing again. What decides whether a piece of work is governance is the authority it is done under, not the seniority of the person doing it.
