entries.title: Responding to an audit request
entries.description: The auditor picks the sample, you produce the evidence, and everything after that is about how you handle what they find. Fieldwork, sampling, findings and the response that closes them.
sources: IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Standard 2310
AICPA, SSAE No. 18, AT-C section 205
ISO/IEC 17021-1:2015 - Requirements for audit and certification bodies

prev.title: Evidence that holds up in audit

sections.text: What to do when the evidence is not there
Handling a finding you disagree with
The habit that makes audits boring

blocks.html:
An audit is a sampling exercise. The auditor selects which instances of a
control they want to see, you produce them, and the quality of the programme
shows in how few surprises that produces.
The single most useful thing to understand going in: you do not choose the sample. A programme that has collected its best evidence rather than all of it discovers this in week one of fieldwork.

Planning. Scope, period, control list, timetable. This is the moment to correct a misunderstanding about scope, and the last cheap moment to do it.

Fieldwork. Requests arrive, usually in batches, usually with a turnaround of a few days each. Someone must own the queue. Two to four weeks for a first external audit.

Findings. Draft findings come with a right of reply. Read the wording closely: the difference between “the control was not operating” and “evidence of operation was not retained” is large and often negotiable on fact.

Response and closure. Management response, remediation plan, dates. Then either closure or carry-forward to the next cycle.

blocks.text: What to do when the evidence is not there

blocks.html:
Say so, immediately, in writing.

The instinct is to reconstruct: regenerate the report today and present it as though it were produced in March. Auditors are extremely good at spotting this, it converts a control finding into an integrity finding, and integrity findings follow a programme for years.

The right move is to state that the instance is missing, say why, say what has changed so the next period is complete, and let it be a finding. A programme that self-reports a gap is treated very differently from one caught concealing the same gap.

blocks.text: Handling a finding you disagree with

blocks.html:
Two kinds of disagreement, handled differently.

Factual. The auditor has the control wrong, or has tested the wrong system. Answer with evidence, not argument, and expect it to be resolved.

Judgement. You both agree what happened and disagree about severity. This is what the management response is for. Say what you accept, say what you dispute and why, and record it. You will not usually win, and the record still matters: it is the thing you point at next year when the same finding is raised against a control you deliberately chose not to change.

Testing a subset of a control’s instances to conclude on the whole population.
Because the auditor selects the sample, evidence must be complete rather than
representative.

blocks.text: The habit that makes audits boring

blocks.html:
Run one internally, first, on a handful of controls, with someone who did not operate them pulling the evidence. It takes two days, finds most of what the real audit would find, and moves the discovery from fieldwork to a quiet Tuesday.

Programmes that do this describe audits as administrative. Programmes that do not describe them as the worst month of the year, and both are accurate.

entries.title: The management assertion
entries.description: In a SOC 2 attestation, management, not the auditor, writes the assertion that the system is described fairly and the controls were suitably designed.
sources: AICPA, SSAE No. 18, AT-C section 205
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100)
AICPA, Description Criteria (DC section 200)
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, clause 9.3 (management review)

sections.text: The assertion is management's, the opinion is the auditor's
Where ISO 27001 puts the same accountability

blocks.html: In an attestation engagement such as SOC 2, management provides a written assertion: its own statement that the system is described fairly and the controls were suitably designed. The practitioner then opines on that assertion: the words are management’s, not the auditor’s.

For a Type II the assertion reaches further: it states that those controls operated effectively across the whole reporting period, not merely that they were well designed on one day. The report is built on top of this statement. The practitioner’s opinion is a conclusion about management’s assertion, so a weak or overstated assertion is management’s exposure and does not transfer to the firm that examined it.

blocks.text: The assertion is management's, the opinion is the auditor's

blocks.html:
These are two separate statements by two separate parties, and running them together is the most common misreading of a SOC 2 report. The assertion comes first: management describes the system and states that the description is fair and the controls suitably designed. The opinion is written on top of it: the practitioner tests, then concludes on whether management’s assertion is fairly stated. Under SSAE 18, AT-C section 205, the examination is of a subject matter for which the responsible party has made an assertion; without that assertion there is nothing for the practitioner to report on.

Aspect The assertion The opinion
Written by Management The practitioner, a licensed CPA firm
States The description is fair and controls were suitably designed Whether that assertion is fairly stated, on the evidence tested
Order Comes first Built on the assertion
Carries the exposure Management owns it The firm answers for its own testing

items.html: The system description matches the system that actually ran: its boundaries, the services in scope and the controls in place. Overstate the boundary and the assertion is signed over a system that does not exist.
The controls, as designed, would meet the applicable Trust Services Criteria if they operated as described. This, together with fair presentation, is the whole of a Type I.
For a Type II, that the controls operated effectively throughout the stated period. This is the part the practitioner tests against a sample.

Which criteria each half is measured against. The description is assessed for fair presentation against the description criteria (DC section 200); the controls are assessed against the Trust Services Criteria. Naming both keeps the report from being read against the wrong bar.

blocks.html:
A Type I assertion covers the fair presentation of the system description and the
suitability of control design at a point in time; a Type II adds that those
controls operated effectively across a period. The same Type I / Type II split is
used for SOC 1 reports.

blocks.text: Where ISO 27001 puts the same accountability

blocks.html: ISO/IEC 27001 has no direct equivalent. Certification produces a certificate from an accredited body, not an opinion on a statement management signed. The accountability lives in different machinery: clause 9.3 requires top management to review the information security management system at planned intervals, and the Statement of Applicability records which controls apply and the justification for including or excluding each. Both put a management decision on record. Neither is a signed assertion a practitioner then opines on, so an ISO certificate should never be described as resting on a management assertion.

Scope overstated. The description claims systems, locations or services the controls do not actually cover, and management signs it anyway. When the sample reaches the part that was never really in scope, the gap is management’s: it asserted something untrue.

Effectiveness the evidence cannot support. Management asserts that controls operated throughout the period when the evidence covers only part of it. A Type II assertion is that the controls operated effectively across the whole period, in all material respects, not a claim resting only on the instances that happened to be captured.

Treated as boilerplate. The assertion is read as text the auditor drafted and management merely countersigned. It is the opposite: the statement management owns and the document the whole report is built to opine on. A programme that lets the firm word its assertion has misunderstood who is exposed.

items.q: What is the difference between the management assertion and the auditor's opinion?
items.html: The assertion is management’s statement; the opinion is the practitioner’s conclusion about that statement. Management writes the assertion first: that the system is described fairly and the controls were suitably designed, and for a Type II operated effectively over the period. The CPA firm then tests and issues an opinion on whether the assertion is fairly stated. One is the claim, the other is the verdict on the claim, and they are written by different parties.

items.q: Who signs the management assertion?
items.html: A member of management with authority over the system in scope, commonly an executive such as the chief executive, chief technology officer or head of security, depending on who owns the system description. It is signed by the organisation being examined, never by the audit firm. The signature is the point: it records that management, not the practitioner, stands behind the description and the controls.

items.q: Is there a management assertion in an ISO 27001 audit?
items.html: Not in the SOC 2 sense. ISO/IEC 27001 certification produces a certificate from an accredited body rather than an opinion on a signed statement. The nearest accountability sits in the management review required by clause 9.3 and in the Statement of Applicability, both of which record management decisions, but neither is a written assertion the auditor opines on.

entries.title: Change management as a control
entries.description: Change management is the control that changes to production are authorised, tested and documented before release. The record it leaves, and how it fails.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 8.32 (change management)
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (criterion CC8.1)
ITIL 4, change enablement

blocks.html: Change management is the control that changes to production are authorised, tested and documented before release, so no change reaches a live system without a record of who asked, who approved, what was tested and when it went out.

An unauthorised change to production is a common way a control that looks healthy on paper turns out not to be operating. It is also among the first things an auditor tests, because a weak change process quietly undermines every other control: each of them assumes that production only changes through a path someone approved.

The value of the control is not the paperwork. It is that the paperwork cannot be produced honestly after the fact, so a change is either evidenced as authorised or it is unsupported, and to an auditor an authorisation that cannot be evidenced is one that did not happen.
A valid change leaves a single record that links four things, each attributable to a named person and each dated by the system rather than typed in afterwards.

items.html: What is being changed and why, raised before the work starts. A request opened after deployment is not a request; it is a reconstruction.
A named approver who is not the person who built the change, recorded before release. This is the authorisation the whole control exists to capture.
Evidence that the change was exercised before it reached production: the test that ran, its outcome and where it ran. “Tested: yes” is not a test result.
When the change went live, who released it and to which system. This is the line that ties the approved change to the thing now running.

blocks.html: Read as a chain, the record answers request, approval, test then deployment for every change, and an auditor sampling releases reads it in that order. A change missing any link is the link the finding names.

The person who builds a change must not be the sole approver and deployer of it. A change approved by its own author records an authorisation that never happened: there was no second judgement, only a signature the requester wrote for themselves. The issue is segregation of duties, not which line reviews: a second reviewer in the same first line is fine; the author signing for themselves is not.

Segregation here is not bureaucracy. It is the difference between a control that catches a bad or malicious change before release and one that only documents it afterwards. The approver need not be senior; they need to be someone other than the author, with enough context to refuse.

ITIL 4 and many control frameworks sort changes into three paths, and the point of the split is to match the weight of the process to the risk of the change rather than force everything through one gate.

Type Path Approval Review
Normal Assessed and approved through the standard route Before release, by someone other than the author At release
Standard Pre-authorised, low-risk and repeatable Granted once, to the change type On the pre-authorisation, periodically
Emergency Expedited for genuine urgency Compressed, by an emergency approver Retrospective, and mandatory

The boundaries (what counts as low-risk, how fast an emergency has to be) are the organisation’s own to set; the three-way split is the part that travels. The emergency path exists for real incidents where waiting for normal approval would do more harm than the change. Authorisation is compressed (an emergency approver signs quickly), not removed; deferring approval to a retrospective review is an exceptional contingency, not the design. It is also the one most often abused, because it is the fastest route through the gate.

Four failure modes account for most change-management findings, and a tester who knows them looks for them first.

The emergency back door. When a large share of changes come through the emergency path, the path has stopped being for emergencies. It has become the route the organisation uses to skip approval, and a rate (emergency changes as a proportion of all changes) is the single most revealing number in the process.

Approver equals requester. The record shows an approval, but the approver and the requester are the same person, or the same shared account. There is a signature and no authorisation. This is the failure segregation exists to prevent, and it survives in programmes that check the box for “approved” without checking who approved.

“Tested” with no test. The change record asserts the change was tested and carries nothing that shows a test ran: no result, no environment, no output. An assertion of testing is not evidence of testing, and an auditor treats the two very differently.

Standing approvals. A blanket or standing approval authorises a category of change rather than a change, so everything inside the category ships without a fresh decision. Standard changes are the bounded, reviewed version of this; a standing approval that is really an open door is not.

Each of these is a control deviation before anyone has named it. When a tester samples releases and finds one that reached production with no approval on file, or an approval signed by its own author, that is the deviation the report records, and the emergency queue is a place testers commonly look first.

A dated record produced by the operation of a control, sufficient for a reviewer
who was not present to conclude that the control ran. A change record is
evidence in exactly this sense, which is why “tested: yes” with nothing behind
it fails.

items.q: What is a change management control?
items.html: It is the control that a change to production is authorised, tested and documented before it is released, so that no change reaches a live system without a record of who requested it, who approved it, what was tested and when it went out. ISO/IEC 27001’s Annex A control 8.32 and the Trust Services criterion CC8.1 both frame it this way. The control is operating when that record exists for every change and the approver is never the author.

items.q: What is an emergency change?
items.html: An emergency change is one released through an expedited path because genuine urgency (an active incident, a live outage) makes waiting for normal approval more harmful than the change itself. Authorisation is expedited, compressed to an emergency approver, and only exceptionally deferred to a mandatory retrospective review. The path is legitimate and necessary; it is also the one most often abused, so the proportion of changes that use it is worth watching.

items.q: What evidence does an auditor want for change management?
items.html: The change record: the request, the approval by someone other than the requester, the test result and the deployment, each attributable to a named person and dated by the system. For a sample of changes across the whole period, not the best one. A change with a missing approval, an approval by its own author or a “tested” flag with no test behind it is recorded as a deviation.

entries.title: Backup and restore testing
entries.description: The control is the proven restore, not the existence of a backup. What a real restore test involves, and the failure modes an untested backup hides.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 8.13 (information backup)
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (criteria A1.2 and A1.3)
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems

sections.text: What the restore has to prove
What a real restore test involves

blocks.html: The control is the restore test, not the existence of a backup. An untested backup is an assumption, and the only proof a backup works is a restore that produced usable data inside the required time.

A backup that has never been restored is a cost with an unproven benefit. It occupies storage, sits on the control list and reassures nobody who has actually needed one, because the ways a backup fails live almost entirely on the restore side: media that cannot be read, a key nobody kept, a set that was always missing a table. None of those show up while the backup job is the only thing anyone watches.

This is why an auditor testing information backup under ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A control 8.13 (which requires backup copies to be maintained and regularly tested), or recovery under Trust Services criterion A1.3, asks to see a restore that happened rather than a backup schedule that runs. The schedule is the assumption; the restore is the evidence.

blocks.text: What the restore has to prove

blocks.html: A restore test is where the recovery point objective and recovery time objective stop being aspirations. The business impact analysis sets both: how much data the organisation can afford to lose (the RPO) and how long it can afford to be without the activity (the RTO). Those numbers are derived from the impact of the outage, not picked by whoever runs the backup tool. A restore either returns data recent enough to meet the RPO, within the restore-time budget the RTO allows, or it does not. The full activity recovery time is proven by an end-to-end recovery exercise, of which the data restore is one part; see business continuity at 3.6. Nothing short of an actual restore tells you whether the data half will hold.

The maximum tolerable data loss, expressed as a length of time rather than a
volume, the point in the past back to which data must be recoverable. A restore
that returns data older than the RPO has failed even if every file it produces
opens cleanly.

blocks.text: What a real restore test involves

blocks.html:
A real restore test recovers the data into a clean, separate environment (never over the top of live production and never back into the system that just failed), and then someone confirms the recovered data is complete and usable. Usable means opened, queried and reconciled against a known record; a job that reports success has told you it finished writing, not that what it wrote can be read back. The restore is timed, from start to usable, and that figure is measured against the RTO. Then the result is documented (what was restored, from which copy, how long it took, what was checked) so the next audit reads a record instead of a memory.

A full restore recovers everything; a sampled restore recovers a defined subset. Sampling is legitimate and often the only affordable way to test often, but the sample has to exercise the real path (the same media, the same decryption, the same sequence) or it proves only that the easy part works.

Dimension Full restore Sampled restore
Scope The whole dataset or system A defined subset of files or records
Proves The recovery path end to end The path works for what was sampled
Cost Time, and a full-size clean environment Cheaper and faster, so run more often
The trap Rare, so the RTO stays untested between runs A sample that skips the hard parts proves nothing

Every one of these passes the backup dashboard.

Green for years, then nothing to restore. The jobs report success for so long that no one questions them, and the first real restore meets missing media, a decryption key nobody held or a set that turns out to have never been complete. The dashboard measured that the job ran, not that its output could be recovered.

Testing the flag, not the restore. The “test” checks that the backup job finished with a success code instead of performing an actual restore. This proves the software can write a file. It says nothing about whether that file reconstructs into working data.

Restoring into the same failure. The restore is run back into the environment that failed, reusing its configuration, its keys and its dependencies. It works, and proves nothing about recovering when that environment is the thing that is gone, which is the scenario a backup exists for.

Works in the lab, never timed. The restore succeeds but was never run against the clock, so the RTO is a number in a plan that no exercise has ever met. A recovery time nobody has measured is a guess, and it is usually optimistic.

items.q: What is the difference between a backup and a restore test?
items.html: A backup is the copy; a restore test is the proof the copy is worth keeping. The backup is made by a scheduled job and confirmed by that job reporting success, which only means data was written somewhere. The restore test reads that data back into a separate environment and confirms it reconstructs into something complete, usable and recent enough to meet the RPO. One is an activity that runs; the other is the control that shows the activity was worth running.

items.q: How often should you test restores?
items.html: Often enough that the gap between two tests is shorter than the time it would take a silent failure to matter, and always after a material change to the system, the backup method or the encryption. A yearly full restore with lighter sampled restores in between is a common shape, and higher-tier systems are tested more often, but those figures are examples, not a rule from any standard. The real cadence follows the criticality set in the BIA and the rate at which the environment changes; a system that was re-platformed last month should not be relying on a restore proven against the old one.

items.q: What does a restore test prove?
items.html: That a specific backup, restored by a specific path, produced data that was complete, usable and recent enough to meet the RPO, within the restore time the RTO budget allows, on the day it was run. Proving the full activity recovery time still needs an end-to-end exercise; a data restore is one part of it. It does not prove the next restore will succeed, which is why the test is repeated and why its result is documented each time. A single successful restore retires the assumption for one configuration; it does not retire it forever.

mainEntity.name: What does a restore test prove?

acceptedAnswer.text: That a specific backup, restored by a specific path, produced data that was complete, usable and recent enough to meet the RPO, within the restore time the RTO budget allows, on the day it was run. Proving the full activity recovery time still needs an end-to-end exercise; a data restore is one part of it. It does not prove the next restore will succeed, which is why the test is repeated and why its result is documented each time. A single successful restore retires the assumption for one configuration; it does not retire it forever.

entries.title: Control deviations and exceptions in testing
entries.description: A control deviation is a tested instance where a control did not operate as designed, what a SOC 2 report calls an exception, and why it is not a waiver.
sources: AICPA, SSAE No. 18, AT-C section 205 (exceptions)
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100)
IIA, International Professional Practices Framework, Standard 2320

sections.text: A deviation is not a waiver
What one deviation says about the population

blocks.html: A control deviation is an instance in the tested sample where the control did not operate as designed. In a SOC 2 report these are called exceptions, and a single one can put the whole control’s conclusion in question.

A deviation is a finding about the control, not about the one instance that failed. The auditor never sees the whole population (they test a sample and conclude back to everything that sample stands for), so a deviation bears on the conclusion for the whole population, not just the one instance that failed. How you treat it, more than the deviation itself, is what the auditor watches next.

blocks.text: A deviation is not a waiver

blocks.html:
The two get confused because both describe a control that was not met, and the confusion is expensive. A policy waiver is a decision made before the fact: a named approver signs off, in advance, that a specific gap will run for a bounded period with a compensating control. A deviation is a failure discovered after the fact, in testing, that nobody authorised.

Recasting a deviation as a waiver once the auditor has found it is the move that turns a control finding into an integrity finding. Back-dating an approval to cover an instance that already failed is not exception management; it is fabricated evidence, and it follows a programme far longer than the deviation ever would.

A planned, pre-authorised and time-bound exception, signed before the gap opens
and paired with a compensating control. A deviation is the opposite in every
respect: unplanned, unauthorised and found only after the control has already
failed.

blocks.text: What one deviation says about the population

blocks.html:
The auditor tests a sample (say 25 change tickets out of a year’s several thousand) and concludes on the whole population from it. One deviation in that sample of 25 is not one late change to be corrected in place; it puts the operating-effectiveness conclusion for every change the sample stood for in question, and commonly prompts the auditor to expand testing to see how far it reaches. The figures here are illustrative, and this sampling is judgemental rather than statistical, so it supports a conclusion about the population, not a precise failure rate: estimating an actual rate would need a valid probability sample.

This is why “we fixed the ticket” is the wrong instinct. Correcting the sampled instance leaves the population (and the conclusion the sample was testing) exactly where they were.
The question that decides the response is whether the deviation is a one-off or the visible edge of a control that does not work.

items.html: A single instance failed for a reason that does not recur: a one-time manual slip, a cycle with the reviewer on leave and no cover. The design holds; one operation of it did not.

The deviation reflects a design or operating failure that will recur: the control has no step that would have caught the case, or the step exists and is routinely skipped. Every untested instance is now suspect.

blocks.html: Root cause is what tells the two apart, and you cannot assert “isolated” without having found one. A deviation labelled isolated with no analysis behind it reads to an auditor as systematic with the analysis skipped.

A response answers why the control failed and what changes because of it; it does not argue that the failure should not have counted. Three parts carry it.

Root cause. Why the instance failed, established by analysis rather than assumed. Until it is known, isolated versus systematic cannot be answered and the remediation is a guess.

Remediation. What changes so the failure does not recur, across the population and not only for the sampled instance. A fix that touches one ticket and leaves the process untouched has remediated nothing.

A statement of what failed. Whether the control’s design was inadequate or a sound design was not operated. The two lead to different fixes, and an honest answer to which it was is worth more than any argument that the deviation should not count.

Four moves recur, and each one makes the finding worse.

Arguing it away. Spending the response explaining why the deviation does not really count instead of finding why it happened. The auditor has already recorded it; the only open question is the cause, and the effort spent on the argument is the effort that would have shrunk the finding.

Back-dating a waiver. Producing an approval, dated before the failure, to reclassify a deviation as a planned exception. This converts a routine control finding into an integrity finding and is the most damaging response available.

Assuming one means one. Treating a single exception in a small sample as a single isolated problem. One deviation in a sample of 25 speaks to the whole population the sample stood for, and because the sample is small and judgemental it rarely proves the problem is contained to the instance that failed.

Fixing the instance, not the population. Remediating the sampled item and leaving every other instance as it was. The sample stood for the population; the response has to reach the same population.

items.q: What is a control deviation?
items.html: A control deviation is an instance, found while testing a control, where the control did not operate as it was designed to. In SOC 2 and other examination reports these are called exceptions. Because the auditor tests a sample and concludes on the whole population, a deviation bears on whether the control operated effectively across everything the sample stood for, not just the instance that failed, so it is not a single fault to be corrected in place.

items.q: What is the difference between a deviation and a policy exception?
items.html: Timing and authorisation. A policy exception, or waiver, is planned: a named approver signs off in advance that a specific gap will run for a bounded period, with a compensating control. A deviation is unplanned: a failure discovered after the fact, in testing, that nobody authorised. Reclassifying a deviation as an exception once an auditor has found it (by back-dating the approval) turns a control finding into an integrity finding.

items.q: Does one exception fail a SOC 2 control?
items.html: Not automatically. A single exception does not by itself mean the criterion was not met; the service auditor evaluates the cause of the exception, whether it is isolated or systematic and what it implies for the rest of the population before concluding. One exception can contribute to a qualified opinion when its effect is material, and it can also be judged isolated and immaterial, which is why the root cause and the response matter more than the count.

entries.title: Continuous control monitoring
entries.description: Continuous control monitoring is automated, ongoing proof that a control is operating, taken from the system itself instead of screenshotted once a quarter.
sources: AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (criterion CC4.1)
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, clause 9.1 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation)
NIST SP 800-137 - Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM)

sections.text: What automation suits, and what it does not
What it feeds, and what it does not replace

blocks.html: Continuous control monitoring is automated, ongoing checking that a control is operating, pulling the signal straight from the system rather than screenshotting it once a quarter. Continuous compliance is the broader goal it feeds (staying provably within requirements over time), which takes acting on what the monitoring finds, not watching alone.

It closes the gap between “we do this” and “we can show we did this” to near zero for the controls it covers, because the evidence 4.2 is produced at the moment the control operates rather than gathered in the four weeks before fieldwork. What it cannot do is exercise judgement, so it earns its place on the controls a machine can check and leaves the rest exactly where they were.

Point-in-time evidence answers one question: did the control run on the day someone looked. Continuous control monitoring answers a harder one: has it run every day since, and can you see the moment it stopped. The record is pulled at the point of operation, continuously, from the system that enforces the control rather than assembled by hand before an audit.

That is the whole value. Evidence 4.2 collected this way is dated and attributable by construction, and complete for the period its coverage actually spans, provided the monitoring itself has no gaps and its telemetry can be trusted. The programme stops sampling its own best month and starts holding the full population it covers.

blocks.text: What automation suits, and what it does not

blocks.html:
Automation suits a control whose correct state a machine can read without interpretation. It does not suit a control whose correctness is a person’s judgement, and wiring one of those to a green tick produces a light with no thought behind it.

Suits continuous monitoring Does not
MFA coverage across privileged accounts A manager’s review of an exception
Encryption configuration on a data store A risk-acceptance decision
Access still matching the joiner-mover-leaver record Whether a vendor is trustworthy
Patch currency against a baseline Whether a policy is the right policy

The left column is machine-checkable: there is a correct state and the system can report the current one against it. The right column is not. A tool can confirm that a review was recorded; it cannot confirm the review was any good, and treating the record of a judgement as the judgement itself is how a green dashboard hides a hollow control.

blocks.text: What it feeds, and what it does not replace

blocks.html: A continuously monitored control is a natural source for a leading indicator. Coverage trending down (privileged accounts without a second factor creeping from two per cent to four) is an early warning while there is still time to act, not a surprise discovered at quarter end.

A leading metric that warns exposure is moving toward appetite before it becomes
an incident. A continuously monitored control is one of the cleanest feeds for
one, because the coverage figure updates itself.

It does not replace the audit. An auditor still tests, still selects the sample and still concludes independently, but tests against a population that is already instrumented, where the evidence exists for every instance rather than the ones that were remembered. Continuous monitoring makes fieldwork shorter and duller. It does not make it unnecessary, and a programme that treats a platform’s green dashboard as an audit opinion has confused the two.

Watching the tool, not the control. A monitor that confirms the scanner is online says nothing about whether the scan is finding anything. The signal has to be the operation of the control, not the availability of the thing that checks it.

Alerting on everything. A monitor that fires on every deviation, at any severity, trains everyone to ignore it. Within a month the alerts are a filtered folder and a real breach sits in it unread. Thresholds and routing are part of the design, not an afterthought.

“Continuous” that is really monthly. A check that runs on a schedule slow enough to miss the thing it watches is point-in-time sampling with a dashboard. If a control can drift and be restored between runs, the gap is invisible and the word is marketing.

Coverage mistaken for effectiveness. Buying a compliance-automation platform and counting the controls it touches measures reach, not operation. A control can be monitored, green and not working; coverage is the count of controls watched, effectiveness is whether the watched control does its job.

items.q: What is continuous control monitoring?
items.html: It is automated, ongoing checking that a control is operating, taken from the system that runs the control rather than reconstructed by hand before an audit. Instead of confirming a control worked on the day someone screenshotted it, it confirms the control has stayed in its required state and shows the moment it did not. It suits controls with a machine-checkable state (MFA coverage, encryption settings, patch currency 4.10) and is poorly suited to controls that turn on human judgement.

items.q: What is the difference between continuous monitoring and continuous compliance?
items.html: Continuous monitoring is one activity inside continuous compliance, not the whole of it. Monitoring reads a control’s condition on an ongoing basis. Continuous compliance is the broader practice of staying provably within requirements over time: it takes evaluating what the monitoring surfaces and remediating what it finds, not monitoring alone. Monitoring makes the state visible; holding it is more than watching.

items.q: Can continuous monitoring replace an audit?
items.html: No. It feeds an audit rather than removing the need for one. An auditor still selects a sample, tests independently and forms an opinion, but does it against a population that is already instrumented, so fieldwork is shorter and holds fewer surprises. A platform’s green dashboard is evidence for an audit, not a substitute for the auditor’s own testing.

entries.title: Security questionnaires (SIG, CAIQ)
entries.description: A security questionnaire is a standardised set of questions used to assess a vendor's security posture. The SIG and CAIQ are the common templates.
sources: Shared Assessments, Standardized Information Gathering (SIG) Questionnaire
Cloud Security Alliance, Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ) and STAR
ISO/IEC 27036-2:2022 - Cybersecurity, supplier relationships, Part 2: Requirements

sections.text: Why a completed questionnaire is not assurance
Tier the questionnaire to the risk

blocks.html: A security questionnaire is a standardised set of questions used to assess a vendor’s security posture (the SIG and the CAIQ are the common templates), and it is a diligence artefact, not assurance in itself.

The questionnaire is where third-party diligence usually starts, and it is where weak programmes stop. Treating the returned document as the assessment confuses the instrument for the finding: three hundred answered questions with nothing sampled behind them tell you what a vendor is willing to assert, not what is true.

The same document sits on two desks, and most people only ever meet one side of it.

Sending. As part of third-party diligence, the questionnaire goes out to a prospective or existing vendor to probe its security posture before and during the relationship. It is one instrument of the wider vendor due diligence at 3.8, not the whole of it: a completed questionnaire narrows what still needs verifying, it does not close the assessment.

Answering. As the vendor being assessed, you complete other organisations’ questionnaires to win and keep their business. For a company that sells to enterprises this is a standing workload measured in hundreds of questions a quarter, and it turns into a revenue-blocking task the moment a deal waits on it.

blocks.text: Why a completed questionnaire is not assurance

blocks.html:
The answers are self-attested. A vendor asserting that access is reviewed quarterly and data is encrypted at rest has told you what it believes to be true; it has shown you nothing. Assurance arrives only with the artefact behind the answer: an independent audit report such as SOC 2, an ISO 27001 certificate scoped to the service you are buying or an actual configuration export.

A “yes” with nothing behind it is a claim, not a control. A SOC 2 report and an ISO 27001 certificate answer different questions (see 5.1), and a certificate scoped to the wrong entity proves nothing about the service in front of you. The questionnaire tells you what to verify; the evidence is what verifies it.

blocks.text: Tier the questionnaire to the risk

blocks.html:
Sending a three-hundred-question SIG to a vendor that stores none of your data and touches none of your systems is questionnaire theatre: it burns the vendor’s time and yours, and nobody reads the result. Depth of questionnaire should follow the risk tier set in third-party risk management: a lightweight set for a routine supplier, the full instrument reserved for a vendor inside a recovery time objective or holding production data. The SIG ships in exactly this spirit, with a shorter SIG Lite for lower-tier suppliers and the full SIG Core for the ones that can actually hurt you.

Dimension SIG CAIQ
Author Shared Assessments Cloud Security Alliance
Scope Broad third-party risk across many control domains Cloud service security, mapped to the Cloud Controls Matrix
Form Configurable question set, from SIG Core down to SIG Lite Yes/no control assertions against CCM domains
Standing Licensed content set, maintained and updated Freely available, underpinning CSA STAR registry listings

Redrafting the same three hundred questions by hand every time is how the workload becomes unbearable and how the answers go stale. The fix is a reviewed knowledge base (every standard question with an approved answer and a link to the evidence behind it) that a response can be assembled from and then tailored to the asker.

It needs a named owner who keeps it current. An answer library nobody maintains is a catalogue of last year’s claims, and the drift is invisible until a customer’s auditor asks to see the control behind an answer that stopped being true two releases ago.

A completed questionnaire treated as assurance. The document comes back, gets filed and closes the assessment, with no report, certificate or export sampled behind a single answer. The programme has collected assertions and recorded them as facts.

Answers that drift from reality. The questionnaire is refreshed once a year while the environment changes every week. Between refreshes the answers describe a posture the organisation no longer has, and nobody notices until an incident or an audit finds the gap.

Questionnaire theatre. Hundreds of questions issued and returned, none validated. The volume signals diligence and delivers none: a longer questionnaire that nobody checks is weaker than a short one that is verified.

One questionnaire for every tier. A low-risk vendor is sent the same instrument as a critical one, so the routine supplier is over-assessed and the critical one is assessed no harder than the rest. Effort decouples from risk, and the review that mattered gets the same cursory read as the ninety that did not.

items.q: What is a security questionnaire?
items.html: A standardised set of questions an organisation sends a vendor to assess its security posture, or receives and completes when it is the vendor being assessed. The SIG and the CAIQ are the two common templates. It is a diligence artefact (a structured way to ask) and not assurance in itself, because the answers are self-attested until evidence is produced behind them.

items.q: What is the difference between a SIG and a CAIQ?
items.html: The SIG (Standardized Information Gathering, from Shared Assessments) is a broad third-party-risk questionnaire covering many control domains, licensed as a maintained content set and configurable from a full SIG Core down to a shorter SIG Lite. The CAIQ (Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire, from the Cloud Security Alliance) is narrower and cloud-specific: yes/no control assertions mapped to the Cloud Controls Matrix and freely available, and a submitted CAIQ is what backs a Level 1 listing in the CSA STAR registry. Use the SIG for general supplier diligence; expect the CAIQ from a cloud provider.

items.q: Is a completed security questionnaire enough assurance?
items.html: No. A completed questionnaire is a set of claims, not evidence they are true. Assurance comes from what stands behind the answers: an independent audit report such as SOC 2, a certification such as ISO 27001 scoped to the service in question or a direct artefact like a configuration export. Treat the questionnaire as the thing that tells you what to verify, then verify the answers that matter.

blocks.html:
The assessment of a supplier’s security, financial and regulatory standing before
and during the relationship, scaled to the risk tier. A questionnaire is one
instrument of that diligence, not the whole of it: verifying what the answers
claim is the rest.

entries.title: Vulnerability management
entries.description: The lifecycle of discovering, prioritising, remediating and verifying technical vulnerabilities on deadlines set by severity, not a one-off scan report.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 8.8 (management of technical vulnerabilities)
NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 - Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Planning
FIRST, Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS)
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (criterion CC7.1)

sections.text: CVSS is not risk on its own
The link to KRIs and continuous monitoring

blocks.html: Vulnerability management is the lifecycle of discovering, prioritising, remediating and verifying technical vulnerabilities on time limits set by severity, a continuous programme, not a scan report filed and forgotten.

The scan is the easy part. What separates a programme from a report is everything after the finding: a decision about which vulnerabilities matter, a deadline to fix them by, and a rescan that proves each one is actually closed. A scanner that runs every week feeding a queue that never empties is not vulnerability management: it is a list that grows.

items.html: Authenticated scanning, penetration testing and vendor and disclosure feeds find what is exposed. An unauthenticated scan sees the front door; an authenticated one sees the missing patches behind it.
CVSS is the starting point, adjusted for active exploitation, exposure and asset criticality. A base score ranks the finding in the abstract; context ranks it on your estate.
Patch, or apply a mitigating control, within a time limit set by severity. The SLA is the commitment; without one the finding has no deadline and no owner.

Rescan (or authoritative version or configuration evidence) to confirm the fix closed the vulnerability rather than moved it. “Remediated” in a ticket is a claim; a clean rescan is evidence that holds up.

blocks.text: CVSS is not risk on its own

blocks.html:
A CVSS score measures the vulnerability, not the risk it poses to you. The base score is a property of the flaw (how hard it is to exploit and what it grants), computed the same way for every organisation on earth. Risk is that score meeting your estate.

Illustratively, a CVSS 9.8 on an internal host reachable only from an administrative network, sitting behind a compensating control, may matter less than a 6.5 on an internet-facing system with a public exploit in active use. The scores are examples, not thresholds. Three things sit on top of the base score and change the order: active exploitation, whether a working exploit exists and is being used; exposure, whether an attacker can reach the asset at all; and the criticality of the asset itself.

Severity then sets the clock. A programme might commit to fixing critical findings within 7 days, high within 30 and medium within 90, but those windows are illustrative. The real ones are the organisation’s own decision, written down and agreed before the first breach rather than argued after it.

A scanner and a penetration test both discover, and neither is a substitute for the other. A scanner enumerates known weaknesses against a signature database; a test tries to exploit what it finds and chains several weaknesses into a path a scanner would report as three unrelated mediums.

Vulnerability scan Penetration test
Method Enumerates known weaknesses Exploits and chains them
Cadence Continuous or scheduled Point in time
Coverage Broad and automated Deep and targeted
Tells you What is probably wrong What an attacker could do
Blind to Anything with no signature Whatever is out of scope

A programme that runs scans and calls it testing has confirmed neither what is present nor what is exploitable.

blocks.text: The link to KRIs and continuous monitoring

blocks.html: Two other entries connect here. The count of critical vulnerabilities open past their SLA can be a key risk indicator 3.11: the SLA defines when one is overdue, and the indicator’s own threshold (how many overdue is too many) is a separate appetite decision, with a named owner and a response when it breaches. And vulnerability state (new criticals, SLA breaches and scan coverage) is a strong candidate for continuous monitoring (4.8) rather than a quarterly snapshot, because the exposure changes daily as new vulnerabilities are disclosed against software that has not moved.

A leading metric that warns exposure is moving toward appetite before it becomes
an incident. The count of critical vulnerabilities still open past their SLA is a
candidate: the SLA sets what counts as overdue, and it earns the name once it has
its own threshold, owner and response.

Scanning with no remediation SLA. The report is produced on schedule and nobody acts on it, because no deadline attaches to any line. A finding with no date is a finding no one owns.

Prioritising by CVSS base score alone. Ranking the queue by base score puts a theoretical critical on an unreachable host above a medium being exploited on the perimeter today. Strip out exploitability and exposure and the order is wrong in exactly the cases that matter.

No rescan, so “remediated” is unverified. A ticket closed on a promise is not a closed vulnerability. Patches fail to apply, roll back on reboot or fix one instance and miss four identical ones; only a rescan, or authoritative evidence of the fixed version, tells the difference.

Counting scanned assets as covered. An unauthenticated scan reaches a host but sees almost nothing installed on it. Reporting that host as assessed records coverage the scan never had, and the missing patches behind it never enter the queue.

items.q: What is vulnerability management?
items.html: Vulnerability management is the continuous lifecycle of finding technical vulnerabilities, deciding which ones matter, fixing them within a time limit set by severity and rescanning to confirm the fix held. It is a programme, not a scan: the scan is one input, and the value is in the prioritisation, the remediation SLA and the verification that follow it.

items.q: What is the difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?
items.html: A scan enumerates known weaknesses automatically against a signature database: broad, fast and repeatable. A penetration test tries to exploit what is found and chain several weaknesses into an attack path, which a scanner cannot do. Both discover, and neither replaces the other: the scan gives coverage, the test gives depth and confirms what is genuinely exploitable.

items.q: How do you prioritise vulnerabilities?
items.html: Start from the CVSS base score, then adjust for three things it does not know: whether a working exploit exists and is being used, whether an attacker can actually reach the asset and how critical that asset is. A medium score on an exposed system under active exploitation outranks a critical on an isolated host behind a compensating control. CVSS ranks the flaw; context ranks the risk.

mainEntity.name: What is vulnerability management?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vulnerability management is the continuous lifecycle of finding technical vulnerabilities, deciding which ones matter, fixing them within a time limit set by severity and rescanning to confirm the fix held. It is a programme, not a scan: the scan is one input, and the value is in the prioritisation, the remediation SLA and the verification that follow it.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?

A penetration test tries to exploit what is found and chain several weaknesses into an attack path, which a scanner cannot do. Both discover, and neither replaces the other: the scan gives coverage, the test gives depth and confirms what is genuinely exploitable.

entries.title: Asset management as a control
entries.description: Asset management is the maintained inventory of what the organisation owns and runs, with an owner for each item. Nearly every other control depends on it.
keywords: what is asset management in cyber security
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A controls 5.9, 5.10, 5.11
CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1, Controls 1 and 2
NIST SP 800-53r5, family CM (Configuration Management) and CM-8

sections.text: Inventory and CMDB are not the same thing

blocks.html: Asset management is the maintained, owned inventory of everything the organisation runs (hardware, software, data stores, cloud services and the business services built on them), kept current enough that other controls can rely on it.

It is listed first in the CIS Controls and near the front of ISO 27001’s Annex A for one reason: every control that follows takes the asset list as input. You cannot patch what you do not know you run, grant least-privilege access to a system nobody recorded, back up an undocumented database or scope an audit against an inventory that is wrong. A gap in the asset register is a gap in every downstream control at once.

The hard part is not building the list. It is keeping it true. An inventory is a control only while it reflects reality this week; a spreadsheet last reconciled at the previous audit is a document, not a control.
Wider than the hardware most people picture.

items.html: Servers, laptops, mobile devices, network kit, and anything with an IP address on the corporate network, including the devices nobody provisioned.
Operating systems, applications, libraries and firmware, each with a version, so a new CVE can be matched to what is actually installed.
Repositories and their classification: where regulated or sensitive data lives, which is what a DLP or access-review programme scopes against.
Accounts, subscriptions, SaaS tenancies and the resources inside them. The fastest-growing category and the one least often fully captured.
The customer-facing or revenue-bearing services that sit on top, mapped to the technical assets they depend on, so an outage or a risk can be described in business terms.

blocks.html:
The named individual accountable for an asset’s classification, its acceptable
use and the risk decisions about it. Not the person who administers it day to
day: the person who answers for it. An asset with no owner is the one that goes
unpatched.

blocks.text: Inventory and CMDB are not the same thing

blocks.html: A configuration management database records relationships (this service runs on those hosts, which depend on that database) and supports change and incident management. An asset inventory records existence, ownership and classification and supports risk and compliance. Mature organisations reconcile the two; small ones should not try to run a full CMDB before the basic inventory is reliable.

One-time discovery. A scan is run, the results are pasted into a sheet, and nothing reconciles it afterwards. Cloud resources and personal devices appear faster than the annual refresh catches them, so accuracy decays from the day the snapshot is taken.

No owner field, or a team name in it. “IT” owns 400 assets, which means nobody does. When a vulnerability lands, there is no individual to task and the remediation clock does not start.

Shadow IT uncounted. A department buys a SaaS tool on a card. It holds customer data, it is in nobody’s inventory, and it surfaces for the first time during a breach or a due-diligence questionnaire.

Classification missing. The list has every host but does not say which ones hold regulated data, so every downstream control has to treat all assets alike and effort cannot be prioritised.

items.q: What is asset management in cyber security?
items.html: The practice of keeping an accurate, owned inventory of all hardware, software, data and services the organisation uses, so that security controls (patching, access control, monitoring, backup, incident response) can be applied completely. It is the foundational control: everything else assumes the list is right.

items.q: What is the difference between an asset inventory and a CMDB?
items.html: An asset inventory answers “what do we have, who owns it, how sensitive is it”. A CMDB (configuration management database) answers “how are these things connected and what changed”. The inventory serves risk and compliance; the CMDB serves change and incident management. They overlap but are built for different questions.

items.q: How often should the asset inventory be updated?
items.html: Continuously for anything that can be discovered automatically (network scans, cloud APIs, endpoint agents feeding the inventory in near real time), with a periodic manual reconciliation, at least quarterly, for the categories that cannot be discovered, such as third-party SaaS and data classification.

items.q: Who is the asset owner?
items.html: The named person accountable for decisions about an asset: its classification, who may use it, and whether an identified risk to it is accepted or treated. It is a business-accountability role, not the system administrator who operates it.

entries.title: Identity and access management
entries.description: IAM is the set of controls deciding who has an account, what it can reach, and how that is proven: the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle and the access review.
keywords: what is identity and access management
sources: NIST SP 800-53r5, family AC (Access Control)
AICPA Trust Services Criteria, CC6.1-CC6.3
NIST SP 800-63-3 - Digital Identity Guidelines

blocks.html: Identity and access management is the set of controls that decides who holds an account, what that account is allowed to reach, and how both are proven, from the moment a person joins to the moment their access is removed.

It is the control domain auditors probe first, because it produces the clearest evidence of whether the organisation does what its policies say. An access list is a fact: either the leaver still has a login or they do not, either the finance system enforces segregation of duties or it does not. There is little room for a narrative.

Two ideas run under everything in the domain. Least privilege: an identity gets the minimum access its role needs and no more. Accountability: every action traces to one person, which is why shared and generic accounts are a standing finding.
Most IAM failures are timing failures in this one process.

items.html: Access is provisioned from an approved role template, granted on the start date and not before, with the approval recorded. Over-provisioning here (“give them what the last person had”) is how entitlement creep starts.

On a role change, old access is removed as new access is added. The step almost always skipped is the removal, so people accumulate rights as they move around and end up with a set nobody would approve from scratch.

Access is revoked on the last working day (ideally by disabling the identity centrally so every connected system follows), and privileged credentials are rotated. Delay here is the highest-severity gap in the domain.

blocks.html:
A control ensuring no single person can both initiate and approve the same
sensitive transaction: raise a payment and release it, write code and deploy it
to production. Enforced through role design and tested by looking for identities
that hold both sides.

The recurring control that catches what the lifecycle missed. On a set cadence, quarterly for privileged and financially significant systems and at least annually for the rest, each system’s access list goes to the person accountable for that system, who confirms every entry is still needed or flags it for removal.

A review is only evidence if three things are true: the reviewer is the business owner and not the IT team that grants the access, the flagged removals are actually actioned and re-checked, and the review covers the whole population rather than a sample. A signed-off review where nothing was ever removed is a signal that nobody looked.

• Multi-factor authentication on anything internet-facing and on all administrative access. Its absence on a remote-access path is a finding on almost every framework.
  • Privileged access management: administrative rights granted just in time, for a bounded window, through a checkout that logs the session, rather than standing admin accounts.
  • Access models: RBAC assigns entitlements to roles and roles to people, and is the practical default. ABAC decides access from attributes (department, location, data tag) at request time, and suits large or highly dynamic estates at the cost of more design effort.

Leaver access left live. The account is disabled weeks late, or in the directory but not in three SaaS tools that provision separately. Every access review starts by hunting for these.

Privilege creep through moves. Nobody removes on role change, so long-tenured staff hold access spanning every team they have passed through: the classic segregation-of-duties breach.

Rubber-stamp reviews. The owner approves 200 lines in one click, removes nothing, and the review is filed. It satisfies the letter of the control and none of its purpose.

Shared accounts. A db-admin login used by four engineers. When something breaks at 2am, the logs cannot say who did it.

items.q: What is identity and access management?
items.html: The discipline of managing digital identities and what they are permitted to do: creating and removing accounts, assigning the minimum access each role needs, enforcing strong authentication, and periodically proving the access that exists is still appropriate. It underpins almost every other security and compliance control.

items.q: What is the joiner-mover-leaver process?
items.html: The lifecycle of a person’s access: provisioned on joining from an approved role template, adjusted on a role change with old rights removed as new ones are added, and fully revoked on leaving. The mover and leaver steps are where most access findings originate, because removal is the part that gets skipped.

items.q: What is the difference between an access review and recertification?
items.html: They are the same control under two names: a periodic check where the owner of a system confirms each person’s access is still required and removes what is not. “Recertification” is the term common in identity-governance tooling; “access review” or “user access review” is the term auditors use.

items.q: What is least privilege?
items.html: The principle that an identity is granted only the access its function requires, for only as long as it requires it, and nothing more. It limits the damage a compromised or misused account can do and makes access reviews tractable, because there is less to justify.

entries.title: Security awareness and education
entries.description: Security awareness is the programme that turns policy into behaviour: role-based training, phishing simulation, and metrics that measure reporting, not clicks.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 6.3; clause 7.2 (competence) and 7.3 (awareness)
NIST SP 800-53r5, control AT (Awareness and Training) family
NIST SP 800-50r1 - Building a cybersecurity and privacy learning program, 2024
ENISA, Cybersecurity culture guidelines, 2022

blocks.html: Security awareness and education is the programme that turns written policy into day-to-day behaviour, teaching staff to recognise the situations that lead to incidents and, more importantly, to report them quickly.

It is a required control (ISO 27001 Annex A 6.3, the NIST AT family, and a line in nearly every regulation), but it is the one most often run as a compliance box. An annual slide deck with a quiz at the end satisfies the auditor’s question “do you train staff” and changes almost nothing about what people do when a convincing email arrives.

The distinction that matters is between awareness and culture. Awareness is knowing the rule. Culture is a workplace where reporting a mistake is met with thanks rather than blame, so people raise the click they just made instead of hiding it. A programme that drives the first without the second produces staff who know they did something wrong and say nothing.

items.html: Developers get secure-coding and dependency risk; finance gets invoice fraud and payment authorisation; executives get targeted social engineering and travel risk. One generic course for everyone wastes the audience it does not fit.
Training at joining, before access to sensitive systems, then short and frequent reinforcement rather than one long annual event people click through.
Realistic simulated phishing sent on a schedule, used to teach and to measure the report rate, not to punish, and not to generate a “gotcha” statistic for a board slide.
A warning at the moment of risk (an external-sender banner, a large-payment confirmation step) which changes behaviour more reliably than a course remembered months later.
Time to report a simulated phish, proportion of recipients who report, repeat-clicker trend. Completion percentage measures attendance, not risk.

blocks.html:
The reframing of awareness as a risk domain: identify which behaviours cause
loss, measure them, target interventions at the highest-risk groups, and track
the residual. It moves the programme from “everyone did the training” to
“the behaviour that causes incidents is trending down”.

The click rate on a phishing simulation is the number every board asks for and the weakest one to lead with. It moves with email difficulty, time of day and seasonal workload, and a low rate can simply mean the lure was obvious.

The stronger measure is the report rate and the time to first report. An organisation where 60% of recipients report a phish within ten minutes can absorb the 5% who clicked, because the incident response team gets its warning early. One where nobody reports is exposed regardless of the click rate, because the first sign of trouble will be the breach itself.

Annual-course thinking. One 45-minute module, once a year, completion tracked to 100%, no measurement of whether anything changed. It is the format auditors have learned to look past.

Phishing as punishment. Clickers are named to their managers or assigned extra training as a penalty. Reporting drops immediately, because owning up now has a cost.

No role targeting. The finance team, who are the actual target of invoice fraud, get the same generic content as everyone else and nothing about the scenario that will be used against them.

Blame culture. The policy says “report immediately”, and the last person who did was disciplined. The next person will not.

items.q: What is security awareness training?
items.html: A programme that teaches staff to recognise and respond to security risks in their actual work (phishing, social engineering, data handling, physical security) and to report suspected incidents quickly. It is a required control under ISO 27001, NIST and most regulations, and is intended to change behaviour, not just record attendance.

items.q: What is the difference between security awareness and security culture?
items.html: Awareness is whether people know the rules. Culture is whether the environment makes following them, and admitting mistakes, the natural choice. A programme can raise awareness while a blame culture suppresses the reporting that makes awareness useful.

items.q: What is the best metric for a security awareness programme?
items.html: The rate and speed at which staff report suspicious messages, not the click rate on phishing simulations. A high report rate gives the incident team early warning; the click rate is noisy and easily gamed by making the simulation obvious. Completion percentage measures attendance only.

items.q: Should phishing simulation results be used to discipline staff?
items.html: No. Using them punitively causes people to stop reporting, which removes the programme’s main benefit. Simulations should be framed as practice, with repeat-clicker patterns handled as a coaching and targeting problem rather than a disciplinary one.

entries.title: Data loss prevention
entries.description: DLP is the set of controls that detects and blocks sensitive data leaving approved channels. Why it depends on classification and generates false positives.
keywords: data loss prevention vs data leakage prevention

quick_facts.acts on: Data in use, in motion, at rest

sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 8.12 (Data leakage prevention)
NIST SP 800-53r5, controls SC-7, SC-28, AC-4
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Articles 5(1)(f) and 32

sections.text: The three states, and where controls sit

blocks.html: Data loss prevention is the set of controls that detects, and where configured blocks, sensitive data moving out of approved channels: a customer list attached to a personal webmail, source code pushed to a public repository, a card number pasted into a chat tool.

DLP only works on data it can recognise, which is why it is downstream of classification. A tool told to watch for “confidential” material has to be given a definition it can match: a regex for account numbers, a fingerprint of a document set, an exact-match list of customer records. The quality of that definition, not the product, decides whether the control catches real leaks or drowns the team in noise.

It also cannot tell intent from accident. The same alert fires whether an employee is stealing a database on their last day or a salesperson is emailing a contract to the client who asked for it. Every DLP programme is therefore a tuning programme: the initial deployment is the easy 20%, and classifying data and cutting false positives is the rest.

blocks.text: The three states, and where controls sit

items.html: On the endpoint: copy to USB, print, screen capture, paste into an unmanaged application. Endpoint DLP agents enforce here and are the only place some channels can be seen at all.
Leaving the network: email, web upload, API. Network and email DLP inspect this traffic; encryption to destinations the inspection point cannot see is the standing blind spot.
Sitting in a store: a shared drive, a SaaS tenancy, an object bucket. Discovery scans find sensitive data in the wrong place so it can be moved or removed before it leaks.

blocks.html:
The scheme that labels data by sensitivity (public, internal, confidential,
restricted) and the rules attached to each label. DLP enforces those rules;
without the scheme it has nothing to enforce and defaults to blunt pattern
matching.

Almost every failed rollout is one that switched to blocking on day one. Legitimate business workflows move sensitive data constantly, and a blocking rule tuned on assumptions rather than observed traffic stops deals, invoices and support cases within hours. The programme is then switched off under pressure and the control is lost entirely.

The workable sequence is: deploy in monitor-only mode, watch real traffic for weeks, build an allowlist of the legitimate flows the alerts reveal, and only then enable blocking on the narrow set of cases that are unambiguous: restricted data to personal webmail, card data to file-sharing sites. Widen from there as confidence grows.

Blocking from the start. Rules go live in enforcement mode, break routine work, and the business demands the tool be disabled.

No classification behind it. The tool matches generic patterns only, so it misses the sensitive document that contains no account numbers and flags every email that mentions a price.

Alerts with no triage owner. Thousands of low-quality alerts, nobody assigned to work them, and the real exfiltration is somewhere in the queue that nobody reads.

Unmanaged channels. Endpoint agents on laptops only, so data walks out through a personal phone, a screenshot or a channel the inspection point cannot decrypt.

items.q: What is data loss prevention?
items.html: A category of security control that identifies sensitive data and monitors or prevents it leaving authorised locations and channels. DLP operates on data in use (endpoints), in motion (network and email) and at rest (stored repositories), and depends on a data classification scheme to know what to protect.

items.q: What is the difference between endpoint DLP and network DLP?
items.html: Endpoint DLP runs as an agent on user devices and can see local actions (copying to USB, printing, pasting into applications) that never touch the network. Network DLP inspects traffic leaving the organisation, mainly email and web uploads. Comprehensive programmes use both, because each covers channels the other cannot.

items.q: Why does DLP generate so many false positives?
items.html: Because it matches patterns and cannot judge intent or context. A rule that catches account numbers also catches every legitimate email that contains one. Reducing false positives requires accurate data classification and weeks of tuning against real traffic, which is the bulk of the effort in any DLP programme.

items.q: Should DLP be set to block or just alert?
items.html: Start in alert-only mode to learn the legitimate data flows, then enable blocking narrowly for the cases that are never acceptable, such as restricted data sent to personal email. Switching straight to blocking usually breaks business processes and gets the tool disabled.
