acceptedAnswer.text: Start in alert-only mode to learn the legitimate data flows, then enable blocking narrowly for the cases that are never acceptable, such as restricted data sent to personal email. Switching straight to blocking usually breaks business processes and gets the tool disabled.

entries.title: Incident response
entries.description: Incident response is the prepared process for detecting, containing and recovering from a security incident, then learning from it. The six phases.
sources: NIST SP 800-61r2 - Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (r3 draft, 2025)
ISO/IEC 27035-1:2023 - Information security incident management, principles
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A controls 5.24-5.28
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 33

blocks.html: Incident response is the prepared process for detecting a security incident, containing it, recovering normal operation and learning from it, written, rehearsed and resourced before anything happens, because an incident is the worst time to design the response.

The distinction from ordinary operations is that an incident has a confirmed or strongly suspected breach of confidentiality, integrity or availability, and a clock. Regulators attach deadlines (72 hours to notify a data-protection authority under GDPR, tighter still under DORA and the SEC rules), and those clocks start at detection, not at the point the organisation feels ready to talk. A response that is being invented while the clock runs will miss them.

Incident response also has an evidence obligation the rest of security does not. Actions taken during containment can destroy the forensic record of how the attacker got in, and can prejudice a later legal or insurance claim. The plan has to say when to preserve and when to prioritise recovery, and who decides.
NIST SP 800-61 gives the model almost every plan follows.

items.html: The plan, the playbooks, the contact tree, the retainer with a forensics firm, the logging that will actually be needed, and the exercises that prove all of it works. Everything expensive happens here, before the incident.
Recognising that an event is an incident, from monitoring, a user report or a third party, and establishing scope: which systems, which data, how far in.

Stopping the spread. Short-term isolation first (disconnect, disable, block), then a longer-term hold while eradication is planned. The point to decide whether to preserve evidence or move straight to recovery.
Removing the cause (the foothold, the malicious account, the vulnerability that was used) so the same route cannot be taken again immediately.
Restoring systems to normal, from known-good backups where needed, with heightened monitoring to catch a return.
A blameless account of what happened, what worked, what did not, and the specific changes now owned by named people with dates. The phase skipped most often and the one that pays back.

blocks.html:
A step-by-step procedure for one incident type: ransomware, business email
compromise, a lost laptop, a public data exposure. The plan is the framework
that applies to everything; the playbook is what the responder actually follows
at 3am for this scenario.

Every plan needs a severity scale defined in advance (typically SEV1 to SEV3 or similar) keyed to concrete criteria: data categories involved, systems affected, regulatory exposure, whether the incident is ongoing. The scale drives who is woken, whether legal and communications are engaged, and whether the board is told. Deciding severity during the incident, with no scale, produces either panic escalation of everything or a serious breach handled by one tired analyst.

A plan never exercised. A document exists, approved and filed, and the first time anyone reads it properly is during a live incident. The contact numbers are stale, the roles are unclear and the forensics retainer was never signed.

Containment that destroys evidence. Machines are wiped and rebuilt for speed, and with them goes the only record of how the attacker got in: the same route is used again, and the insurance claim is weakened.

No lessons-learned discipline. The incident is closed, everyone is exhausted, the review is skipped or produces vague actions with no owner. The next incident is the same incident.

Regulatory clock missed. Nobody owned the notification assessment, so the 72-hour window under GDPR passed while the technical team was still working the containment.

items.q: What are the phases of incident response?
items.html: The NIST model has six: preparation; detection and analysis; containment; eradication; recovery; and post-incident review (lessons learned). Some frameworks compress eradication and recovery into one, giving a four-phase version, but the sequence and intent are the same.

items.q: What is the difference between an incident response plan and a playbook?
items.html: The plan is the overall framework (roles, severity scale, escalation, legal and regulatory obligations) that applies to any incident. A playbook is a specific procedure for one scenario, such as ransomware or business email compromise, that a responder follows step by step. An organisation needs one plan and several playbooks.

items.q: How quickly must a data breach be reported?
items.html: It depends on the regime. Under the EU GDPR, a personal-data breach must be notified to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of the organisation becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to result in risk to individuals. Other regimes (DORA, the SEC cyber rules, sector regulators, contracts) impose their own, often shorter, clocks.

items.q: What is a post-incident review?
items.html: A structured, blameless examination held after the incident is closed, covering the timeline, what helped and hindered the response, the root cause, and a set of specific improvements each assigned to an owner and a date. It is what turns an incident into a reduction in future risk rather than just a bad week.

entries.title: Penetration testing
entries.description: A penetration test is an authorised, scoped attempt to exploit weaknesses in a system to prove real impact. How it differs from a vulnerability scan.
keywords: black box vs white box pentest

quick_facts.needs: A signed scope and rules of engagement

sources: NIST SP 800-115 - Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
PCI DSS v4.0.1, Requirement 11.4 (penetration testing)
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A control 8.8 (management of technical vulnerabilities)
PTES - Penetration Testing Execution Standard

blocks.html: A penetration test is an authorised, time-boxed, scoped attempt to exploit weaknesses in a system the way a real attacker would, chaining findings together to reach a defined objective and demonstrate concrete impact, not just list what is theoretically wrong.

The word most people get wrong is exploit. A vulnerability scan reports that a door looks unlocked. A penetration test opens it, walks through, and shows what is in the room. That difference (proven impact versus flagged presence) is why a framework such as PCI DSS mandates a real test annually and does not accept a scan in its place.

A penetration test is a point-in-time assurance activity, not a security programme. It tells you what an attacker could have done to that scope, on that date, with that much time. It does not keep the system secure between tests; vulnerability management does that.

rows.a: Yes, several low issues into one critical path
Low, findings are verified by exploitation
Narrative of attack paths, rated by real impact

blocks.html:
A broader, objective-based engagement testing detection and response as well as
prevention, usually without the defenders knowing, over weeks rather than days.
A penetration test asks “can this be broken into”; a red team asks “would we
notice, and could we stop it”.

The test is only as useful as its scope, and the scope is a governance artefact, not a technical detail.

  • Targets: the exact systems, applications, IP ranges and accounts in and out of bounds. A test scoped to one application will not find the flat network behind it: that has to be a deliberate choice, recorded.
  • Knowledge level: black box (the tester starts blind), grey box (given low-privilege credentials and some documentation) or white box (full access to source and design). Grey box usually returns the most findings per day of effort, because the tester does not spend the budget on reconnaissance.
  • Rules of engagement: permitted hours, techniques excluded (denial of service, social engineering, physical), the emergency contact, and explicit written authorisation from someone who owns the systems. Testing without that authorisation is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions.
  • Handling of live data and third parties: cloud providers and SaaS vendors often require advance notice or forbid testing of shared infrastructure entirely.

The finding count is not the headline. What matters is the attack narrative: the path from external position to the objective, and the one or two links in that chain that, if broken, would have stopped it. A report with thirty low-severity findings and no viable path is a better result than one with three lows that chain into domain admin.

Then the retest. Findings are remediated, the tester re-checks the specific issues, and a retest report records what closed and what did not. A penetration test with no retest leaves the assurance question half-answered.

Scoped to nothing. The scope is narrowed until the test cannot find anything serious, then the clean report is shown to customers as proof of security.

Scan sold as a test. An automated scan with light manual validation is delivered as a “penetration test” at test prices. PCI assessors and mature customers can tell the difference from the report.

No remediation or retest. The report is filed, the findings are not tracked in the risk register, and the same issues appear in next year’s test.

Point-in-time treated as continuous. The annual test passes and the organisation assumes it is secure for twelve months, with no vulnerability management running in between.

items.q: What is the difference between a penetration test and a vulnerability scan?
items.html: A vulnerability scan is an automated check that lists known weaknesses. A penetration test is a mostly manual engagement where a tester actively exploits weaknesses, chains them together and demonstrates real impact against a defined objective. Scans run continuously and produce a list; tests run periodically and produce an attack narrative.

items.q: How often should penetration testing be done?
items.html: At least annually, and after any significant change to the environment: a new application, a major architecture change, a migration. Regulated regimes are specific: PCI DSS requires external and internal testing at least annually and after significant change. High-risk or fast-changing systems may warrant more frequent testing.

items.q: What is the difference between black box, grey box and white box testing?
items.html: They describe how much the tester is told. Black box: no prior knowledge, closest to an external attacker but slow. White box: full access to source, configuration and design, most thorough per unit of time. Grey box: limited credentials and some documentation, and usually the most cost-effective for application testing.

items.q: Is a penetration test the same as a red team exercise?
items.html: No. A penetration test aims to find and prove exploitable weaknesses in a defined scope, usually openly and over days. A red team exercise is objective-driven, covert, runs over weeks, and tests whether the security team detects and responds as well as whether the controls hold.

entries.title: How to read a framework
entries.description: Four kinds of document get called a framework, and they answer different questions. Which one you are holding determines what you can do with the output.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information security management systems, requirements
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, 2024
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100)
COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

sections.text: The two questions that sort them
What overlaps and what does not

blocks.html:
Four different kinds of document are called frameworks, and they are not
alternatives. Which kind you are holding decides what its output is worth to
whoever asked for it.
The question “which framework should we do” is nearly always answered by who is asking and what they will accept, not by the merits of the documents.

items.html: Specifies requirements a management system must meet. An accredited body audits against it and issues a certificate. ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 9001, ISO 22301.
Criteria a practitioner tests your described controls against, producing a report rather than a certificate. SOC 2 against the Trust Services Criteria.
A vocabulary and structure for describing where you are. Not a bar to clear, and nothing certifies against it. NIST CSF 2.0, with its six functions.
A model of how control and risk should reach a governing body. Used to design a programme, not to test one. COSO ERM, the IIA’s Three Lines Model.

blocks.text: The two questions that sort them

blocks.html:
What does it produce? A certificate travels and can be published. A report is read, usually under NDA, and says considerably more. A profile or a maturity score says where you are and binds you to nothing. A model produces a design.

Who audits it? An accredited certification body, a licensed practitioner, yourself, or nobody. This is what determines whether the output means anything to a third party: a self-assessed anything is worth exactly the trust already placed in you.

Three things to find before anything else.

The scope clause. Every certifiable standard has one, and it is where the real negotiation happens. A certificate covering one product line is not a certificate covering the company, and the scope statement is printed on it.

The shall/should boundary. In a standard, “shall” is a requirement and “should” is a recommendation. Auditors test the first and ask about the second. Reading a standard without noticing which is which produces a programme that gold-plates recommendations and misses requirements.

The annex’s status. ISO 27001’s Annex A is a reference control set you justify including or excluding, not a checklist you complete. Treating it as mandatory is the single most expensive misreading in the discipline.

The oversight of the certification bodies themselves, by a national
accreditation body. An unaccredited certificate is a document a company bought.

blocks.text: What overlaps and what does not

blocks.html:
The controls overlap heavily: access, change, vulnerabilities, incidents, vendors, backups. The shells do not: ISO wants a management system with internal audit and management review; SOC 2 wants a system description and the auditor’s own testing; NIST CSF wants neither and gives you a profile.

Budget for one control programme and as many reporting shells as you have buyers. See 5.2 for the artefact that makes that affordable.

entries.title: ISO 27001 vs SOC 2
entries.description: ISO 27001 certifies a management system and produces a certificate. SOC 2 is an attestation over control operation and produces a report. Which one your buyer is actually asking for.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information security management systems, requirements
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100), 2017, revised 2022
AICPA, SSAE No. 18, AT-C section 205

sections.text: The overlap, and why it pays

blocks.html:
ISO/IEC 27001 certifies that a management system exists and works, and produces
a certificate. SOC 2 attests that specific controls operated over a period, and
produces a report someone reads. They answer different questions for different
buyers.
The question “which should we do first” is nearly always settled by who is asking for it, not by the merits of either standard.

sides.name: ISO/IEC 27001
sides.html:
An accredited body audits your ISMS against the standard and issues a
certificate you can publish. Annex A supplies a reference control set you
justify including or excluding.

sides.name: SOC 2
sides.html:
A licensed CPA firm tests the controls you describe against the Trust Services
Criteria and writes a report, usually shared under NDA. No fixed control list -
you describe your own, then prove them.

rows.b: Type I point in time; Type II a period

blocks.html: The fixed-control-list row is the structural difference and the one that surprises people. ISO 27001 hands you a reference set of controls in Annex A and asks you to justify inclusions and exclusions in a Statement of Applicability. SOC 2 hands you criteria and asks you to describe the controls you have chosen to meet them. One is a checklist you argue with; the other is an essay you must then prove.

The document recording which Annex A controls apply, which do not, and the
justification for each decision. Required by ISO/IEC 27001 clause 6.1.3 d).

A distinction only SOC 2 has, and the one most often got wrong in sales conversations.

Type I says the controls were suitably designed at a point in time. It is a snapshot, achievable quickly, and a sophisticated buyer will note that it proves nothing about operation.

Type II says the controls operated effectively across a period, commonly three to twelve months. This is what enterprise procurement means when it says “SOC 2”. A first Type II usually covers a shorter window, then extends to twelve months on the next cycle.

blocks.text: The overlap, and why it pays

blocks.html:
The control sets overlap substantially. Access review, change management, vulnerability management, incident response, vendor management and backup do work for both, with the same evidence.

What does not transfer is the shell around them. ISO 27001 requires management system machinery (scope, policy, risk assessment methodology, internal audit, management review, corrective action) that SOC 2 has no equivalent of. SOC 2 requires a system description and a control matrix in a specific form, plus an auditor’s own testing, which ISO does not.

Budget for one control programme and two reporting shells. Organisations that budget for two programmes spend roughly twice what they need to and produce two inconsistent control inventories, which is worse than the cost.

If your buyers are North American technology companies, they will ask for SOC 2 and many will not recognise an ISO certificate. If they are European, or enterprise procurement anywhere, they will ask for ISO 27001. If they are both, do the control work once and sequence the reporting: SOC 2 Type I first for speed, ISO 27001 next for reach, SOC 2 Type II on the following cycle.

entries.title: Building a control crosswalk
entries.description: A crosswalk maps one framework's requirements onto another through your own controls. How to build one that survives a revision, and why mapping framework-to-framework directly is the wrong shape.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A
AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100)
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, informative references, 2024

sections.text: Hub and spoke, not point to point
What a revision does to it

blocks.html:
A crosswalk lets one control answer several frameworks at once. Built correctly
it is the reason a second certification costs a fraction of the first; built
incorrectly it is a spreadsheet that has to be thrown away at the next revision.
The critical decision is the shape. Almost every published crosswalk maps framework A directly to framework B, and almost every useful internal one maps both through your own control inventory.

blocks.text: Hub and spoke, not point to point

blocks.html:
Direct mapping produces one artefact per pair. Three frameworks means three mappings; four means six. Each is maintained separately and they drift.

Mapping through your controls means one artefact. Each control lists the requirements it satisfies across every framework you carry. Adding a fourth framework adds one column, not three documents.
The last row is where the confusion comes from. Vendors publish framework-to-framework crosswalks because they are marketable. They are a useful starting reference and a poor operating artefact.

Take the control inventory from 4.1. For each framework, walk its requirements and record against each control the requirements it satisfies. Three outputs, as always: mapped, unmapped requirements, and controls nothing requires.

Two rules keep it honest. A mapping is a claim that this control, as written, satisfies that requirement. If it only partly does, record it as partial and name the gap, because a partial mapping recorded as full is exactly what fieldwork finds. And every mapping cites the requirement identifier, not its paraphrase, so a revision can be diffed.

blocks.text: What a revision does to it

blocks.html:
ISO 27001 moved from 114 Annex A controls in 2013 to 93 in 2022, restructured into four themes. Organisations with a hub-and-spoke crosswalk re-mapped one column. Organisations with three pairwise mappings rebuilt all of them.

Assume a revision every three to five years per framework and build for it.

A control that satisfies part of a requirement, recorded with what it does not
cover. The honest form, and the one that stops a gap being discovered during
fieldwork.

For a company adding SOC 2 to an existing ISO 27001 programme, the control work is largely done and the crosswalk shows exactly which parts. What remains is the system description, the auditor’s testing, and the handful of criteria ISO does not reach.

The saving is not the certificate. It is that the second audit examines a programme that already runs, rather than a programme assembled to be examined.

entries.title: The statement of applicability
entries.description: The SoA records which ISO 27001 Annex A controls apply, which do not, and why - a decision record, not an inventory. Required by clause 6.1.3 d).
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, clause 6.1.3 d)
ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A
ISO/IEC 27002:2022 - Information security controls

sections.text: How it relates to your other artefacts

blocks.html:
The statement of applicability records which Annex A controls apply to your
ISMS, which do not, and the justification for each decision. ISO/IEC 27001
clause 6.1.3 d) requires it, and the auditor reads it before anything else.

It is a decision record, not a control inventory. That distinction is where most first attempts go wrong: a document listing 93 controls with “implemented” beside each says nothing about why any of them applies to you.

items.html: The Annex A identifier, from the 2022 revision’s 93 controls across four themes: organisational, people, physical, technological.
Yes or no. Not “partially”: a control either applies to your scope or it does not.
Why. For an inclusion this is usually the risk it treats or the obligation it meets; for an exclusion it is why the scope does not reach it.
Whether it is in place, and where the detail lives, a pointer to your own control inventory rather than a description.

blocks.html: The justification column is the one that gets skimmed and the one that is read hardest. “Applicable, best practice” is not a justification. “Applicable, treats R-014, remote access to production” is.

Excluding a control is legitimate and expected. A company with no physical premises excludes several physical controls; a company that writes no software excludes secure development controls.

What is not legitimate is excluding a control because it is inconvenient. The justification is tested, and the obvious tell is an exclusion that contradicts the scope statement: no development controls, in a scope covering a product the company builds.

Where an exclusion is genuine, the phrasing that survives is the one that ties back to scope rather than to circumstance: not “we do not currently do this”, but “this activity is outside the ISMS scope defined in clause 4.3”.

blocks.text: How it relates to your other artefacts

blocks.html:
The SoA is the bridge between the risk assessment and the control inventory. The risk assessment says what needs treating; the SoA says which Annex A controls are in play as a result; the inventory says what you actually do and who owns it.

Keeping them as three artefacts is correct. Merging the SoA into the inventory produces a document that is neither a decision record nor an operating list, and which has to be untangled at the next audit.

The boundary of the management system, stated under clause 4.3. Everything in
the SoA is a decision made relative to it, which is why an exclusion that
contradicts scope fails immediately.

Review it whenever the scope changes, whenever the risk assessment produces a new treatment, and at the annual management review. A SoA carrying last year’s scope is the most common documentation finding in surveillance audits, and it is entirely avoidable.

entries.title: The Trust Services Criteria
entries.description: The AICPA control criteria a SOC 2 report is tested against, in five categories. Only Security is mandatory; the other four are chosen by relevance.
sources: AICPA, Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100), 2017, revised 2022
AICPA, Description Criteria (DC section 200)
COSO, Internal Control - Integrated Framework, 2013

sections.text: Two sets of criteria, two jobs

blocks.html: The Trust Services Criteria are the AICPA control criteria a SOC 2 examination is measured against, grouped into five categories (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality and Privacy), of which only Security is mandatory. The other four are included when they are relevant to the service.

Which categories a report covers is a scoping decision, not a fixed list, and it is one of the biggest levers on what a SOC 2 costs and how long it takes. A report can be scoped to Security alone and be a complete, valid SOC 2 report. Adding a category adds criteria, adds the controls that meet them and adds the evidence an auditor must test.

Before the 2017 revision these were called the trust services principles; the criteria themselves are published by the AICPA as TSP section 100.

Category Mandatory? What it covers
Security Yes, the common criteria Systems and information are protected against unauthorised access, unauthorised disclosure and damage. Present in every SOC 2 report.
Availability Optional The system is available for operation and use as committed or agreed.
Processing Integrity Optional System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely and authorised.
Confidentiality Optional Information designated as confidential is protected as committed.
Privacy Optional Personal information is collected, used, retained, disclosed and disposed of in line with the entity’s own privacy notice.

Security is the only category that must be in scope, and it is met by the common criteria, the CC series, which every SOC 2 report includes. The other four are selected by relevance to the service and to the commitments the entity has actually made to its customers. Most reports are Security only, or Security with Availability and often Confidentiality. Adding Privacy is often the largest single increase in scope, because it brings in a whole additional body of criteria about personal information.

A common misconception is that a SOC 2 report covers all five categories. It does not. Only Security is mandatory; a category appears only when the entity chooses it, and a report scoped to Security alone is not a lesser or partial SOC 2. Note also that Confidentiality and Privacy are different jobs: Confidentiality protects any information the entity has agreed to treat as confidential, whatever its subject; Privacy is specifically about personal information and the entity’s handling of it.

The common criteria are called common because they apply to every engagement regardless of which categories are in scope, and because they constitute the whole of the Security category on their own. In the 2017 criteria, revised 2022, they run from CC1 to CC9.

The first five families, CC1 to CC5, are built directly on the five components of the 2013 COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework: the control environment (CC1), communication and information (CC2), risk assessment (CC3), monitoring activities (CC4) and control activities (CC5). CC6 to CC9 are additional criteria the AICPA layered on for information security specifically: logical and physical access controls (CC6); system operations (CC7); change management (CC8) and risk mitigation (CC9).

Each optional category then adds a short supplemental series on top of the common criteria, rather than replacing anything.

items.html: A single supplemental series covering capacity, environmental protections and backup, recovery and incident handling that keep the system available as committed.

Criteria that inputs, processing and outputs are complete, valid, accurate, timely and authorised. Most relevant where the completeness or accuracy of processing is itself part of the service commitment.
Criteria that information the entity has agreed to treat as confidential is protected through its lifecycle and disposed of when no longer needed.

Eight supplemental groupings: notice and communication; choice and consent; collection; use, retention and disposal; access; disclosure and notification; quality; and monitoring and enforcement. Controls are evaluated against these criteria in light of the entity’s privacy commitments and notice, not as a legal-compliance opinion on any privacy law.

blocks.text: Two sets of criteria, two jobs

blocks.html: The Trust Services Criteria are not the only criteria a SOC 2 report is written against, and confusing them with the other set is a genuine misreading. The Trust Services Criteria are what the controls are evaluated against: whether the controls that meet Security and any other category in scope are suitably designed and, in a Type 2 report, operating effectively. The description criteria (DC section 200) govern something different: whether the system description management writes is presented fairly. One measures the controls; the other measures the account of the system those controls sit in. They are separate documents doing separate jobs.

The criteria (DC section 200) for fair presentation of the system description in a SOC 2 report: its boundaries, the services in scope and the controls in place. The system description is assessed against these, while the controls are assessed against the Trust Services Criteria; the management assertion addresses both.

Category selection is the main lever on scope and cost, so choose by two things: what the entity genuinely commits to in its customer contracts and what its buyers are actually asking for. If customers ask for uptime commitments, Availability earns its place. If the service holds confidential customer data under contract, Confidentiality does. If a report is being read alongside an ISO 27001 certificate, the sensible sequence is to scope the categories the buyer names rather than every category available.

Privacy is the category most often added for the wrong reason. It signals maturity, so it gets bolted on, but it demands a real privacy programme measured against a published notice, and an auditor who finds no such programme will report the gap. Over-scoping does not strengthen a report; it enlarges the surface on which it can fall short.

“SOC 2 covers all five categories.” It does not. Only Security is mandatory, and the other four appear only when the entity selects them. A report scoped to Security, or to Security and Availability, is a complete SOC 2 report. Reading the absence of Privacy or Processing Integrity as a deficiency is a mistake buyers and sellers both make.

Privacy read as a legal-compliance opinion. The Privacy category tests handling of personal information against the entity’s own privacy notice and commitments. It is not an opinion on GDPR, on any national privacy law or on the adequacy of the notice itself. A SOC 2 Privacy report does not certify legal compliance, and it should never be sold or read as if it did.

Bolting on a category with no real programme. Adding Privacy or Processing Integrity to look thorough, without the controls those criteria require, invites a qualified opinion or an exception in the very area meant to impress. Categories are commitments the report then has to prove.

Confusing the two sets of criteria. Judging the system description against the Trust Services Criteria, or the controls against the description criteria, measures each thing against the wrong bar. Controls answer to the Trust Services Criteria; the fairness of the description answers to DC section 200.

items.q: Is Privacy required in a SOC 2 report?
items.html: No. Security is the only mandatory category. Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality and Privacy are each optional and included only when relevant to the service and to the commitments the entity has made. Privacy is a substantial addition, because it brings its own supplemental criteria (P1 to P8) about personal information, so it is added when there is a real privacy programme to report on, not by default.

items.q: Does SOC 2 cover all five Trust Services Criteria?
items.html: Not unless the entity scopes all five in. A SOC 2 report always includes Security, the common criteria present in every report, and then whichever of the other four categories the entity has selected. Most reports are Security only, or Security with Availability and Confidentiality. Treating every SOC 2 as a five-category report misreads what has actually been examined.

items.q: What is the difference between the Trust Services Criteria and the description criteria?
items.html: The Trust Services Criteria (TSP section 100) are what the controls are tested against. The description criteria (DC section 200) are what the system description is tested against for fair presentation. They are different documents doing different jobs in the same report: one governs the controls, the other governs the account of the system the controls operate in.

entries.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
entries.description: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework organises cyber risk into six functions and maps to control sets rather than listing them; it certifies nothing.
sources: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, 2024
NIST, CSF 2.0 Reference Tool / Informative References

sections.text: Profiles turn the framework into a plan

blocks.html: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary, outcome-based structure for organising and communicating a cyber risk-management programme, built around six functions (govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover) rather than a catalogue of controls to implement.

Version 2.0, published in 2024, made two changes worth knowing before anything else. It widened the stated audience from critical-infrastructure operators to organisations of every size and sector, and it added GOVERN as a sixth function that wraps the other five. The framework certifies nothing: its value is a common structure for a programme and a shared vocabulary for reporting cyber risk to leadership, and through GOVERN it ties that risk to enterprise governance (2.0).
The Core organises everything the framework covers into six functions. Five are operational; GOVERN sits around them and sets the terms they operate under.

items.html: Sets and monitors the organisation’s cybersecurity strategy, expectations and policy. Added in version 2.0 and positioned around the other five.
Establishes a current understanding of assets, suppliers and the risks that bear on them.
Puts safeguards in place to keep those risks from being realised.
Finds and analyses possible attacks and compromises.
Acts on a detected incident to contain and mitigate it.
Restores the assets and operations an incident has affected.

blocks.html:
The Core is a three-level hierarchy (functions divide into categories, and categories into subcategories), and the subcategories are outcomes, not controls. A subcategory states a result to achieve, such as “identities and credentials are managed”, and says nothing about the mechanism that achieves it.

The mechanism lives elsewhere. NIST and third parties publish Informative References (non-exhaustive mappings from the Core outcomes to control sets such as NIST SP 800-53, ISO/IEC 27001 and the CIS Controls), so the framework points at controls rather than listing them. Treating a subcategory as a control to tick off, rather than selecting controls to achieve it, misreads what the document is. Mapping those references onto your own control inventory is a crosswalk (5.2), and the framework is built to sit at one end of one.

The framework defines four tiers describing how rigorous an organisation’s cyber risk governance and management are. They are not maturity levels, and tier 4 is not a target every organisation should reach: you choose the tier that fits the risk you carry and the resources you have. The construct they are most often confused with is control maturity (5.9), which rates how well a given control is embedded rather than how an organisation governs risk overall.

Tier Name Character of risk governance
1 Partial Risk managed ad hoc and reactively, with little organisation-wide awareness.
2 Risk Informed Risk practices approved by management but not established organisation-wide.
3 Repeatable Practices set formally as policy and updated as risk and business change.
4 Adaptive Practices adapt continuously from lessons learnt and predictive indicators.

Four descriptions (partial, risk informed, repeatable and adaptive) of the rigour of an organisation’s cyber risk governance. Deliberately not maturity levels, and no single tier is the right answer for everyone; a small firm may sit at tier 2 by design.

blocks.text: Profiles turn the framework into a plan

blocks.html:
A profile records how the functions, categories and subcategories apply to a particular organisation. Two profiles do the real work: a Current Profile describing the outcomes you achieve today, and a Target Profile describing the outcomes you intend to achieve. The gap between them is the input to an action plan: what to close, in what order and at what cost.

These are Organisational Profiles, specific to one organisation. A Community Profile is a shared baseline built for a sector or a common use case: a starting Target Profile that organisations facing the same risk can adopt rather than draft from scratch.

Read as a maturity ladder. Teams treat the tiers as levels to climb and set tier 4 as the goal. The tiers describe how rigorous risk governance is, not how advanced an organisation is, and choosing a lower tier deliberately is a legitimate outcome of a risk decision.

Mistaken for a control catalogue. Because subcategories read like requirements, they get implemented directly and the Informative References go unread. The subcategory names the outcome; the control that delivers it is chosen separately (often via the Informative References into 800-53, ISO/IEC 27001 or the CIS Controls), and skipping that choice leaves a programme with outcomes stated but no controls behind them.

A Current Profile with no target. A profile of today, drawn up and never paired with a Target Profile, produces a description and no plan. The gap between current and target is the whole mechanism; on its own a Current Profile documents posture but sets no direction.

Chasing a certificate. Procurement asks for “CSF certification” and a supplier offers one. Neither exists. What exists is a self-assessment against the framework, or a third-party assessment of it, and calling either a certification misrepresents what has been done.

items.q: Is the NIST Cybersecurity Framework mandatory?
items.html: No. It is voluntary. It was written first for critical-infrastructure operators and, from version 2.0, for organisations of any size and sector, but it imposes no obligation on the private sector by itself. A regulator, a contract or a board can require a particular organisation to use it, in which case the requirement comes from that instrument and not from the framework.

items.q: Can you get NIST CSF certified?
items.html: No. There is no CSF certification and no certificate to hold up. You can assess yourself against the framework, or have a third party assess you, and you can record your Current and Target Profiles, but none of that is an accredited certification in the sense that ISO/IEC 27001 is. A supplier claiming to be “CSF certified” is describing an assessment, not a certificate.

items.q: What changed in NIST CSF 2.0?
items.html: Two things stand out. GOVERN was added as a sixth function, wrapping the other five and tying cyber risk to the organisation’s wider risk management and governance. And the scope widened from critical infrastructure to organisations of every size and sector. The 2024 revision also expanded the supporting resources, including the online Reference Tool that publishes the Informative References.

entries.title: The two COSO frameworks
entries.description: COSO publishes two frameworks, not one: the 2013 Internal Control model behind SOX and SOC 2, and a broader 2017 enterprise risk framework.
keywords: COSO internal control vs enterprise risk management
which COSO framework does SOC 2 use
sources: COSO, Internal Control - Integrated Framework, 2013
COSO, Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance, 2017

blocks.html: A COSO framework is one of two distinct reference models published by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. The two are the Internal Control - Integrated Framework (2013) and Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017), routinely confused as though they were a single document.

Because both carry the COSO name, a requirement, a contract clause or an audit request that cites “the COSO framework” without a year is ambiguous: the two answer different questions for different audiences. Neither is certifiable. Both are reference models an organisation adopts and assesses itself against, not a bar an accredited body signs off.
Both are built from five components, which is part of why they are mixed up. The components are different sets doing different work.

items.html: The model management uses to assess internal control. Five components (control environment; risk assessment; control activities; information and communication; and monitoring activities) sit above 17 principles. It underpins internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) for SOX section 404, and its five components are what the SOC 2 Common Criteria (CC1-CC5) are organised around.

items.term: Enterprise Risk Management - Integrating with Strategy and Performance (2017)
items.html: The model for governing risk across the enterprise. Five components (governance and culture; strategy and objective-setting; performance; review and revision; and information, communication and reporting) sit above 20 principles. It is broader than internal control, tying risk-taking to strategy and performance rather than to the soundness of a control set.

blocks.html:
The two are often set side by side, so the distinction is worth stating plainly.

Dimension Internal Control - Integrated Framework (2013) Enterprise Risk Management (2017)
Purpose Whether internal control, especially over financial reporting, is designed and operating soundly How the whole enterprise takes and manages risk against its strategy and objectives
Structure Five components, 17 principles Five components, 20 principles
Typical use SOX section 404, external financial audit, SOC 2 Common Criteria Board risk oversight, risk appetite, strategy-linked risk

The one-line test is what each answers. The 2013 framework answers whether internal control is sound; the 2017 framework answers how the enterprise takes risk against its strategy. Internal control is a component of good risk management, not the whole of it, which is why ERM is the wider model and ICIF the narrower discipline it partly contains.

A published reference framework an organisation adopts to structure and assess its own control or risk, rather than a standard an accredited body certifies it against. COSO’s Internal Control - Integrated Framework serves internal control; COSO ERM serves enterprise risk. Neither certifies an organisation.

Which framework is in play is settled by the audience, not by preference.

Financial reporting and control attestation. SOX section 404 requires management to assess ICFR against a recognised control framework, and does not name COSO. In practice COSO’s Internal Control - Integrated Framework is the near-universal choice among US issuers, to the point that “COSO” in a SOX context almost always means the 2013 internal control model. The SOC 2 Common Criteria (CC1-CC5) align to its five components, so a SOC 2 examination rests on ICIF whether or not the report says so.

Board-level risk governance. Risk appetite, strategy-linked risk and board-level oversight (the province of governance) sit in COSO ERM. It is the United States and COSO-world counterpart to ISO 31000, the international risk-management standard covered under clause 3.0; the two cover overlapping enterprise-risk ground and serve as alternatives or complements depending on governance needs.

Treating “COSO” as one framework. The most common error, and the reason this entry exists. “COSO” names a body that publishes at least two frameworks; a policy, RFP answer or control narrative that cites “the COSO framework” without naming Internal Control (2013) or ERM (2017) has not actually said which model it means.

Reaching for ERM to pass a SOX or SOC 2 audit. ERM is enterprise risk governance, not a control framework for financial reporting. A team that adopts the 2017 model expecting it to satisfy section 404 or the SOC 2 Common Criteria has taken up the wrong document. The SOC 2 Common Criteria (CC1-CC5) are based on the 2013 internal control framework; SOX section 404 requires a recognised internal-control framework, for which the 2013 framework is the near-universal US choice rather than a statutory mandate.

Expecting a certificate. Neither framework is certifiable. There is no accredited COSO certification for an organisation: both are reference models you adopt and assess yourself against, and a vendor badge claiming otherwise is not one.

Citing the superseded ERM. The 2017 model replaced an earlier 2004 version built around eight components and a cube diagram. Training and documentation that still describe eight components, or the cube, are describing the superseded framework rather than the current five-component, 20-principle one.

items.q: What is the difference between COSO and COSO ERM?
items.html: “COSO” is the body, the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission, and it publishes two frameworks. In everyday use “COSO” usually means the Internal Control - Integrated Framework (2013), the internal control model behind SOX section 404 and the SOC 2 Common Criteria. “COSO ERM” means the separate Enterprise Risk Management framework (2017), which governs risk-taking across the enterprise against its strategy. They are different documents answering different questions, so the safe habit is to name the year.

items.q: Is COSO required for SOX compliance?
items.html: SOX section 404 requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting against a recognised control framework, and does not name COSO specifically. In practice COSO’s Internal Control - Integrated Framework is the near-universal choice among US issuers, to the point that “the framework” in a SOX context is almost always the 2013 COSO model. It is a strong default rather than a legal mandate, and it is not something an organisation is certified against.

items.q: Which COSO framework does SOC 2 use?
items.html: The 2013 Internal Control - Integrated Framework. The SOC 2 Common Criteria (CC1-CC5) map to its five components, so a SOC 2 examination rests on COSO ICIF even though the report is issued against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. COSO ERM (2017) is the enterprise risk framework and is not what SOC 2 is built on.

entries.title: NIST SP 800-53
entries.description: NIST SP 800-53 is a catalogue of security and privacy controls, not a framework you certify against. What Revision 5 changed and where it fits.

quick_facts.Mandatory: US federal and applicable contractor systems

sources: NIST, SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations (2020)
NIST, SP 800-37 Rev. 2 - Risk Management Framework

blocks.html: NIST SP 800-53 is the US National Institute of Standards and Technology’s catalogue of security and privacy controls for information systems and organisations, a control set that other processes draw from, not a framework an organisation is certified against.

The current revision is Revision 5, published in September 2020. It is the control content underneath much of US federal security practice: the Risk Management Framework selects from it, FedRAMP builds its cloud authorisation baselines on it and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (5.5) points at it through its Informative References. What 800-53 does not do is tell you which of its controls apply to you, or issue a certificate when you implement them.

800-53 is a menu. Revision 5 organises the controls into 20 control families, each with a two-letter identifier, and every family holds a set of related controls stated as requirements. The document tells you what a control is; it does not tell you which controls to select, in what order to implement them or whether you have implemented them well. Those decisions live in other documents, which is exactly what makes 800-53 a catalogue rather than a framework you work through (5.0).

The families cover the breadth of an information-security programme. A representative sample of the 20:

items.html: Who and what may reach a system, and on what terms.
Generating, protecting and reviewing the records that show what happened.
Establishing and holding a known-good configuration for systems and components.
Preparing for, detecting and handling security incidents.
Identifying and analysing the risk that bears on a system.
Protecting information in transit and the boundaries around it.
Handling personally identifiable information lawfully and openly. Added in Revision 5.
Managing the risk carried in by suppliers and components. Added in Revision 5.

blocks.html: PT and SR are the two families Revision 5 added; the rest carry over from earlier revisions.

A published set of controls an organisation selects and tailors from, rather than a standard an accredited body certifies it against. 800-53 is the large US example; a process such as the Risk Management Framework, or a framework such as the CSF, draws its actual control content from a catalogue like this one.

Three changes matter before anything else. Privacy controls were integrated into the main catalogue: the separate privacy appendix of earlier revisions was retired, so security and privacy controls now sit in one consolidated list rather than sending you to a second appendix. Controls were made outcome-based and consolidated: the phrase “the information system” was removed as the implied actor, so a control now applies to whatever entity (a person, a process or a system) is responsible for the outcome, rather than assuming a machine does the work. And the PT and SR families were added, making privacy transparency and supply-chain risk first-class parts of the catalogue.

The fourth change is structural and the one most often missed. The control baselines (the low, moderate and high starting sets) were moved out of 800-53 in Revision 5 into a companion publication, SP 800-53B. In Revision 5 the baselines are not inside 800-53 at all.

“800-53” is used loosely to mean three different documents, and the distinction is load-bearing.

Document What it is What it gives you
SP 800-53 The control catalogue The controls themselves
SP 800-53A Assessment procedures How to assess whether a control is met
SP 800-53B Control baselines Low, moderate and high starting sets, driven by FIPS 199

Impact level comes from FIPS 199, which categorises a system as low, moderate or high; FIPS 200 sets the minimum security requirements; 800-53B turns that categorisation into a starting baseline of controls. All three sit inside the NIST Risk Management Framework, described in SP 800-37 Revision 2, whose seven steps are prepare, categorise, select, implement, assess, authorise and monitor. 800-53 supplies the menu the select step draws from, 800-53B supplies the starting baseline and 800-53A supplies the procedures the assess step runs.

A baseline is a starting point, not a verdict. Controls are then tailored to context (added, removed or adjusted for the system in front of you), and overlays provide ready-made baselines for a specific community or technology so that tailoring does not start from scratch each time.

800-53 is one of three documents a team reaches for, and they are not interchangeable. Choosing between them starts with what shape of answer you need.

Document Shape Reach for it to
NIST SP 800-53 A large catalogue you select and tailor from Draw the control content an authorisation or programme needs
CIS Controls (5.8) A prioritised shortlist Start from a defensible minimum in priority order
NIST CSF 2.0 (5.5) Outcomes that reference control sets Structure and communicate a programme; it points at 800-53 for the controls

The CSF and 800-53 are complementary rather than rival: the framework names an outcome and 800-53 supplies a control that delivers it. The CIS Controls trade comprehensiveness for a running order, which is the opposite bet from 800-53’s breadth.

Called a certification. There is no 800-53 certificate for an organisation. What exists is an assessment against the controls (for example the assessment behind an authorisation to operate), not an accredited certification. This is the sharp contrast with ISO 27001, which is certifiable; a supplier claiming to be “800-53 certified” is describing an assessment, and often overstating even that.

Assuming every control applies. The catalogue holds far more controls than any one system needs, and treating it as a checklist to satisfy in full misreads it. Baselines and tailoring exist precisely so that most controls do not apply to most systems; the work is selecting and tailoring, not implementing everything.

Confusing 800-53 with 800-53A or 800-53B. Since Revision 5 the baselines live in 800-53B and the assessment procedures in 800-53A. Citing “800-53” for a baseline, or for how to assess a control, sends the reader to the wrong document: the catalogue states the controls but not their baselines and not how to test them.

Treated as mandatory for a private company. 800-53 is mandatory for US federal information systems, and often for federal contractors, through FISMA. It does not reach a private company with no federal nexus, where it is voluntary, widely adopted and referenced through the CSF Informative References and FedRAMP among others, but not required by FISMA.

items.q: Can you get NIST 800-53 certified?
items.html: No. There is no 800-53 certification for an organisation and no certificate to hold up. A system can be assessed against the controls (most visibly as part of an authorisation to operate), but that assessment is not an accredited certification in the way ISO/IEC 27001 is. A vendor describing itself as “800-53 certified” is describing an assessment rather than a certificate.

items.q: Is NIST 800-53 mandatory for my company?
items.html: It depends on whether you touch the US federal government. FISMA makes 800-53 mandatory for federal information systems and frequently for federal contractors handling government data. A private company with no such nexus is under no FISMA obligation to use it; there it is voluntary, though it is widely adopted and referenced by other frameworks and by FedRAMP.

items.q: What is the difference between 800-53, 800-53A and 800-53B?
items.html: 800-53 is the control catalogue itself. 800-53A is the companion that gives the procedures for assessing whether a control is met. 800-53B holds the low, moderate and high control baselines, which moved out of 800-53 in Revision 5. Three documents, three jobs: the controls, how to test them and where to start.

entries.title: CIS Controls
entries.description: The CIS Controls are a prioritised, prescriptive set of 18 controls and 153 safeguards, tiered by Implementation Group and not certifiable.
sources: Center for Internet Security, CIS Critical Security Controls v8 (2021)
CIS, Implementation Groups and the Community Defense Model

sections.text: Implementation Groups: choose a tier by risk
Prescriptive and prioritised, not a catalogue

blocks.html: The CIS Controls are a prioritised, prescriptive set of cyber-defence actions maintained by the Center for Internet Security, a non-profit. Version 8 organises 18 controls into 153 measurable safeguards, ordered so an organisation knows not just what to do but in what order to do it.

Formerly the SANS Top 20 and later the CIS Critical Security Controls, the set has been renamed more than once but keeps the same job: tell a defender which actions cut the most risk first. It is free to adopt and certifies nothing. Where an outcomes framework such as NIST CSF (5.5) states results to achieve and leaves the controls to you, the CIS Controls hand you the actions and the order, which is why they read less like a standard to interpret and more like a roadmap to work through. Read them against how to read a framework (5.0) before adopting.

Version 8, published in 2021, introduced the structure the Controls still use. It cut the count from 20 controls in version 7 to 18 and made the safeguard (not the control) the unit that matters. A control is a theme; a safeguard is one specific, measurable action inside it, and version 8 defines 153 of them.

items.html: A theme or category of defensive activity (18 in version 8) such as inventory of enterprise assets or data protection.
A single, measurable action inside a control. The safeguard, not the control, is what gets an owner and evidence; version 8 holds 153.

blocks.html: The reorganisation in version 8 is the change worth understanding. Earlier versions grouped controls partly by who owned the asset. Version 8 groups them by the activity being performed, so a single control now spans whatever devices, users or cloud services that activity touches, which matches how a modern estate actually runs. A later refresh, version 8.1 (2024), realigned the mappings to NIST CSF 2.0 and sharpened the governance and asset-class framing.

blocks.text: Implementation Groups: choose a tier by risk

blocks.html:
Not every enterprise is expected to implement all 153 safeguards. Implementation Groups (IG1, IG2 and IG3) are a prioritisation overlay that sorts every safeguard into a tier, so an organisation can start with what matters most and add the rest as its risk and resources justify.

The groups are nested. IG1 is a subset of IG2, which is a subset of IG3, and every safeguard is assigned to the lowest group that requires it. IG1 is the foundational baseline (CIS calls it essential cyber hygiene) and holds 56 of the 153 safeguards in version 8.

Group What it is Chosen when
IG1 Essential cyber hygiene; the 56-safeguard baseline every enterprise should meet Always; it is the floor
IG2 IG1 plus safeguards for more sensitive data and more complex operations Regulated or sensitive data is held across departments
IG3 IG2 plus the remaining safeguards The organisation must withstand sophisticated, targeted attacks

The foundational tier of the CIS Controls (56 safeguards CIS calls essential cyber hygiene), meant as the baseline every enterprise should meet. It is chosen by an organisation’s resources and data sensitivity, not climbed towards: IG1 done well is a legitimate end state, not a rung below IG3. Distinct from a maturity level, which rates how well a control is performed rather than which safeguards are in scope.

Which group you target is a risk decision, not a maturity climb. It is set by the organisation’s resources and the sensitivity of the data it holds, not by an ambition to reach IG3. A small business that meets IG1 well has arrived somewhere legitimate, not paused partway up a ladder. Reading IG3 as the destination is the most common way the model is misused, and it is close kin to the mistake of treating control maturity (5.9) as a ladder to level 5.

blocks.text: Prescriptive and prioritised, not a catalogue

blocks.html:
What distinguishes the CIS Controls from most other frameworks is that they tell you what to do and in what order. A large control catalogue such as NIST SP 800-53 (5.7) gives you a superset to select and tailor from; an outcomes framework such as NIST CSF (5.5) states results and leaves the mechanism open. The CIS Controls sit at the prescriptive, prioritised end: the safeguards are the actions, and the Implementation Groups set the priority.

Aspect CIS Controls NIST 800-53 NIST CSF
Form Prioritised action list Control catalogue Outcome statements
Tells you What to do, in what order The full menu to tailor The result to achieve
First move Work IG1 Pick a baseline, then tailor Set target outcomes

Prescriptive does not mean isolated. CIS publishes mappings from the Controls to NIST CSF, NIST 800-53, ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS and others, so the set can act as an implementation-ordered layer that crosswalks to whichever compliance framework you owe. You work the safeguards in priority order, and the mapping shows which obligations each one helps satisfy, a way to sequence hardening while still tracking against the standard you are held to.

Two CIS products are constantly confused. The CIS Controls tell you what to do. The CIS Benchmarks are a separate product: secure-configuration guidance for specific technologies, such as a given operating system, browser or cloud service, down to individual settings. A control might say to configure enterprise assets securely; the matching Benchmark is the setting-by-setting document telling you how to harden a particular version of a particular system. Both come from CIS. They answer different questions, and neither is a substitute for the other.

IGs treated as a maturity ladder. The three groups get read as levels to climb, with IG3 as the goal. They are a prioritisation overlay keyed to risk and resources, not rungs: IG1 met properly is a legitimate end state for many organisations, and reaching for IG3 without the data sensitivity or threat exposure to justify it spends effort where the risk does not warrant it.

Controls confused with Benchmarks. A team hardens its servers to the CIS Benchmarks and reports that it has “done CIS”, or adopts the Controls and assumes its systems are configured. The two are different products answering different questions (what to do versus how to configure one specific system), and neither covers the other’s ground.

IG1 hygiene skipped to chase advanced safeguards. Attention goes to sophisticated IG3 safeguards while basic hygiene in IG1 (asset inventory, account management and patching) is left incomplete. The safeguards are ordered for a reason: the IG1 baseline blocks the most common attacks for the least effort, and building advanced defences on top of an incomplete baseline leaves the front door open behind them.

A certificate expected. Someone asks to see the organisation’s “CIS certification”. There is none. The Controls are free to adopt and not certifiable; you can self-assess, and CIS offers configuration-assessment tooling such as CIS-CAT that scores systems against the Benchmarks, but none of that is an organisational certification of the kind ISO/IEC 27001 provides.

items.q: Do I have to implement all 153 safeguards?
items.html: No. The safeguards are tiered into Implementation Groups so you start where your risk and resources put you. IG1, the 56-safeguard essential-hygiene baseline, is the floor every enterprise should meet; IG2 and IG3 add the rest for organisations holding more sensitive data or facing more capable attackers. Meeting IG1 well is a legitimate place to stop, not a partial result.

items.q: Are the CIS Controls the same as the CIS Benchmarks?
items.html: No, and conflating them is the most common CIS mistake. The Controls are a prioritised list of what to do across a programme; the Benchmarks are secure-configuration guides for specific technologies: how to harden a particular operating system, browser or cloud service. Both come from CIS, but one sets the actions and the other details the settings for a single system.

items.q: Can my organisation get CIS certified?
items.html: No. There is no CIS certification for an organisation. The Controls are free to adopt and you can assess yourself against them; CIS also sells assessment tooling like CIS-CAT that checks systems against the Benchmarks. None of that is an accredited certificate. If you need one, it comes from a framework such as ISO/IEC 27001, which the Controls can be mapped to.

entries.title: Control maturity
entries.description: Control maturity rates how repeatably and how well documented a control is. It is not the same as effectiveness or coverage and is not an assurance opinion.
sources: ISACA / CMMI Institute, Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI)
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, 2024 - Implementation Tiers

sections.text: Maturity is not effectiveness, and not coverage

blocks.html: Control maturity is a rating of how consistently, how well documented and how repeatably a control or process is performed, a measure of the process behind a control, not of whether that control works on any given day. It is scored on a scale, most often the five levels adapted from the Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI), and it is not an assurance opinion.
The score is useful for one thing: deciding where to invest to make a control more reliable. It is misused for almost everything else, usually by being read as a statement that the control works.

Most maturity models in governance, risk and compliance use a five-level scale derived from CMMI. Each level describes how the process behind the control is run, from improvised to continuously improved. Some models add a level 0 for a control that does not exist at all.

Level Name What it looks like
0 Non-existent Added by some models. The control is not performed and there is nothing to assess.
1 Initial The work gets done, but the process is unpredictable, reactive and dependent on individuals rather than a repeatable method.
2 Managed Planned, performed, monitored and controlled at the level of individual projects, with policies and records, but not yet standardised across the organisation. This is the level older CMM-based models called “repeatable”.
3 Defined Documented as an organisation-wide standard and performed consistently, whoever runs it.
4 Quantitatively managed Controlled using statistical and other quantitative techniques against defined objectives, so process performance is understood in numbers rather than merely tracked.
5 Optimising Continuously improved using that measurement; change is deliberate rather than reactive.

A score is only as good as the rubric behind it. Level 3 has to mean the same evidence for two different assessors, or the number cannot be rolled up or compared over time.

blocks.text: Maturity is not effectiveness, and not coverage

blocks.html:
This is the point the whole entry turns on. Three different questions are routinely collapsed into one number, and they measure different things.

Dimension The question it answers What a good score still hides
Maturity How repeatable and well documented is the process behind the control? Whether the control actually stops anything.
Effectiveness Did the control achieve its objective across the period? Whether it will survive staff turnover or scale.
Coverage How much of the estate does the control reach? Whether it works where it does reach.

A high-maturity control can still fail on a given day: the process is repeatable, but the run in question missed. A low-maturity, ad hoc control can still catch the risk once, by luck or by an individual’s diligence. Maturity describes the machine, not the output on any particular day, and it yields no assurance on its own.

Whether a control actually achieved its objective across a period of operation, the question an auditor tests, and the source of assurance. Distinct from maturity, which describes only how the process is run.

CMMI offers two representations, and the difference matters when someone reports a level. The continuous representation gives selected process areas their own capability levels, useful when you want to know how one area stands. The staged representation gives an organisational unit a single maturity level once it satisfies a required set of process areas, one benchmark for the whole.

A capability level describes one area; a maturity level describes the organisation. A claim like “we are level 4” means nothing until it says level 4 of what: one control, one domain or the organisation as a whole.

Maturity earns its place as a planning tool, not a scorecard. Three disciplines make it work.

Set a target by risk, not a target of level 5. Maturity costs money to build and money to hold. Decide, per control or per domain, what maturity the risk it carries actually justifies. A low-risk control held at level 5 is spending that a higher-risk control still at level 2 needed. Not everything needs to be optimised.

Track trajectory, not just position. For prioritisation the direction over time often tells you more than the absolute level. A control moving from 2 to 3 is being invested in; one static at 4 for three years may be coasting.

Prioritise by the gap. The distance between current and target maturity, weighted by the risk behind each control, is a defensible way to sequence investment. The controls with the widest risk-weighted gaps go first.

Maturity levels are sometimes confused with NIST CSF Tiers, which are a related but distinct governance construct. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework defines four Tiers (Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable and Adaptive) describing the rigour of an organisation’s cybersecurity risk governance rather than the maturity of an individual control. NIST is explicit that the Tiers are not maturity levels and that Tier 4 is not a target every organisation should set; the right Tier is the one that meets the organisation’s goals and reduces risk to an acceptable level. Read a maturity model the same way, and read it against how to read a framework before you adopt one.

Rated on opinion, with no rubric. Without defined evidence for each level, a maturity score is a feeling written as a number. Two assessors score the same control two levels apart, the roll-up is noise and the year-on-year comparison measures nothing but who did the assessing.

Reported as an assurance opinion. A maturity score says the process is repeatable and documented; it says nothing about whether the control operated effectively over the period. Presenting “level 4” to a board as though it were assurance overstates what was measured. Assurance comes from effectiveness testing, not from a maturity rating.

Level 5 set as the target for everything. Driving every control to Optimising diverts budget and attention from controls that carry real risk and are still at level 2. Uniform targets are the most common way a maturity programme wastes money.

High maturity mistaken for “we are secure”. A control can be documented, measured and continuously improved and still be the wrong control, or aimed at a risk that no longer matters. A mature process around an obsolete control is a well-run irrelevance. Maturity of a process is not evidence of a defended organisation.

items.q: What is the difference between control maturity and control effectiveness?
items.html: Maturity measures the process: how consistently, how well documented and how repeatably a control is performed. Effectiveness measures the outcome: whether the control achieved its objective across a period. A control can score high on maturity and still fail on a given day, and a barely-documented control can still catch a risk once. A maturity score is not an assurance opinion; effectiveness testing is where assurance comes from.

items.q: What are the five levels of a maturity model?
items.html: Most models use the five levels adapted from CMMI: 1 Initial (unpredictable and reactive), 2 Managed (planned and controlled per project, not yet standardised), 3 Defined (standardised across the organisation), 4 Quantitatively managed (controlled with quantitative techniques) and 5 Optimising (continuously improved). Some models add a level 0, Non-existent, for a control that is not performed at all.

items.q: Should every control reach maturity level 5?
items.html: No. Target maturity should be set by the risk each control carries, not raised uniformly. Holding a low-risk control at level 5 costs money to build and maintain that a higher-risk control still at level 2 needed more. The goal is the right maturity for each control and a closing gap over time, not level 5 everywhere.

sources_html: ISACA / CMMI Institute, Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI)
NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, 2024 - Implementation Tiers
