entries.title: HIPAA Security Rule
entries.description: The HIPAA Security Rule sets US federal standards for protecting electronic health information through administrative, physical and technical safeguards.
keywords: what is the hipaa security rule

quick_facts.Full name: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act

sources: HIPAA Security Rule, 45 CFR Part 160 and Part 164 Subparts A and C
HHS Office for Civil Rights, Security Rule guidance

sections.text: What it protects and who it binds
The risk analysis is the foundation
Enforcement, and the certification that does not exist

blocks.html: The HIPAA Security Rule is the part of US federal law that sets national standards for protecting electronic protected health information (ePHI) through administrative, physical and technical safeguards. It is technology-neutral and scales to the size and complexity of the organisation.

HIPAA (the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) was enacted in 1996; the Security Rule itself was finalised in 2003, with compliance required from 2005. It is codified at 45 CFR Part 160 and Part 164, and it governs one thing narrowly: ePHI, health information created, held or moved in electronic form. The broader Privacy Rule covers protected health information in every form, paper included, and the two are routinely conflated. This entry is the Security Rule.

The distinction that matters most sits underneath all of it: this is law, not a contract. Non-compliance is enforced by a federal regulator, and the safeguards are written to be assessed as legal obligations rather than as a supplier’s promise. Everything below follows from that.

blocks.text: What it protects and who it binds

blocks.html:
The Rule protects ePHI, and it binds two classes of party. Covered entities are health plans, health-care clearinghouses and health-care providers who transmit health information electronically in connection with a transaction for which HHS has adopted a standard. Business associates are the vendors that create, receive, maintain or transmit ePHI on a covered entity’s behalf: a cloud host, a billing processor, a managed-service provider.

Business associates were not always directly on the hook. The 2013 HIPAA Omnibus Rule, implementing the HITECH Act, made them directly liable to the regulator for the Security Rule, rather than liable only through the contract with the covered entity that engaged them. A vendor handling ePHI is answerable to the regulator in its own right, and a covered entity that treats its vendors’ compliance as the vendors’ problem alone has misread the position.
The Rule groups its standards into three families of safeguards, plus organisational requirements and a documentation regime.

items.html: The largest group: assigned security responsibility, workforce training, contingency planning and the required risk analysis that governs how ePHI is protected.
Controls over physical access to the systems and facilities that hold ePHI: facility access controls; workstation use; workstation security; and device and media controls.
The technology controls on the ePHI itself: access control, audit controls, integrity, authentication and transmission security.
The contracts that bind the parties who handle ePHI, most visibly the business-associate agreement.
The written policies behind the safeguards and the records that evidence them, retained for six years.

blocks.html: The documentation family is not administrative overhead. It is the raw material a compliance function turns into evidence (see what compliance produces (4.0)), and an unwritten control is, for enforcement purposes, close to an absent one.

Each standard carries one or more implementation specifications, and every specification is marked either required or addressable. The single most expensive misreading of the Security Rule is treating “addressable” as “optional”. It is not.

For an addressable specification an organisation must assess whether the safeguard is a reasonable and appropriate control in its own environment, and then do one of two things: implement it; or, where it is genuinely not reasonable and appropriate, document why not and implement an equivalent alternative measure where reasonable to do so. Assessing nothing and implementing nothing is not one of the options. Reading specification language precisely is a general framework skill, not a HIPAA quirk (see how to read a framework (5.0)).

A status on an implementation specification meaning the organisation must decide whether the safeguard is reasonable and appropriate for its environment, then either implement it or record why it is not reasonable and appropriate and put an equivalent alternative measure in place where reasonable. It does not mean optional and it does not license inaction.

blocks.text: The risk analysis is the foundation

blocks.html:
A risk analysis (an accurate and thorough assessment of the risks to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of ePHI) is itself a required administrative safeguard, at 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A). It is not a preliminary; it is the control the rest of the programme is built on. Which addressable specifications are reasonable, where scarce effort should go first, and what “reasonable and appropriate” means for this organisation are all decided from the risk analysis.

This is what the risk function produces (3.0) pointed at a single dataset. It is also, done badly or not at all, one of the most common findings in enforcement: a risk analysis that covers one system and ignores the rest, or that was run once and never revisited, is a recurring theme in settled cases.

blocks.text: Enforcement, and the certification that does not exist

blocks.html:
The Security Rule is enforced by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR). Because HIPAA is a law, the consequences of non-compliance are legal: civil monetary penalties tiered by culpability (from a genuinely unknowing breach up to wilful neglect) and, in some cases, criminal penalties. That is the sharp contrast with PCI DSS (5.11), which imposes similar-looking security requirements but binds through a private contract with the card brands rather than through statute: different enforcer and different teeth.

One consequence is worth stating plainly, because it costs organisations real money: there is no official HIPAA certification. No government body certifies HIPAA compliance, and no certificate confers it. An organisation can undergo a third-party assessment or make an attestation, and either can be useful, but “HIPAA certified” is not a government credential and a vendor advertising one is describing an assessment at best.

Reading “addressable” as “optional”. Addressable specifications demand an assessment and then either implementation or a documented, equivalent alternative. Skipping one because it is “only addressable” is a straightforward finding waiting to be made.

Skimping the risk analysis. A required safeguard treated as a formality (narrow scope, stale date, no follow-through) undermines every decision that should have flowed from it, and it is among the most cited failings in enforcement.

Assuming a “HIPAA certification” exists. It does not. Buying or claiming one wastes money and can mislead partners; the honest statement is that an independent assessment was performed against the Rule.

Confusing the Security Rule with the Privacy Rule. The Security Rule governs ePHI: electronic data. The Privacy Rule governs protected health information in every form, and covers uses and disclosures the Security Rule never touches. A programme built for one is not automatically compliant with the other.

Forgetting business associates are directly liable. Since the 2013 Omnibus Rule a vendor handling ePHI answers to the regulator itself, not only to the covered entity that hired it. A business-associate agreement allocates responsibility; it does not move a vendor’s ePHI outside the Rule’s reach.

items.q: Is HIPAA a law or a framework?
items.html: HIPAA is a US federal law, enacted in 1996, and the Security Rule is a regulation issued under it. That is why it is enforced by a regulator with civil and, in some cases, criminal penalties, rather than through a contract the way PCI DSS is. It is not a voluntary framework you adopt; if you handle ePHI as a covered entity or business associate, it applies to you.

items.q: Does "addressable" mean I can skip the control?
items.html: No. Addressable means you must assess whether the safeguard is reasonable and appropriate for your environment, then either implement it or document why it is not and put an equivalent measure in place where reasonable. The one response that is never compliant is doing nothing and recording nothing.

items.q: Can my company get HIPAA certified?
items.html: No. There is no official HIPAA certification and no government body issues one. You can have an independent assessor evaluate your safeguards against the Security Rule, and that can be worth doing, but the result is an assessment or attestation, not a government-recognised certificate. Treat any “HIPAA certified” badge as marketing.

entries.title: PCI DSS
entries.description: PCI DSS is the card brands' contractual security standard that any organisation storing, processing or transmitting cardholder data must meet.

quick_facts.Full name: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

sources: PCI Security Standards Council, PCI DSS v4.0.1 (2024)
PCI SSC, Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) Instructions and Guidelines

sections.text: What it is and who enforces it
The six goals and twelve requirements

blocks.html: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) is a set of security requirements that any organisation storing, processing or transmitting cardholder data must meet. It is maintained by the PCI Security Standards Council and enforced contractually by the card brands, not by any law.

The standard applies equally to merchants and to the service providers that handle card data on their behalf. What varies is not whether it applies but how much of it applies and how that is proven, both of which follow from how card data moves through the business.

blocks.text: What it is and who enforces it

blocks.html:
PCI DSS is published and maintained by the PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC), a body founded in 2006 by the five major card brands: Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover and JCB. The Council writes the standard; it does not enforce it.

Enforcement runs through contracts. A merchant’s obligation to comply is a term of its agreement with its acquiring bank, and the acquirer in turn is bound by the operating rules of the card brands. PCI DSS is not a law. The common belief that “PCI is a legal requirement” is wrong in most jurisdictions: it is a private contractual scheme. That distinction matters because the consequences are contractual too: an acquirer can levy fines, raise transaction fees or ultimately withdraw a merchant’s ability to accept cards, and after a breach the brands can pass assessment and recovery costs down the chain. A few jurisdictions reference PCI DSS in statute, but the standard itself is industry rule rather than legislation.

The cardholder data environment (CDE) is the people, processes and systems that store, process or transmit account data. That environment, and any connected-to or security-impacting system component that is not effectively isolated from it, falls within PCI DSS scope.

blocks.text: The six goals and twelve requirements

blocks.html: PCI DSS groups its detailed controls under six goals, which resolve into twelve numbered requirements.

items.term: Build and maintain a secure network and systems
items.html: Requirements 1 and 2: network security controls and secure configurations, in place of default passwords and settings.
Requirements 3 and 4: protect stored account data and encrypt cardholder data in transit across open, public networks.
Requirements 5 and 6: protection against malicious software and secure development, patching and change control.
Requirements 7, 8 and 9: least-privilege access, unique identification with authentication and restriction of physical access.
Requirements 10 and 11: logging and monitoring, plus regular security testing including internal and external vulnerability scans and penetration tests.
Requirement 12: the governing policies, risk assessment and programme that hold the rest together.

blocks.html: Requirements 6 and 11 are the ones a GRC function will already recognise: between them they cover secure software, patching and the scanning-and-testing cycle that a standing vulnerability management programme produces. The evidence a merchant gathers for those requirements is largely the same evidence vulnerability management generates on its own account.

PCI DSS v4.0 was published in 2022; v4.0.1 (2024) is the current revision. v4.0 ran alongside the retired v3.2.1 through a transition period, and a large block of future-dated v4.0 requirements took effect on 31 March 2025.

The headline change is a second route to meeting a requirement.

Defined approach. Implement the requirement as written and be assessed against that wording. This is the traditional model and stays available for every requirement.

Customised approach. Meet the stated security objective of a requirement by controls of your own design, then evidence that they achieve the objective. The assessor validates the design against a controls matrix and a targeted risk analysis rather than against prescriptive text. It suits mature organisations and adds documentation burden; it is not a shortcut.

v4.0 also introduces targeted risk analyses, which let an organisation set the frequency of certain recurring activities from documented risk rather than a fixed interval, and it expands multi-factor authentication, extending MFA to all access into the CDE rather than only remote or administrative access.

Validation scales with volume. Each card brand sorts merchants into four merchant levels by annual transaction count, and Level 1 also captures any merchant that has suffered a breach, whatever its size. Service providers sit in a separate two-level scheme. The thresholds below are the common shape; each brand sets and can vary its own.

Merchant level Who it covers Typical validation
Level 1 Highest volume, commonly more than 6 million transactions of a brand a year, and any merchant after a breach Annual on-site assessment by a QSA (or, where the brand permits, an Internal Security Assessor (ISA) with the required officer sign-off) producing a Report on Compliance (ROC) and an Attestation of Compliance (AOC); quarterly ASV scan where externally accessible in-scope systems exist
Level 2 Commonly 1-6 million transactions a year Annual Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) and AOC; quarterly ASV scan where externally accessible in-scope systems exist; some brands require assessor involvement
Level 3 Commonly 20,000-1 million e-commerce transactions a year Annual SAQ and AOC; quarterly ASV scan where externally accessible in-scope systems exist
Level 4 Fewer than 20,000 e-commerce, or up to 1 million other transactions a year Annual SAQ and AOC; quarterly ASV scan where externally accessible in-scope systems exist

The SAQ is a self-assessment, and the type (A, A-EP, B, B-IP, C, C-VT, D or P2PE) depends on how the merchant handles card data: a fully outsourced e-commerce page; a payment page that partly touches your systems; standalone terminals and so on each map to a different questionnaire and a different set of applicable requirements. It is the same idea as any security questionnaire used as a self-assessment, but the SAQ is PCI-specific and unrelated to the vendor-assessment templates such as the SIG or CAIQ. Where in-scope system components are externally accessible, quarterly scans by an Approved Scanning Vendor (ASV) are required (Requirement 11.3.2), subject to the applicable SAQ and validation rules.

The single largest determinant of cost and effort is not the standard’s depth but how much of the business the CDE touches. Everything that stores, processes or transmits account data (and everything connected to it without segmentation) is in scope. Shrink that footprint and both the applicable requirements and the SAQ shrink with it.

Three techniques do most of the work. Tokenisation replaces the card number with a non-sensitive token so downstream systems never hold real account data. Point-to-point encryption (P2PE), using a validated solution, encrypts the card data at the point of capture so your own systems only ever handle ciphertext. Outsourcing the card handling itself (a hosted payment page or a redirect to a compliant service provider) moves the sensitive processing outside your environment entirely.

None of these makes compliance disappear. The belief that “using a PCI-compliant processor makes us compliant” is a common and expensive error: outsourcing narrows your scope, often down to the shortest questionnaire (SAQ A), but you still complete the validation your brand or acquirer requires (an SAQ and AOC when eligible, or a ROC where directed) and still carry the requirements that remain: how you integrate the processor, who has access and how you govern the relationship.

Treating PCI as a law. It is a contract with your acquirer, not a statute. Teams that wait for a regulator to act miss that the enforcement lever (fines, fees, loss of card acceptance) sits with the bank and can move faster than any regulator would.

Assuming a compliant processor confers compliance. A compliant service provider reduces your scope; it does not complete your validation. You still submit your own SAQ and AOC for the slice of the flow you own.

Never segmenting the CDE. Left flat, a network puts every connected system in scope, which turns a small card footprint into an enterprise-wide assessment. Segmentation reduces the assessed scope and effort, but it does not by itself change a merchant’s brand or acquirer validation level: it will not turn a required ROC into an SAQ.

Reading validation as a point rather than a programme. A ROC or SAQ describes a moment; v4.0’s business-as-usual emphasis exists because controls decay between annual assessments. Compliance evidenced once a year and ignored for the other eleven months is the ordinary way a breached-but-“compliant” merchant is made.

items.q: Is PCI DSS a legal requirement?
items.html: In most jurisdictions, no. PCI DSS is a contractual standard imposed by the card brands and enforced through your acquiring bank, not a law passed by a legislature. The obligations are real (an acquirer can fine a merchant, raise its fees or withdraw card acceptance, and the brands can pass breach costs down the chain), but they flow from contract and brand operating rules rather than statute.

items.q: What are the PCI DSS merchant levels?
items.html: There are four merchant levels, set by each card brand according to annual transaction volume, with Level 1 the highest. Level 1 also captures any merchant that has suffered a breach. Level 1 typically requires an annual on-site assessment by a QSA producing a Report on Compliance and an Attestation of Compliance; Levels 2 to 4 typically validate through a Self-Assessment Questionnaire and Attestation of Compliance, with quarterly ASV scans where card data reaches internet-facing systems.

items.q: Does using a PCI-compliant payment processor make my business compliant?
items.html: No. It narrows your scope but does not remove your obligation. Outsourcing card handling to a compliant processor can reduce you to the shortest questionnaire, often SAQ A, but you still complete the validation your brand or acquirer requires for your part of the flow, usually an SAQ and AOC. How you integrate the processor, who can access the environment and how you govern the relationship all remain yours to validate.

entries.title: SOC 1 vs SOC 2 vs SOC 3
entries.description: SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3 are AICPA attestation reports on a service organisation's controls: financial-reporting, security and a public trust summary.
sources: AICPA, SOC 1 - SSAE 18 (AT-C section 320)
AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria
AICPA, AT-C section 205 - Assertion-Based Examination Engagements

blocks.html: System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports are a suite of attestation reports defined by the AICPA and issued by a licensed CPA firm on a service organisation’s controls. The three in common use (SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3) answer different questions for different readers.

The numbers invite the reader to rank them, as though SOC 3 were a beginner’s SOC 2 and SOC 1 the serious one. They are not a ladder. SOC 1 and SOC 2 cover different subject matter, and SOC 3 is a public version of a SOC 2 rather than a weaker one. Choosing the right report starts with knowing which question each was built to answer.

SOC 1 reports on a service organisation’s controls that are relevant to its user entities’ internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). It is performed under SSAE 18 (AT-C section 320), and its audience is the user entity’s own management and their financial-statement auditors. It is a restricted-use report. A payroll bureau or a claims processor produces a SOC 1 because its processing feeds directly into its customers’ financial statements. SOC 1 is not the “financial” report you hand a prospect to prove security: it is specifically about financial-reporting controls.

SOC 2 reports on controls relevant to the Trust Services Criteria: security, which is mandatory, and optionally availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. It is performed under AT-C section 205 and is a detailed report: it sets out the system and the controls, and in a Type II report the auditor’s tests of operating effectiveness and their results, the evidence that lets a reader weigh the controls rather than take an assertion on trust. It is restricted-use, shared with management, customers and regulators, typically under NDA. This is the report an enterprise security team means when it asks a vendor for “your SOC report”.

SOC 3 covers the same subject matter and the same Trust Services Criteria as a SOC 2, but is a short, general-use report. It carries the auditor’s opinion and management’s assertion but omits the system description, the control listing and the test results. Stripped of that detail, it can be distributed freely: published on a website as a public trust summary. A SOC 3 is a public companion to a SOC 2, not a lower grade of assurance on the same criteria.

Beyond these three, the AICPA also defines reports such as SOC for Cybersecurity and SOC for Supply Chain. They serve narrower purposes and sit outside the SOC 1 / SOC 2 / SOC 3 comparison this entry draws.

Dimension SOC 1 SOC 2 SOC 3
Subject / criteria Controls relevant to user entities’ internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) Trust Services Criteria: security, plus optional availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy Same subject and criteria as SOC 2
Standard SSAE 18 (AT-C 320) AT-C 205 AT-C 205
Audience & distribution User management and their financial-statement auditors; restricted-use Management, customers and regulators; restricted-use, usually under NDA Anyone; general-use, freely publishable
Level of detail Detailed: system and controls; a Type II adds operating-effectiveness tests and results Detailed: system and controls; a Type II adds operating-effectiveness tests and results Short: opinion and assertion only, no description, control listing or results
Type I / II Applies Applies Does not apply
Typical use Given to a customer’s auditors when your service touches their financial statements Shared with customers and prospects reviewing your security Public trust summary on a website

A further distinction cuts across SOC 1 and SOC 2, but not SOC 3. A Type I report tests whether the controls were suitably designed at a single point in time; a Type II tests whether they also operated effectively across a period, commonly three to twelve months. Enterprise procurement asking for “a SOC 2” almost always means a Type II, because a Type I speaks only to the suitability of design at a point in time, not to operating effectiveness.

Two forms a SOC 1 or SOC 2 report can take. A Type I opinion addresses the suitability of the design of controls at a point in time; a Type II addresses design and operating effectiveness over a period, and so carries the auditor’s tests and their results. SOC 3 has neither form. How the two bear on the management assertion is set out separately.

When you rely on a counterparty’s SOC report, check the Type first and the period it covers second. A Type I, or a Type II over a short or stale window, supports far less weight than a clean cover page implies.

“SOC 2 certified.” There is no such thing. SOC 2 is an attestation (an opinion expressed in a report by a licensed CPA firm) not a certification, and nothing is issued that an organisation is “certified” against. The certifiable security standard is ISO 27001; where a claim of certification is what matters, that is the one to reach for. Saying “SOC 2 certified” signals to a knowledgeable reader that the speaker has not read one.

Reaching for SOC 1 when you mean security. SOC 1 is about controls over financial reporting, not information security. A prospect asking about your security posture wants a SOC 2. Commissioning a SOC 1 to answer a security questionnaire spends real money on the wrong report and answers a question nobody asked.

Treating SOC 3 as a lesser SOC 2. A SOC 3 is not a cut-price or entry-level SOC 2. It is examined against the same criteria and carries the same opinion; what it drops is the confidential detail, so that it can be published. Reading the absence of a system description as weaker assurance mistakes distribution for rigour.

Ignoring Type I versus Type II when relying on a report. A Type I says only that the controls were designed suitably on one day. Accepting it as evidence that controls operated across the whole year is a common and consequential misread. Check the Type, then the period it covers, before you lean on someone else’s report.

items.q: A customer is asking for "our SOC report": which one do they mean?
items.html: Almost always a SOC 2, and almost always a Type II. SOC 1 comes up only when your service affects the customer’s financial statements (a payroll or billing processor, say), in which case their auditors, not their security team, will ask. If in doubt, ask whether they want it for a financial-statement audit (SOC 1) or a vendor security review (SOC 2).

items.q: Can I say we are "SOC 2 certified"?
items.html: No. SOC 2 produces an attestation report with an auditor’s opinion, not a certificate, so “certified” is incorrect and reads as a tell that the report has not been understood. Say instead that you “have a SOC 2 report” or “completed a SOC 2 Type II examination”. The certifiable standard is ISO 27001.

items.q: Is a SOC 3 weaker than a SOC 2?
items.html: No. A SOC 3 is assessed against the same Trust Services Criteria and carries the same auditor’s opinion as the SOC 2 it accompanies. It simply leaves out the system description, control listing and test results so that it can be shared publicly. Treat it as the public summary, not a lower tier of assurance.

entries.title: GDPR
entries.description: GDPR is the EU's binding data-protection law, not a voluntary framework. What it requires, who it binds, and why "GDPR certified" overstates the position.
sources: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation)
European Data Protection Board, guidelines on the GDPR

blocks.html: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is the European Union’s binding data-protection law (Regulation (EU) 2016/679, in force since 25 May 2018) governing how personal data about people in the EU is handled. It is legislation, not a voluntary framework.

That single fact changes what the rest of this part means. Most other documents in this part are things an organisation elects to adopt; GDPR, like the HIPAA Security Rule, applies whether or not anyone has decided to engage with it, and a regulator can act without a contract or a customer asking it to. It appears among the frameworks because most organisations run their obligations under it as a compliance programme, but the obligation itself is statutory.

Reading GDPR as one more optional standard is the mistake everything else follows from. Its reach also does not stop at the EU border. Article 3 makes the Regulation extraterritorial: it binds a controller or processor established outside the EU whenever they offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour. A company with no European office, billing in dollars, is caught the moment it targets or tracks people in the Union.

This is the honest reason GDPR sits in this part and also the reason it does not behave like its neighbours. PCI DSS is a contract with the card brands; ISO 27001 is a certificate you choose to pursue. GDPR is neither: it is law, and the only comparable neighbours here are other statutory regimes such as the HIPAA Security Rule. If you are unsure which kind of document you are holding, how to read a framework sorts them.

A framework, in the sense used across this part, is a document an organisation chooses to adopt and be measured against. GDPR is not one: it applies by operation of law, with or without any decision to take it on.

GDPR splits responsibility between two roles, and the split decides who answers for what. The controller decides the purposes and means of processing (the why and the how) and carries the primary legal accountability. A processor processes personal data on the controller’s behalf and only on its documented instructions, typically a supplier running a service. The distinction is not cosmetic: it determines who owes which duty, and the two must have a written contract under Article 28 governing the processing. A vendor that quietly starts deciding its own purposes for the data has become a controller in its own right, with a controller’s liabilities.
Article 5 sets out seven principles that every act of processing has to satisfy.

items.html: Process on a valid legal basis, do not mislead the data subject and be open about what happens to their data.
Collect data for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and do not reuse it in ways incompatible with those.
Hold only the data the purpose actually needs, and no more.
Keep personal data correct and current, and correct or erase what is wrong.
Keep data in identifiable form no longer than the purpose requires.
Secure the data against unauthorised access, loss or damage, the security principle.
Be able to demonstrate compliance with the other six, not merely assert it.

blocks.html:
Accountability is the principle that turns the rest into work you can show. The controller must be able to produce the records, assessments and evidence that demonstrate compliance, because under GDPR being compliant and being able to prove it are the same requirement.

Article 6 then says every act of processing needs a lawful basis, and there are six: consent, a contract with the data subject, a legal obligation, protection of someone’s vital interests, a public task and legitimate interests. At least one must apply before processing begins, and the basis has to be fixed up front; you cannot reach for a different one afterwards to justify what you have already done. Consent is only one of the six and often the weakest, because it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and it can be withdrawn at any moment. For routine business processing a contract, a legal obligation or legitimate interests is usually the sounder footing.

GDPR also gives data subjects a set of enforceable rights over their own data: the right to be informed; access to it; rectification of inaccurate data; erasure, the “right to be forgotten”; restriction of processing; data portability; objection to processing; and rights concerning solely automated decision-making and profiling. The rights are not absolute (several carry exemptions), but a controller has to be able to recognise a request, respond within the statutory deadline and explain any refusal.
The principles and rights translate into a handful of concrete duties a supervisory authority will expect to see met.

items.html: Article 30: a documented inventory of what personal data you process, why, where it flows and how long you keep it.

items.term: Data protection by design and by default
items.html: Article 25: build data protection into systems and processes from the outset, and default to the least data and the tightest sharing.
Article 35: a structured risk assessment required before high-risk processing, such as large-scale profiling or systematic monitoring.

Articles 33 and 34: unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk, notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and generally within 72 hours of becoming aware; under Article 34, tell affected individuals without undue delay where the breach is likely to result in a high risk to them.

Article 37: appoint one where you are a public authority (other than a court acting judicially), or where your core activities involve large-scale regular and systematic monitoring or large-scale processing of special-category or criminal-conviction data.

blocks.html: The 72-hour clock is the one that catches people out. It runs from awareness of the breach, not from the end of the investigation, so the notification often goes in while the facts are still incomplete.

GDPR is enforced by national supervisory authorities (the data protection authorities, one or more per member state, such as Ireland’s Data Protection Commission or France’s CNIL). Where processing crosses borders, a lead authority coordinates through a one-stop-shop mechanism. Their power is real: administrative fines run in two tiers, each set at the higher of a fixed ceiling or a percentage of worldwide turnover.

Tier Maximum fine Applies to
Lower EUR 10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher Breaches of specific obligations such as records, security and DPO duties
Higher EUR 20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher Breaches of the core principles, lawful-basis rules and data-subject rights

There is no single certificate that makes an organisation “GDPR compliant”. Article 42 provides for approved certification mechanisms that can help demonstrate compliance for specific processing, but no scheme signs off the whole Regulation, and “GDPR certified” presented as a blanket badge is marketing rather than a legal status.

Following the UK’s departure from the EU, the UK GDPR is the retained domestic version, broadly mirroring the EU text and enforced by the Information Commissioner’s Office. An organisation handling both UK and EU data is generally subject to both regimes at once.

Treating it as optional. The commonest error is filing GDPR alongside the voluntary standards and waiting to be asked. It is directly applicable law: the duty exists the moment you process the data, and a supervisory authority needs no contract or complaint to act.

Assuming distance is protection. “We are not in the EU, so it does not apply” ignores Article 3. Offer goods or services to people in the EU, or monitor their behaviour, and you are in scope with no European office at all, and may additionally have to appoint an EU representative under Article 27.

Leaning on consent for everything. Consent is one lawful basis of six, and often the most fragile, because it can be withdrawn and must clear a high bar to be valid. Processing that would sit comfortably on contract, legal obligation or legitimate interests is left exposed when it is bolted to a consent the data subject can revoke at will.

Buying a “GDPR certification”. No product or audit makes an organisation compliant with the whole Regulation. Article 42 schemes can evidence compliance for a defined activity, but a vendor selling blanket “GDPR certification” as proof of compliance is overstating what it can deliver, and relying on it leaves the actual obligations unmet.

items.q: Does GDPR apply to my company if it is based outside the EU?
items.html: It can. Article 3 gives GDPR extraterritorial reach: if you offer goods or services to people in the EU, or monitor their behaviour, you are in scope even with no EU establishment. Where you have no EU presence you may also have to appoint an EU representative under Article 27. Being outside Europe is not, by itself, a reason the Regulation does not reach you.

items.q: Do I always need consent to process personal data?
items.html: No. Consent is only one of six lawful bases, and often not the best. For much routine processing a contract, a legal obligation or legitimate interests gives you a stronger footing, and consent means honouring a withdrawal at any time. You need one valid basis, fixed before processing starts, not necessarily consent.

items.q: Can I get my organisation "GDPR certified"?
items.html: Not in the sense the phrase implies. There is no official certificate that renders an organisation compliant with the whole Regulation. Article 42 allows approved schemes that can evidence compliance for particular processing, and those can help, but any vendor selling blanket “GDPR certification” as proof of overall compliance is overstating what it means.

entries.title: ISO/IEC 27001 explained
entries.description: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard for an information security management system. Clauses 4-10, Annex A 2022, and the certification path.
sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 - Information security management systems - Requirements
ISO/IEC 27002:2022 - Information security controls (guidance for Annex A)
ISO/IEC 27006 - Requirements for bodies providing audit and certification of an ISMS
ISO/IEC 27001:2022/Amd 1:2024 - climate action amendment

blocks.html: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard for an information security management system, a documented, risk-driven way of running security that an accredited body can audit and certify. It certifies the system, not any product, team or piece of software.

The distinction between the management system and the controls is the thing to hold onto. Clauses 4 to 10 are the requirements: they describe the machine, its scope, leadership, risk assessment, objectives, internal audit, management review and corrective action. Annex A is a reference list of 93 controls the risk assessment can draw on. You are certified against the clauses. Annex A is where you shop, guided by your risks, and your choices are recorded in the Statement of Applicability.

A certificate says an accredited auditor examined that machine and found it running: risks are being assessed, controls are being chosen and operated, and the organisation is finding and fixing its own failures. It does not say the organisation cannot be breached.

items.html: Define the scope: which parts of the organisation, which locations, which services. Identify interested parties and their requirements. A scope drawn too wide is unauditable; drawn too narrow it is worthless to a customer.
Top management owns the ISMS, sets the policy, and assigns roles. “Management commitment” is audited by evidence (attendance at reviews, resourcing decisions), not by a signed statement.
The risk assessment methodology, the risk assessment itself, the risk treatment plan, and measurable security objectives. The 2022 version also requires that changes to the ISMS be planned.
Resources, competence, awareness, communication, and control of documented information.
Actually running the risk assessment and treatment on the planned cadence and whenever something significant changes.
Monitoring and measurement, internal audit, and management review. This is where most first-time certifications struggle, because it requires records built up over months.
Handling nonconformities with corrective action, and continually improving the ISMS.

blocks.html:
The document listing every Annex A control, whether it applies, and the
justification for each inclusion and exclusion. Required by clause 6.1.3 d) and
the first artefact an auditor asks for.

The 2022 update cut the control count from 114 to 93 and reorganised them from 14 domains into four themes: organisational (37), people (8), physical (14) and technological (34). Eleven controls are genuinely new, including threat intelligence, information security for cloud services, ICT readiness for business continuity, data masking, data leakage prevention, web filtering and secure coding. Organisations certified against the 2013 version had a transition window that closed on 31 October 2025.

A 2024 amendment added climate-change consideration to clauses 4.1 and 4.2, a small wording change, but auditors now expect to see that climate has been considered as a contextual issue.

1. Gap analysis. Measure the current state against the clauses and Annex A.
  2. Implementation. Build the missing management-system machinery and controls. Typically 6-12 months for an organisation starting from little.
  3. Operate for evidence. Run the ISMS long enough to have real records: at least one internal audit, one management review, one cycle of the risk assessment. Usually a minimum of three months.
  4. Stage 1 audit. The certification body reviews documentation and readiness.
  5. Stage 2 audit. The certification body tests the ISMS in operation. A pass, possibly with minor nonconformities to close, leads to the certificate.
  6. Surveillance. Smaller audits in years one and two, a full recertification in year three.

Choose a certification body accredited under ISO/IEC 27006 by a recognised national accreditation body. An unaccredited certificate is not recognised by procurement and is a common false economy.

Buying Annex A, ignoring the clauses. A control set is implemented, the management system around it is not, and Stage 2 fails on clause 9 because there are no internal audit or management-review records.

Scope drawn to flatter the certificate. A narrow scope (one product, one office) gets the certificate cheaply, then a customer reads the scope statement and finds their service is not in it.

Risk assessment as a formality. A generic risk register is produced to satisfy clause 6, disconnected from the SoA, so control choices cannot be traced to any risk.

Certificate treated as the finish line. The ISMS goes quiet after the audit, surveillance year one finds it dormant, and the finding is a major nonconformity.

items.q: What is ISO 27001 in simple terms?
items.html: An international standard that sets out how to run information security as a managed, repeatable system: decide what you are protecting, assess the risks, choose and operate controls, check that it works, and fix what does not. An accredited auditor can then certify that the system is genuinely in place.

items.q: What is the difference between ISO 27001 and ISO 27002?
items.html: ISO 27001 is the certifiable standard: its clauses are the requirements you are audited against. ISO 27002 is a companion guidance document that explains how to implement each Annex A control in detail. You certify against 27001; you read 27002 for implementation advice. You cannot be certified against 27002.

items.q: How long does ISO 27001 certification take?
items.html: For an organisation starting with few formal controls, typically 9 to 18 months: several months to build the management system and controls, a minimum operating period of about three months to generate records, then the two-stage audit. Organisations with mature controls already in place can be faster.

items.q: What changed in ISO 27001:2022?
items.html: The requirement clauses (4-10) changed only slightly. Annex A was restructured from 114 controls in 14 domains to 93 controls in 4 themes, with 11 new controls covering areas such as cloud services, threat intelligence, secure coding and data leakage prevention. A 2024 amendment added climate change as a contextual consideration.

items.q: Does ISO 27001 certification mean a company is secure?
items.html: No. It means an accredited auditor found a working information security management system: risks assessed, controls chosen and operated, failures found and corrected. It is strong evidence of a disciplined approach, not a guarantee against a breach.

entries.title: The ISO management-system certification family
entries.description: ISO 27001 sits in a family of management-system standards that share a structure: 27701, 27017, 27018, 22301, 9001, 42001, 20000-1 and how they relate.
sources: ISO/IEC 27701:2019 - Privacy information management - extension to 27001/27002
ISO/IEC 27017:2015 and ISO/IEC 27018:2019 - cloud security and cloud PII
ISO 22301:2019 - Business continuity management systems
ISO/IEC 42001:2023 - Artificial intelligence management system
ISO/IEC Directives Part 1, Annex SL (Harmonised Structure)

sections.text: The standards a GRC function meets most

blocks.html: ISO/IEC 27001 is one of a family of management-system standards that share the same skeleton (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, evaluation, improvement) so an organisation running one can add another without rebuilding the machinery underneath it.

That shared skeleton is called Annex SL, or the Harmonised Structure. It is why clauses 4 to 10 look almost identical across ISO 27001, ISO 22301 and ISO 9001, and why an internal audit programme, a management review and a corrective-action process built for one can be extended to cover several. The differences are in what each standard asks the management system to do.

Two shapes exist in the family. Some are standalone management systems you certify against directly. Others are extensions or sector code-of-practice documents that ride on top of an existing ISO 27001 certification.

blocks.text: The standards a GRC function meets most

blocks.html:
Standard What it manages Shape Certifiable
ISO/IEC 27001 Information security Standalone management system Yes
ISO/IEC 27701 Privacy (PII as controller or processor) Extension to 27001 Yes, as an extension
ISO/IEC 27017 Security controls for cloud services Code of practice on Annex A Some bodies certify; often audited as an extension
ISO/IEC 27018 Protection of PII in public cloud Code of practice As above
ISO 22301 Business continuity Standalone management system Yes
ISO/IEC 20000-1 IT service management Standalone management system Yes
ISO 9001 Quality management Standalone management system Yes
ISO/IEC 42001 Artificial intelligence management Standalone management system Yes

The common high-level structure and identical core text that ISO requires all new
and revised management-system standards to follow, so that clauses 4-10 align and
multiple systems can be integrated into one.

ISO 27701 adds privacy-specific requirements and two extra control sets (one for organisations acting as a data controller, one for processors) onto a 27001 ISMS. You cannot hold 27701 without 27001 (or certifying to both together). It is the recognised way to show a structured response to GDPR and similar laws, though it is not itself a legal compliance certificate.

ISO 27017 and 27018 are code-of-practice documents for cloud. 27017 gives cloud-specific implementation guidance and seven additional controls; 27018 focuses on personal data in public cloud. Cloud providers commonly hold all three (27001, 27017, 27018) and customers ask for the set.

ISO 22301 is a full, separate management system for business continuity (covered at 3.6) with its own certification. It shares the Annex SL structure with 27001, so the two integrate cleanly.

ISO/IEC 42001, published in 2023, is the first certifiable AI management system standard. It asks an organisation to govern the AI it develops or uses (impact assessment, data governance, transparency, human oversight) through the same management-system pattern. It is becoming a procurement ask for AI vendors the way 27001 did for cloud.

Add a standard when a buyer, a regulator or a genuine risk asks for it, not to collect certificates. Each additional certification is another audit, another surveillance cycle and another set of records to maintain. The economical path is one integrated management system with the scope widened to cover each standard, audited together where the certification body allows it, not several parallel systems with inconsistent risk registers.

items.q: What is the difference between ISO 27001 and ISO 27701?
items.html: ISO 27001 certifies an information security management system. ISO 27701 is a privacy extension that adds data-protection requirements and controller- or processor-specific controls on top of it. You need a 27001 ISMS to hold 27701; 27701 is the structured way to demonstrate privacy management, but it is not a certificate of legal compliance with GDPR.

items.q: What is ISO 42001?
items.html: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for an artificial intelligence management system. It sets out how an organisation should govern its development and use of AI (risk and impact assessment, data governance, transparency, human oversight) using the same management-system structure as ISO 27001. It is certifiable.

items.q: Do ISO 27017 and 27018 replace ISO 27001?
items.html: No. They are codes of practice that add cloud-specific and cloud-privacy guidance to an ISO 27001 ISMS. Cloud providers typically hold ISO 27001 together with 27017 and 27018, and customers ask for all three.

items.q: Can multiple ISO management systems be combined?
items.html: Yes. Because they share the Annex SL structure, standards such as ISO 27001, ISO 22301 and ISO 9001 can be run as one integrated management system with a single internal audit programme, management review and corrective-action process, and audited together. This is the standard approach for organisations holding more than one.

entries.title: The NIST framework family
entries.description: NIST publishes several security frameworks that are often confused: CSF 2.0, SP 800-53, SP 800-171, the Risk Management Framework and the AI RMF.
keywords: what is the NIST Risk Management Framework
sources: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, February 2024
NIST SP 800-53r5 - Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
NIST SP 800-171r3 - Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information
NIST SP 800-37r2 - Risk Management Framework
NIST AI 100-1 - Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework 1.0, January 2023

blocks.html: NIST publishes a family of security and risk documents that do different jobs: CSF 2.0 describes outcomes, SP 800-53 is the control catalogue, SP 800-171 is the baseline for government contractors, the Risk Management Framework is the process that ties them together, and the AI RMF extends the same thinking to AI systems.

The confusion is understandable, because organisations cite “NIST” as if it were one thing. It is a publisher. Most of what it produces is voluntary guidance; some of it becomes mandatory through a contract clause or a federal regulation, not through NIST itself. Knowing which document someone means (and whether it applies to you by choice or by obligation) is the first step in any conversation that starts “we need to be NIST compliant”.

items.html: An outcome framework organised into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. It describes what good looks like, not how to do it, and is used to assess maturity and communicate posture. The 2024 version added Govern and made it explicitly for organisations of any size and sector.

A catalogue of over 1,000 security and privacy controls in 20 families, with three baselines (low, moderate, high). Mandatory for US federal information systems; widely borrowed elsewhere as a control reference. This is the detail CSF points to.

A trimmed set of requirements (110 in revision 2, restructured in revision 3) for non-federal organisations that handle Controlled Unclassified Information under a US government contract. Enforced through the DFARS clause and, increasingly, CMMC assessment.

A seven-step process (Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor) for bringing a system into service with a documented risk decision behind it. This is the “how” that operationalises 800-53.

A voluntary framework for managing risks specific to AI systems, structured as Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. It mirrors the CSF approach and is the reference most US AI-governance programmes start from.

blocks.html:
Information the US government requires to be safeguarded but which is not
classified: contract data, technical drawings, some personal data. Handling it
under a federal contract triggers SP 800-171.

The most common mistake is treating CSF 2.0 and SP 800-53 as two options to choose between. They are layers. CSF gives you the outcome categories and a maturity conversation the board can follow. When you need to say how a category is met, you drop to a control catalogue (800-53, or ISO 27001 Annex A, or the CIS Controls), and CSF 2.0 ships mappings to exactly those. Use CSF to structure the programme and report on it; use a control set to implement it.

• US federal agency or system: 800-53 and the RMF are mandatory.
  • US government contractor touching CUI: 800-171, via your contract, with CMMC assessment arriving as the enforcement mechanism.
  • Everyone else: CSF 2.0 is a free, well-recognised way to structure and benchmark a security programme, with no certification and no obligation. The AI RMF plays the same role for AI risk.

“NIST compliant” with no document named. The requirement is written into a policy or a contract without specifying CSF, 800-53 or 800-171, and two teams spend a quarter building to different targets.

CSF treated as a checklist. The framework is a set of outcomes to assess against, not controls to tick. Scoring every subcategory “implemented” with no control evidence behind it produces a maturity chart that means nothing.

800-53 adopted whole. An organisation with no federal obligation implements the moderate baseline in full, hundreds of controls, most irrelevant to its risk, instead of using it as a reference to draw from.

171 revision confusion. A programme built to revision 2’s 110 requirements is not automatically aligned to revision 3’s restructured set; the transition needs a gap analysis.

items.q: What is the difference between the NIST CSF and NIST 800-53?
items.html: The CSF is an outcome framework: six functions and a set of categories that describe what a good security programme achieves, used for assessment and communication. SP 800-53 is a detailed catalogue of over a thousand controls used to implement those outcomes. CSF is the structure; 800-53 is one of the control sets it maps to. Federal systems must use 800-53; the CSF is voluntary.

items.q: Is NIST CSF mandatory?
items.html: Not in itself. The CSF is voluntary guidance for any organisation. It can become contractually or legally required if a customer, regulator or sector rule points to it, but NIST does not certify or enforce it. SP 800-53 and SP 800-171 are the NIST documents that carry mandatory force, and only in specific federal or contractor contexts.

items.q: What is NIST 800-171 and who needs it?
items.html: SP 800-171 is a set of security requirements for non-federal organisations that store or process Controlled Unclassified Information under a US government contract. It is enforced through the DFARS contract clause and, progressively, through CMMC assessments. If you do not handle CUI for the US government, it does not apply to you.

items.q: What is the NIST Risk Management Framework?
items.html: A seven-step process (Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor) defined in SP 800-37 for putting a system into operation with a formal, documented risk-acceptance decision. It is mandatory for US federal systems and is the process layer that turns the 800-53 control catalogue into an authorised system.

items.q: What is the NIST AI RMF?
items.html: A voluntary framework (NIST AI 100-1) for identifying and managing risks unique to AI systems, organised as Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. It parallels the CSF’s structure and is the common starting reference for US AI-governance programmes, alongside the certifiable ISO/IEC 42001.

entries.description: A map of the security and GRC frameworks beyond ISO and NIST (CIS, COBIT, HITRUST, FedRAMP, Cyber Essentials, Essential Eight, CSA CCM) and what each is for.
sources: CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1, Center for Internet Security
ISACA, COBIT 2019 Framework: Governance and Management Objectives
HITRUST CSF version 11, HITRUST Alliance
FedRAMP authorization requirements, GSA
NCSC Cyber Essentials (UK); ASD Essential Eight Maturity Model (Australia)
Cloud Security Alliance, Cloud Controls Matrix v4

blocks.html: Beyond ISO 27001 and the NIST family, most of the frameworks a GRC function meets fall into four groups: prescriptive control sets, governance models, certifiable industry schemes, and national baselines. Knowing which group a framework belongs to tells you what it is for before you read a line of it.

The field has more frameworks than any organisation should adopt. They overlap heavily, because they are all describing the same small set of security practices from different angles and for different audiences. The skill is not knowing every framework in detail; it is placing a new one quickly (is this a list of controls, a way of governing IT, a certification a customer will ask for, or a floor a government has set) and then deciding whether it adds anything you do not already have.
Frameworks that tell you what to implement, in priority order.

items.html: 18 controls, each broken into safeguards, grouped into three Implementation Groups by organisation size and risk. Ordered by impact, so a small team can start at the top and stop where its resources run out. Covered at 5.8.
A cloud-specific control set with mappings to most other frameworks, paired with the CAIQ questionnaire. The common reference for assessing a cloud provider.
Application-security verification requirements and a maturity model for a secure development programme. Narrower scope, deep in one domain.

A framework for the governance and management of enterprise IT, from ISACA. It is broader than security (it covers IT value, resourcing and performance) and sits above a security control set rather than replacing one. Used where the question is “is IT as a whole well governed”, often to satisfy audit committees.
A service-management framework, not a security one, but its change, incident and problem practices are where several security controls actually live.

blocks.html:
A framework an accredited or licensed third party can assess you against and
issue a recognised certificate or attestation for. ISO 27001, SOC 2, HITRUST,
PCI DSS and FedRAMP are certifiable in this sense; CSF 2.0, COBIT and the CIS
Controls are not.

Scheme Sector and region What it produces
HITRUST CSF US healthcare and its supply chain A certification, at i1 or r2 assurance level, that maps many frameworks into one assessment
PCI DSS Anyone storing or processing card data An Attestation of Compliance; covered at 5.11
FedRAMP Cloud services sold to US federal agencies An authorisation (ATO) based on a tailored 800-53 baseline
TISAX European automotive supply chain A shared assessment result, based on an ISO 27001-derived catalogue
Cyber Essentials Plus UK, any sector; required for some UK government contracts A certificate based on a hands-on technical audit of five control areas

HITRUST is the one worth understanding even outside healthcare, because its model, which takes many overlapping frameworks, harmonises them into a single control set, and assesses once to report against all of them, is the direction multi-framework compliance is heading generally.

Governments set floors for their own suppliers and, often, for the wider economy.

  • Cyber Essentials (UK): five technical control areas, self-assessed or, for Plus, independently tested. A baseline, not a comprehensive framework.
  • Essential Eight (Australia): eight mitigation strategies with a four-level maturity model, mandated for Australian government entities.
  • NIS2 (EU): a directive, not a framework. It imposes risk-management and incident-reporting duties on operators of essential and important services, transposed into each member state’s law.

These are obligations to meet, then build past: clearing Cyber Essentials or Essential Eight Level Two is a starting position, not a security programme.

Pick the framework your buyers, regulators or sector already speak. A US healthcare vendor is asked for HITRUST; a company selling to UK government needs Cyber Essentials; an EU automotive supplier needs TISAX; a SaaS company selling to North American enterprises is asked for SOC 2. Where nothing external dictates the choice, ISO 27001 for a management system and the CIS Controls for an implementation order is a defensible default that maps cleanly to almost everything else. Adopt one primary framework, then use crosswalks (see 5.2) to answer the rest from the same evidence.

items.q: How many cyber security frameworks are there?
items.html: Dozens in active use, but they cluster into a few types: prescriptive control sets (CIS Controls, CSA CCM), governance models (COBIT), certifiable schemes (ISO 27001, SOC 2, HITRUST, PCI DSS, FedRAMP), and national baselines (Cyber Essentials, Essential Eight). Most organisations need one primary framework and crosswalks to the others.

items.q: What is the difference between CIS Controls and NIST CSF?
items.html: The CIS Controls are a prioritised list of specific safeguards to implement. The NIST CSF is a set of outcomes to assess against. CIS tells you what to do next; CSF tells you how mature your programme is. They map to each other, and many organisations use CSF for structure and CIS for the implementation order.

items.q: What is HITRUST?
items.html: HITRUST maintains the HITRUST CSF, a control framework that harmonises ISO 27001, NIST, PCI DSS, HIPAA and others into one set, and runs a certification scheme against it. It is most established in US healthcare and its supply chain, where customers frequently require HITRUST r2 certification from vendors.

items.q: What is FedRAMP?
items.html: A US government programme that standardises security assessment and authorisation for cloud services sold to federal agencies. A cloud provider works with an accredited assessor against a FedRAMP baseline (derived from NIST SP 800-53) to obtain an Authorization to Operate, which other agencies can then reuse.

items.q: Which framework should a company start with?
items.html: If a customer or regulator names one, start there. If not, ISO 27001 for the management system plus the CIS Controls for implementation priority is a solid default that crosswalks to nearly every other framework, so later requirements can be met from the same control work and evidence.

entries.title: What GRC roles exist
entries.description: Analyst, manager, lead, head - plus the four specialisations the work splits into. What each seat does daily, what it pays attention to, and where each one goes next.
sources: IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020
ISACA, State of Cybersecurity, workforce sections, 2025
(ISC)² Cybersecurity Workforce Study, 2025

sections.text: What each seat is measured on

blocks.html:
The titles vary more than the work does. Every seat in this field is
accountable for one or more of the four artefacts, and the useful way to read a
job advert is to work out which.

Salary bands are deliberately omitted here: they move, they are regional, and a number in a reference work goes stale in a way the rest of an entry does not. What follows is what each seat actually does.

items.html: The entry seat. Runs the register day to day, chases evidence, completes customer questionnaires, keeps the policy set current. Most of the week is writing things down so somebody else can act on them.
Owns a framework end to end and the audit relationship that goes with it. First seat with a budget conversation and the first with a genuine right to say no.
Owns the register, the appetite statement and the committee reporting. Divergence point: this seat drifts toward the business, the compliance seat toward the auditors.
Owns the programme and the board narrative. Answers for the function’s opinion rather than its paperwork, and spends more time on resourcing than on controls.

blocks.html:
Third-party risk. The first split in almost every organisation, because the volume of supplier assessments is relentless and unlike the rest of the work.

Privacy. A distinct obligation set with its own regulator, its own artefacts and - where a statutory DPO is required - independence constraints that make it a poor fit for a general compliance seat.

Technology / product compliance. Sits closest to engineering. Owns the controls that live in the pipeline, and needs enough fluency to challenge an architecture decision.

Financial controls / SOX. A different lineage entirely, closer to internal audit and the finance function, with its own qualification path.

blocks.text: What each seat is measured on

blocks.html:
Not by controls implemented, in any function worth working in. Analysts are measured on whether the artefacts are current and legible. Managers on whether audits produce surprises. Heads on whether the board’s picture of risk matches the organisation’s actual position.

An interview question worth asking in the other direction: how do you know this function is working? An answer in terms of coverage percentages describes a function that reports on itself. An answer in terms of decisions made and surprises avoided describes one that is used.

The specialist functions providing expertise, challenge and monitoring to the
first line. Almost every GRC seat sits here.

Sideways more often than up, and that is normal. Risk to privacy, compliance to internal audit, GRC to security architecture, and - increasingly - GRC into product, because the person who understands the obligations understands what the product has to do.

The route out that surprises people is into consulting, where the breadth of a generalist seat is worth more than the depth of a specialist one.
Interested in what a day in the life of a GRC professional actually looks like? Check this out: UnixGuy’s remote GRC work week on YouTube.

entries.title: Breaking into GRC
entries.description: The field hires from IT support, audit, project delivery and law more often than from graduate schemes. What transfers, what has to be learned, and the one artefact that beats a certificate in an interview.
sources: ISACA, CRISC and CISA job practice areas, 2025
(ISC)² Cybersecurity Workforce Study, 2025

sections.text: What each route brings, and what it lacks
The thing that beats a certificate
The gap that actually blocks people

blocks.html:
Almost nobody starts here. The field hires from IT support, internal audit,
project delivery and law, and each route arrives with most of one half of the
job already done.
Knowing which half you already have is the difference between a targeted application and a scattergun one.

blocks.text: What each route brings, and what it lacks

items.html: Brings the ability to read a system you did not build and write down what happened. Lacks the evidence habit - what makes a screenshot admissible, why a date matters, what the auditor asks next.
Brings sampling, testing and the discipline of writing findings that survive challenge. Lacks the design side: this seat has never had to build the control it has spent years testing.
Brings tracking, chasing and getting a dozen people to a date. Lacks the domain - which obligations exist and why they bind.
Brings obligation reading and precision about sources. Lacks the technical literacy to challenge an engineer’s answer without accepting it whole.

blocks.text: The thing that beats a certificate

blocks.html:
One artefact you built, that you can walk somebody through end to end.

A risk you assessed: how it was raised, how you scored it and against what scale, who owned it, what treatment was chosen, who approved it, what evidence closed it. Ten minutes, specific, with the parts that went wrong included.

A candidate who can do that outperforms one with three certificates and nothing to describe, every time, because the interviewer’s actual question is whether you have handled a real artefact or only read about them.

If your current job has none, build one. Assess a risk in your own team’s work, properly, with a documented scale. It is a real artefact even if the organisation never asked for it.

They help with the screening filter and they do not close the interview.

CISA is the most widely recognised in audit-adjacent roles and does not assume a technical background. ISO 27001 Lead Implementer teaches the management-system vocabulary faster than anything else. CRISC maps well to the risk seat. A security certification like Security+ helps only if the gap you are closing is technical literacy.

Sequencing matters more than choice: a certificate taken before you have handled an artefact teaches you vocabulary with nothing to attach it to, and it fades.

blocks.text: The gap that actually blocks people

blocks.html:
Not technical depth. The evidence habit - understanding that the job is not doing the thing but being able to show, months later, to somebody who was not there, that the thing was done.

It is learnable in months and it is the thing hiring managers are listening for. Candidates who talk about what they did are common; candidates who talk about what they kept are not.

entries.title: Interview questions, and how to answer them
entries.description: The eight questions that come up in almost every GRC interview, what each one is really testing, and the shape of an answer that lands.
sources: IIA, The Three Lines Model, 2020
ISO 31000:2018 - Risk management, guidelines

blocks.html:
Every one of these questions has a textbook answer and a real answer. The
textbook answer gets you to the next question; the real answer gets you the job.

What interviewers are testing, almost without exception, is whether you have held the artefact or only read about it. Answers that name a specific instance do that; answers that recite a definition do not.

items.q: What is the difference between GRC and internal audit?
items.html:
The accountability line, not the task list. “GRC reports to management and owns the outcome; internal audit reports to the audit committee and owns the opinion.” Everything about tools and frameworks follows from it.

The follow-up is usually about independence, and the answer they are listening for is that it is structural rather than personal - an auditor who helped fix the gap has lost the opinion they were hired to give, however honest they are. See 1.4.

items.q: Appetite or tolerance - what is the difference?
items.html:
Appetite is how much risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives, set annually by the board, usually by category. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around one specific objective, and it is a number you can cross.

The good answer adds when the distinction bites: at the moment somebody has to decide whether a specific risk gets treated or accepted. See 3.2.

items.q: Walk me through a risk you assessed.
items.html:
The one that matters. Pick a real one, and include what went wrong.

How it was raised. How you scored it, against what documented scale. Who owned it - a person. What treatment was chosen and who had the authority to approve it. What evidence closed it. Then the honest part: what you would do differently, which is where the interview stops being a test.

items.q: How do you handle a control owner who will not give you evidence?
items.html:
They are testing whether you escalate straight away, which is the wrong answer.

Find out why first - usually the request is ambiguous, the system cannot produce what you asked for, or they do not know they own the control. Then make the request specific and easy. Escalation is the third move, not the first, and when it comes it goes with a record of the two attempts before it.

items.q: ISO 27001 or SOC 2?
items.html:
Answer with a question: who is asking for it. North American technology buyers ask for SOC 2; European and enterprise procurement asks for ISO. If both, sequence rather than choose.

Candidates who answer with a preference are describing a document they have read. Candidates who answer with the buyer are describing work they have done. See 5.1.

items.q: Is GRC a technical job?
items.html:
No, but it is a literate one. You need to read a system diagram and challenge an engineer’s answer; you do not need to configure the system.

Worth adding the failure mode, because it shows self-awareness: the risk is not being insufficiently technical, it is accepting an answer you did not understand because asking again felt awkward.

items.q: How would you build a programme from nothing?
items.html:
Register first, even a rough one, because the argument about the scale is easier with real entries in front of it. Then the policy set, then the control inventory with its mapping, then the evidence habit.

Starting with policy is the intuitive answer and the slow one - you end up writing rules for risks you have not established you carry. Saying so demonstrates you have thought about order rather than listing artefacts.

items.q: Where do you see the function failing?
items.html:
An invitation, and most candidates waste it on something generic about tone at the top.

Better: name a failure mode you have seen. Registers where nothing has moved in two quarters. Treatment columns full of “monitor”. Evidence collected in the four weeks before fieldwork. Each of those is specific, checkable, and shows you know what a working function looks like because you know what a broken one looks like.

blocks.html:
Two questions worth more than a dozen polite ones.

How do you know this function is working? Coverage percentages describe a function that reports on itself; decisions made and surprises avoided describe one that is used.

What was the last finding you disagreed with, and what happened? The answer tells you whether the function has standing, or whether it writes what it is asked to write.
